of Health Management, School of Health Studies, Tokai University, Hiratsukashi, Kanagawa, Japan; 3Department of Innovative Food Sciences, School of Food Sciences and Nutrition, Mukogawa Women’s University, Nishinomiya, Hyogo, Japan; and 4Institute for World Health Development, Mukogawa Women’s University, Nishinomiya, Hyogo, Japan ABSTRACT Background: Elevated concentrations of serum inflammatory cytokines, specifically TNF-α and IL-6, as well as C- reactive protein (CRP), are commonly observed

C- reactive protein (CRP), are commonly observed after menopause. Objectives: Because soy isoflavones may have some anti-inflammatory potential, the aim of the present systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was to explore whether soy intake affects serum markers of inflammation in postmenopausal women. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched up to August 2020. All RCTs that met the following criteria were

All RCTs that met the following criteria were included: 1) studies of the effects of soy intake on inflammatory markers; 2) any date of publication; 3) conducted on postmenopausal women; 4) with sufficient quantitative data for meta-analysis. Effect sizes were expressed as weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95% CIs. A total of 24 RCTs assessing the effects of soy intake on serum concentrations of CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 were included in the analysis. A random-effects model was used to determine

A random-effects model was used to determine the overall effect. Results: Soy supplementation significantly reduced CRP by 0.11 mg/L in postmenopausal women (95% CI: −0.22, −0.004 mg/L; P = 0.0414), but did not affect IL-6 or TNF-α. Significant reductions in CRP concentration occurred when natural soy products were given (WMD: −0.23 mg/L; 95% CI: −0.29, −0.17 mg/L; P < 0.001). This is equivalent to a ∼9% reduction in CRP concentration from baseline. Conclusions: Although our meta-analysis found

Conclusions: Although our meta-analysis found evidence that soy products significantly reduce CRP concentrations in postmenopausal women, the mechanisms by which soy foods and their constituents affect inflammatory biomarkers still need to be clarified. This systematic review was registered at www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ as CRD42020179232. J Nutr 2022;152:5–15. 5 vitro experiments have suggested that isoflavones could act as an anti-inflammatory agent, owing to genistein downregulating cytokine-induced signal transduction events in the cells of the immune system (7). Soy (Glycine max Merrill) is the main source of isoflavones in the diet. The chemical structure of isoflavones is very similar to that of 17-β-estradiol, and they show estrogenic activity, which is why they are referred to as phytoestrogens (8). Isoflavones are found primarily in plants

(8). Isoflavones are found primarily in plants in an inactive form, as glycosides (9). After ingestion, isoflavone glucosides are hydrolyzed to aglycones by β-glucosidases in the small intestine, where the metabolites are absorbed completely or further metabolized into other metabolites, such as equol and O-desmethylangolensin, by intestinal microflora in the large intestine (10). Studies show that people differ in their ability to synthesize S-equol (11), with those who are equol producers

S-equol (11), with those who are equol producers showing more favorable responses to diets that contain soy isoflavones (12, 13). Indeed, some studies have suggested that the ability to produce equol is associated with a reduced risk in postmenopausal women of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease—diseases that are caused by inflammation (14). Dong et al. (15) showed in their meta-analysis a slight, although nonsignificant, reduction in CRP concentration by 0.17 mg/L (95% CI: −0.38, 0.04

concentration by 0.17 mg/L (95% CI: −0.38, 0.04 mg/L) when soy isoflavone was compared with controls in 14 trials also conducted among postmenopausal women. However, a number of articles published since have considered the association between soy isoflavone intake and inflammatory markers in postmenopausal women, highlighting the need for a new, more extensive review. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was thus to explore whether soy

trials (RCTs) was thus to explore whether soy intake affects serum markers of inflammation in postmenopausal women. Methods Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guideline and the Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcome principle The literature search, data extraction, and quality assessment were all performed independently and in duplicate by 2 authors (KŁ and JB) using a standardized approach. This systematic review and meta- analysis protocol has been

review and meta- analysis protocol has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) as CRD4202017923. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines were consulted throughout the execution of this systematic review (16). The Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcome (PICO) strategy was used to construct the research question (Supplemental Table 1). Literature sources, search strategy, and

1). Literature sources, search strategy, and selection criteria We systematically searched 3 databases (PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and the Web of Science) up to August 2020 to identify RCTs that examined the effects of soy supplementation on serum CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α concentrations, using the following keywords: postmenopause OR menopause OR postmenopausal OR menopausal OR post-menopause OR post-menopausal OR climacteric AND soy OR soybeans OR soy beans OR soy foods OR soy food OR soy

OR soy beans OR soy foods OR soy food OR soy protein OR soy proteins OR phytoestrogens OR isoflavones AND inflammation OR inflammatory OR C-reactive protein OR high-sensitivity C-reactive protein OR high-sensitivity CRP OR hs-CRP OR interleukin-6 OR interleukin 6 OR IL-6 OR IL6 OR tumor necrosis factor-alpha OR tumor necrosis factor alpha OR TNFalpha OR TNF-alpha OR TNF- α. We included all RCTs that met the following criteria: 1) studied the effects of soy intake on inflammatory markers; 2) had

of soy intake on inflammatory markers; 2) had any date of publication; 3) were conducted on postmenopausal women; and 4) had sufficient quantitative data for meta-analysis. Studies were excluded if 1) they were published in non-peer-reviewed journals; 2) they lacked a control group; 3) their participants used hormone therapy or statins during the intervention; 4) they were reviews, animal studies, observation studies, masters or doctoral theses, commentaries, or letters; or 5) they were not in

commentaries, or letters; or 5) they were not in English. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction was conducted independently by 2 reviewers (KŁ, JB) based on the exclusion and inclusion criteria. Publications were assessed in subsequent stages using titles, abstracts, and full texts. Doubts were resolved by a third reviewer (JR) by consensus. Each selected publication was studied critically. Two authors (KŁ and AS-R) independently assessed the risk of bias of each study using

assessed the risk of bias of each study using the latest version of the Cochrane Collaboration Risk of Bias tool for RCTs and parallel-group trials, and the template for crossover trials (RoB 2) (17), in line with the Cochrane Handbook’s criteria for judging bias risk (18). Studies were assessed across the following 5 domains for parallel-group trials: bias arising from the randomization process; bias due to deviations from the intended interventions; bias due to missing outcome data; bias in

bias due to missing outcome data; bias in measuring the outcome; and bias in selecting the reported result. All signaling questions were answered in the RoB 2 template for crossover trials, and also for the additional domain—the full guidance document instructions were followed. The tool includes algorithms that map the responses to signaling questions onto a proposed risk-of-bias judgment for each domain across 3 levels: low risk of bias, some concerns, and high risk of bias. Two of the

some concerns, and high risk of bias. Two of the authors (KŁ, JB) independently evaluated the eligibility of all the studies retrieved from the databases and extracted the relevant data from each study that was included. During the data abstraction process, if outcome data were found to be missing, attempts were made to contact the authors for relevant information (twice). The following data from each study were abstracted: first author’s name, year of publication, country, study design

name, year of publication, country, study design (including whether parallel or crossover); study duration, number of participants; and daily dose of isoflavones ingested from the diet and supplementation, placebo, and other treatment intervention. We also recorded the following participant characteristics: health status, mean age or age range, BMI, and main outcomes (serum concentrations of CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6). The data for the main outcomes were converted to the same unit (mg/L for CRP and

were converted to the same unit (mg/L for CRP and pg/mL for TNF-α and IL-6). If >1 time point for follow-up was reported, we used the data from the longest follow-up. If the study data were doubled, we used the data with the appropriate unit, or the newest. Data synthesis and statistical analysis In studies where mean changes were not directly reported, they were calculated by subtracting the postintervention data from the baseline value. Missing SD values were imputed using the method of

SD values were imputed using the method of Follmann et al. (19), assuming a correlation coefficient of 0.5. SEs and CIs were converted to SDs for the analysis, in line with the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook (20). Random-effects models provided a summary estimate. Interstudy heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q statistic and quantified with the I2 test. Publication bias was examined through visual inspection of a funnel plot, and further evaluated by Begg and Egger’s tests

and further evaluated by Begg and Egger’s tests (21) (P < 0.05 indicated a significant publication bias). Tests for publication bias are recommended for use when ≥10 studies are included in a meta-analysis (20). Begg and Egger’s tests were thus implemented to evaluate publication bias in the cases of CRP and TNF-α. To explore the possible effects of study designs and participant characteristics on changes on CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 concentrations, we analyzed prespecified subgroups stratified by

we analyzed prespecified subgroups stratified by intervention duration, source and daily dose of isoflavones, health status of participants, region of the world where the study was conducted, and baseline CRP value (taking ≥3 as the cutoff for cardiovascular events). Statistical analysis was carried out using the Statistica data analysis software system, version 13 (TIBCO Software, 2017). Results Search results Supplemental Figure 1 presents a

Search results Supplemental Figure 1 presents a flowchart showing the extraction of studies. Throughout the initial search strategy, we identified 505 articles, and after analysis of their titles and abstracts, a further 43 publications were selected for full- text review. Finally, after excluding publications, 24 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis. The main reasons for exclusions were as follows: trials enrolled postmenopausal women using hormone

enrolled postmenopausal women using hormone therapy during the intervention, trials used other bioactive substances as a control (soy protein, phytate), or data could not be extracted to calculate changes in the outcomes. In addition, we excluded some trials because the inflammatory marker data were extremely high or extremely low. process in sufficient detail, and were judged as having a low risk of bias in this domain (4, 22–36). One study had an unclear risk of bias (37). Fourteen trials had sufficient information on the blinding of participants and personnel (4, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28–36), 2 had unclear information (24, 27), and 1 was judged as having a high risk of bias (37). All the parallel- group studies that were included had a low risk of bias in terms of missing outcome data. In relation to outcome measurement,

outcome data. In relation to outcome measurement, only 1 study demonstrated a high risk of bias (37). Fourteen studies demonstrated a low risk of bias in the selection of the result that was reported (4, 22, 23, 25–33, 35, 36), 1 was unclear (34), and 2 had a high risk of bias (24, 37). To summarize, 2 parallel-group studies were characterized as having an unclear risk (27, 34), 2 as having a high risk (24, 37), and 13 as having a low risk of bias (4, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28–33, 35, 36).

Effect of soy products on serum CRP concentration The 25 experiments included in the meta-analysis measured the effects of soy products on serum CRP concentration.

Begg’s rank correlation test (P = 0.256), Egger’s linear regression test (P = 0.717), and funnel plots (Supplemental Figure 4) suggested that there was no significant publication bias. The concentration of serum CRP before intervention ranged from 1.01 ± 2.06 mg/L to 6.3 ± 11.6 mg/L (34, 38) and after intervention from 0.9 ± 1.5 mg/L to 6.4 ± 10.1 mg/L (29, 38). This is equivalent to a ∼4.4% reduction in CRP concentration from baseline. Discussion In this meta-analysis of 24 articles, we evaluated the effects of soy supplementation on 3 of the most important inflammatory biomarkers—CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α—in a group of 1559 postmenopausal women. It was observed that, during 4– 96 wk of intervention, in response to soy product intake and in contrast to the control, serum CRP concentration in the study group reduced

CRP concentration in the study group reduced significantly by 0.11 mg/L (95% CI: −0.22, −0.004 mg/L; P = 0.0414), which is equivalent to a ∼4.4% reduction in CRP concentrations from the baseline. In comparison, statin therapy lowered median CRP concentration concentrations by 14% (45), whereas simvastatin decreased CRP in postmenopausal women by 4% (46). In a previous meta-analysis, Dong et al. (15) showed a slight, although nonsignificant, reduction in CRP concentration by 0.17 mg/L (95% CI:

in CRP concentration by 0.17 mg/L (95% CI: −0.38, 0.04 mg/L) when soy supple- mentation was compared with controls in 14 trials conducted among postmenopausal women. Including additional trials with larger sample sizes in our analysis strengthened the effects of soy supplementation on serum CRP reduction in the targeted population. Although Wu et al. (47), in their cross-sectional study of Chinese women, found that concentrations of IL-6 and TNF-α were inversely associated with the intake of

were inversely associated with the intake of soy food, we did not observe in our meta-analysis that the serum IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations of postmenopausal women were significantly affected by soy consumption. Analysis of the subgroups, whether by daily dose and isoflavone source, or by duration of follow-up, did not show any significant effect of these variables on IL-6 or TNF-α. However, the subgroup analysis did show a significant reduction in CRP 12 Bajerska et al. TABLE 3 Subgroup

by 0.18 mg/L (95% CI: −0.28, −0.08 mg/L), in comparison with other sources of isoflavones (such as purified phytoestrogens in tablet form or isolated soy protein). They explained that the manufacture of soy products entails a loss of some anti-inflammatory ingredients other than isoflavones (such as specific fatty acids and fiber). Moreover, Azadbakht et al. (43) explained that the favorable effect of soy nuts on markers of inflammation and endothelial function in postmenopausal women with

endothelial function in postmenopausal women with metabolic syndrome may also be associated with the interaction of these favorable soy ingredients. Messina (49) also indicated that, in more refined products such as isolated soy protein, as much as 80%– 90% of the isoflavone content can be lost in processing. On the other hand, the bioavailability of isoflavones from soy- based foods and dietary supplements may differ. For example, Vergne et al. (50) indicated that isoflavone bioavailability is

(50) indicated that isoflavone bioavailability is not affected by isoflavone conjugation pattern, and that the higher bioavailability of isoflavones from soy extracts than from soy- based cheese seen in their study was associated with weakening or breaking of the links between isoflavones and other molecules during manufacturing. Cassidy et al. (51) indicated that people absorb isoflavones from a range of different soy-rich foods in a similar manner, but that the food matrix (whether solid or

but that the food matrix (whether solid or liquid) or form in which they are ingested can alter their pharmacokinetic profiles. They concluded that a liquid matrix of soy products, such as soy milk, yields faster absorption rates and higher peak plasma concentrations than a solid matrix, whereas aglycones in fermented food such as tempeh are absorbed more rapidly than glucoside conjugates (51). It has repeatedly been reported that the effects of soy products on inflammatory markers are more

of soy products on inflammatory markers are more significant in subjects with the ability to metabolize daidzein to equol (15). The prevalence of equol producers is 20%–35% among Western adults, but 50%–55% in Asian populations (15). However, Miura et al. (52) in their study stated that the bioavailability of daidzein and genistein was significantly greater in equol nonproducers than in equol producers, especially after the consumption of soy milk. In our current meta-analysis, the conversion

In our current meta-analysis, the conversion of isoflavones to equol was measured only in 5 studies (28, 35, 39, 40, 53), but only 2 (39, 40) measured how equol production status affects the way soy isoflavone interventions affect inflammatory markers. It is worth noting that neither of these studies found any differences in the responses of inflammatory markers in equol producers and nonproducers during the interventions with soy products. In their meta-analyses, both Asbaghi et al. and

In their meta-analyses, both Asbaghi et al. and Khodarahmi et al. revealed a significant lowering effect of soy supplemen- tation on CRP when isoflavone dosages ranged from 70 to Soy and inflammation in postmenopausal women 13 100 mg/d. However, in our meta-analysis, subgroup analysis based on isoflavone dosage (≥84/<84 mg/d) did not show the beneficial effects of soy supplementation in reducing CRP concentration. This quantity of soy isoflavones corresponds to an intake of ∼35 g of soy nuts or

corresponds to an intake of ∼35 g of soy nuts or 3 glasses of soy milk, which are amounts of soy foods commonly consumed by Asian people (48). Moreover, Charles et al. (23) observed in their clinical trial that the intake of soy isoflavones in amounts similar to those consumed by Asian populations led in postmenopausal women to an increase in the concentration of adiponectin, an insulin-sensitizing adipokine. The inclusion of soy foods into a Western diet may thus play a crucial role in

a Western diet may thus play a crucial role in regulating the inflammation of postmenopausal women. The recent conclusion of the European Food Safety Authority that soy isoflavones do not adversely affect the breast, thyroid, or uterus of postmenopausal women is in support of their safety (49, 54). Our current study has some important strengths. First, the participants in the studies we included formed homogeneous groups and did not use hormone therapy or statins during the intervention.

therapy or statins during the intervention. Second, Begg’s test showed no publication bias for the studies that evaluated the effects of soy isoflavones on CRP and TNF-α. It seems that genetic variation did not influence this effect, because the majority of the trials were conducted in Europe and North America, where women do not habitually consume isoflavones or soy foods and had relatively small differences in genetic susceptibility to isoflavones. All of these facts help greatly to reduce

All of these facts help greatly to reduce the study heterogeneity and to assist in achieving reliable and precise results. However, some limitations should also be considered. Soy supplementation was used in dissimilar dosages and was of different types (natural soy foods, supplements with isoflavones, soy protein). Also, the relatively small or moderate sample sizes in some studies, and insufficient follow-up durations, may have affected the study outcomes. The quality and confounding factors

outcomes. The quality and confounding factors in the description of certain studies may also have affected the bias and outcomes. For example, only several included studies provided the relevant information that women with the presence of inflammation or using drugs with anti-inflammatory activities had been excluded from the study; this factor may potentially influence the outcome. In conclusion, this meta-analysis found evidence that soy supplementation in postmenopausal women significantly

in postmenopausal women significantly reduces serum CRP by 0.11 mg/L, while not affecting IL-6 and TNF-α. Subgroup analysis showed a significant reduction in CRP when natural soy products (such as soy milk, whole soybeans, and soy nuts) were given. The potential mecha- nisms through which natural soy food and its constituents affect inflammatory biomarkers remain to be clarified. The variability in anti-inflammatory effect may be related to the proportions of women who are equol-producers and

proportions of women who are equol-producers and equol- nonproducers, so additional studies are warranted to confirm the potential CRP-lowering effects of natural soy-based food items, especially taking the ability to produce equol into consideration. While a substantial 34 proportion of the absorbed amino acids are captured and metabolized by splanchnic tissues, the 35 majority enter systemic circulation where they become available for uptake by peripheral tissues 36 (e.g., skeletal muscle). The need for temporal sensory methods Traditional sensory profiling methods involve panellists scoring at­ tributes after a single tasting. However, it is recognised that this cannot fully measure sensory experiences due to changes that occur during mastication, bolus formation and oral processing (Visalli & Galmarini, 2022). In

oral processing (Visalli & Galmarini, 2022). In addition to changes occurring in the mouth, the sensory properties of foods and drinks change with consecutive consumption of bites/sips contributing towards a full portion (Visalli & Galmarini, 2022). Temporal sensory methods have been developed to address this dimension to sensory perception. It has been suggested that by considering temporal changes these methods are more realistic and representative of the consumers’ experience (Esmerino et

of the consumers’ experience (Esmerino et al., 2017). There are numerous sensory methods used for this purpose, summarised in a scoping review by Visalli and Galmarini (2022). As with all sensory research, the methodological choice of temporal sensory test involves a compromise between temporal resolution, descriptive and discrimina­ tive capacity, validity, complexity, and reliability (Visalli, Galmarini, & Schlich, 2023). An example of this is the number of sensory attributes to be

of this is the number of sensory attributes to be investigated: single and dual attribute time intensity (TI) tests are able to report on the varying intensity of one or two attributes, respec­ tively, over time. Comparison of temporal sensory methodologies The use of alternative temporal

methodologies The use of alternative temporal sensory methodologies has become increasingly common as a means to address the limitations of time in­ tensity methods (Esmerino et al., 2017). Temporal Dominance of Sen­ sations (TDS) was introduced as a method to capture which sensations were dominant over the consumption period, rather than rating in­ tensity over time (Schlich, 2017). This method allowed multiple attri­ butes to be assessed simultaneously, with one dominant attribute being

simultaneously, with one dominant attribute being selected by each panellist at any time. Later, the Temporal Check All That Apply (TCATA) method was introduced, where panellists were asked to register the presence or absence of multiple attributes over time, as a temporal modification to the Check All That Apply (CATA) method (Castura, Antúnez, Gim´enez, & Ares, 2016). A detailed description of the dynamic sensory profile of products during con­ sumption was provided by TCATA, as panellists

sumption was provided by TCATA, as panellists could report on all at­ tributes they were experiencing (Ares et al., 2016). This method may provide a more rounded profile, as is not based on dominance; however, conflicting evidence has been found regarding its simplicity when compared with TDS. TCATA has been reported to have higher statistical power, suggesting a higher discriminative ability (Meyners, 2020). This may indicate that TCATA is simpler for panellists to perform, as they are

is simpler for panellists to perform, as they are required to select or deselect all attributes they perceive over time, rather than deciding which is the most dominant, as is the case with TDS. Regardless of simplicity, multiple studies have concluded that TCATA provides more detail about flavour and texture perception than TDS (Esmerino et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2018). However, TCATA re­ quires more analytical steps to generate meaningful data compared with TDS, such as considering the

data compared with TDS, such as considering the chance probability of selecting both indi­ vidual and multiple attributes, an aspect often overlooked in discussions on this technique (Meyners & Castura, 2018). Overall, TCATA has gained widespread acceptance and is commonly used by both consumers and trained panellists (Ares et al., 2016). One limitation of TCATA is that intensity information is omitted, and as a result, analysis methods often rely on comparing the duration of attribute

often rely on comparing the duration of attribute selection as well as attribute onsets and offsets (Dietz et al., 2022). To address this limitation, sequential profiling has been utilised, where the progressive profile of 5–7 attributes is investigated through consecutive tastings at regimented time intervals. This method was adapted for use in drinks by Methven et al. (2010) when the sensory profile of oral nutritional supplements (ONS) across 5 attributes was investigated. The ideal number

5 attributes was investigated. The ideal number of attributes for sequential profiling will be context specific, but researchers have impressed the importance of not overwhelming participants with too many attributes (Pineau et al., 2012). Typically, publications have included 5–7 attributes for sequential profiling, with good results recorded from panellists (Methven et al., 2010), indicating that this number is appropriate. In sequential profiling, a low number of attributes (taste, flavour

a low number of attributes (taste, flavour and/or mouthfeel) are scored by participants immediately after tasting and after a 30 s delay to account for after-taste, with the process being repeated for 8–10 consecutive sips to show the evolution of taste and flavour with repeated consumption (Methven et al., 2010). This method enables collection of intensity data for a range of attributes overcoming many of the limitations associated with TI, TDS and TCATA. In this earlier study using ONS, it

and TCATA. In this earlier study using ONS, it was shown that attributes including soya milk flavour, metallic taste and mouthdrying significantly increased with consump­ tion (p < 0.002), negatively impacting liking (Methven et al., 2010). This highlights the need for sequential profiling as the importance of these attributes may have been missed in static profiling, and they can provide additional information to research and development teams trying to minimise or optimise the intensity of

trying to minimise or optimise the intensity of several attributes over time. A previous investigation of these temporal sensory methodologies by Esmerino et al. (2017) compared TDS, TCATA and progressive profiling (a single sip version of sequential profiling) of fermented dairy drinks and found good agreement between the three methods. The study showed that the citation proportion of TCATA had a close relationship with the intensities determined by progressive profiling (Esmerino et al.,

by progressive profiling (Esmerino et al., 2017). However, this was completed using a single-sip tasting experi­ ence by consumers, meaning that the relationship between these methods in a multi-sip context is not known. The current study will build on this work in a multi-sip context to further understand the relation­ ships between these methodologies. 1.3. The potential for researcher bias within temporal sensory studies For the majority of sensory methodologies, there are clear guidelines

sensory methodologies, there are clear guidelines for the selection of attributes, such as using group discussions to generate a consensus vocabulary in quantitative descriptive analysis (QDA™) detailed in the ISO standard 13,299 (ISO, 2016). However, the low number of attributes used for temporal methods means that trun­ cation of the consensus vocabulary is required. For this, guidelines are limited, and in the literature it is often unclear what rationale has been used for attribute

what rationale has been used for attribute selection. A recent review quantified the method by which attributes had been selected for temporal studies; in 40 % of studies attributes were chosen by panellists, 15 % by the researcher, 15 % from references to the literature, 15 % by an alternative panel, and in 15 % of articles the basis for the choice was not reported (Visalli & Galmarini, 2024). This highlights a key limitation in temporal sensory studies and suggests practices could be

sensory studies and suggests practices could be optimised going forward. An example of this in practice can be seen when sequential profiling builds on standard profiling: here it is often unclear how the shortlist of attributes have been selected for inclusion from the extensive consensus vocabulary, with the attribute number decreasing from 25 to 30 to 5–7 based on static profiling data alone such as in the study of Bull et al. (2017). Sequential profiling can also be presented in isolation,

profiling can also be presented in isolation, as in the work of Olatujoye et al. (2020); here, minimal details were given on the generation of attributes and there was little consideration to their rele­ vance for temporal investigations (Olatujoye et al., 2020). In both of these cases, it is likely that the selection of attributes for sequential profiling was influenced by the study aims, panellist discussions, and use of the current literature. However, as there is no standardised, objective

However, as there is no standardised, objective methodology to oversee this process, it should also be considered that this subjective method is open to bias, including influence by dominant panellists or by the researcher guiding panellists’ choices. A recent re­ view on temporal methods concluded that temporal measurements are yet to reach methodological maturity, supporting that there is scope for optimisation and developments in this field (Visalli & Galmarini, 2024). Research is needed to identify an objective method for attribute short­ listing to reduce the scope for researcher bias in this context and to ensure the relevance and suitability of attributes selected for further temporal investigations. 1.4. Aims & hypotheses The authors propose that there is a gap in sensory methodology for the reliable shortlisting of attributes from an extensive consensus vo­ cabulary for use in subsequent temporal studies, such as sequential profiling, when only a small number of attributes can be assessed. It is hypothesised that analysis of TCATA citation proportions may indicate the temporal

citation proportions may indicate the temporal experience of an attribute, providing an objective method to identify attributes likely to display temporal variability to be taken forward into sequential profiling. The primary aim of the study was to investigate whether the use of TCATA citation proportions provide a robust method for attribute selection for use in sequential profiling of whey protein isolate (WPI) model beverages. It is accepted by the authors that the relevant attributes will

by the authors that the relevant attributes will be product-specific: this was best described by Meyners and Castura (2018) in their definition of the term “product space” where all test results depend on the set of products used in the study as these define the product space. For these beverages it was hypothesised that mouth­ drying would significantly build up over time during TCATA and with repeated consumption in sequential profiling, as seen in Bull et al. (2017). By contrast, sweetness

in Bull et al. (2017). By contrast, sweetness has previously shown no changes across a sequential profile (Methven et al., 2010), thus it was hypothesised that sweetness perception would not show significant temporal variability in either method. It was not anticipated how other sensory attributes would be influenced as there is limited previous temporal research of other attributes in these whey models. It was hypothesised that TCATA could identify attributes likely to display temporal

identify attributes likely to display temporal variability which can subsequently be taken forward in the design of temporal intensity sen­ sory studies to increase the relevance of results. The secondary aim of this study was to investigate the use of TCATA as a tool to identify appropriate attributes for further investigation via sequential profiling. (2022), whereas the aim of this study was to use TCATA citation proportions as a means to compare selection within the same product at different timepoints. It was hypothesised that this would provide a preliminary indication of the temporal variability of attributes, which cannot be achieved through analysis of the duration of attribute selection, and facilitate the use of TCATA as a tool for attribute selection for use in sequential profiling, aiding scientific understanding and sensory

aiding scientific understanding and sensory practice. 2. Methodology 2.1. Materials Whey protein isolate (WPI) was provided by Volac Whey Nutrition Ltd. (Hertfordshire, UK). Conclusion It was hypothesised that TCATA may be an objective method to select attributes for sequential profiling from an extended consensus vocabulary, improving on current research practices. This method pro­ vided additional information from TCATA data that was not elucidated by duration selection alone. Using a model whey protein beverage, TCATA was able to identify mouthdrying as relevant for inclusion in sequential profiling through a high

inclusion in sequential profiling through a high citation proportion and an increase in attribute selection over time. Mouthcoating also reached borderline significance so was chosen for further investigation. Sweetness was not shown to be temporally influenced in TCATA. When investigating these attributes in sequential profiling, mouthdrying and mouthcoating significantly increased over time, whereas sweetness did not, echoing the predictions of TCATA. This research demonstrates the use of

of TCATA. This research demonstrates the use of TCATA as an objective attribute selector for sequential profiling. No significant differences were found when comparing a blinded and unblinded pro­ tocol for sequential profiling. Significant levels of panellist variability were reported for all attributes: the authors propose that variation in mouthdrying and salivating perception may be a result of individual variation in salivary flow rate and the response of salivary production to a drying

the response of salivary production to a drying stimulus, highlighting the difficulty in standardisation for these attributes. Overall, this study highlights the ability of TCATA to identify attri­ butes that display temporal variability through analysis of citation proportions. Future research should investigate this methodology in different food contexts, as well as the factors that influence mouthdrying and salivating perception of whey protein beverages. Discussion This study aimed to investigate the influence of RT with free weights and the influence of HPD on body composition, muscle thickness and strength capacity. In addition, initial results of HPD on liver and kidney function in postmenopausal women should be obtained. It has been shown that RT with free weights is a safe method with moderate to strong effects on strength capacity and trivial to moderate effects on body composition and

to moderate effects on body composition and muscle thickness. HPD alone had also a small effect on strength capacity. Maintaining the SMM is important for prolonging functionality and strength in older age [56]. Exercises like everyday movements and maintaining or promoting strength are ideal strategies. This study demonstrates that RT with free weights is a safe method to increase strength and SMM in postmenopausal women. As in previous studies, no high dropout rate could be attributed to the

no high dropout rate could be attributed to the training method [9]. This study was the first to show that RT with free weights significantly increases SMM while reducing FM in postmenopausal women. A significant increase in SMM was observed in both training groups but not in the CP group. An increase of more than one kilo was even observed in both groups. Besides a time*group effect could also observed for TP in FFM to C. These effects are similar to those seen in younger women [57].

are similar to those seen in younger women [57]. Interestingly, the results suggest that postmenopausal women need at least three training sessions per week to increase FFM and SMM. In prior studies with two sessions per week with a similar study design, no significant effect was achieved in FFM and SMM in postmenopausal women but in premenopausal women [9]. However, the significant increase in SMM can be confirmed by the results of Rossato et al. [16]. The TP and CP groups from this study

et al. [16]. The TP and CP groups from this study consumed significantly more protein than both groups of Rossato et al. The high protein group von Rossato et al. consumed only 1.2 g/kg BW [16]. Even if a higher absolute value was achieved in the FMM and SMM in the TP than in T, no significant difference between the groups was detected. Consequently, regular strength training is probably the decisive factor for maintaining or increasing FMM or SMM in untrained postmenopausal women. HPD

FMM or SMM in untrained postmenopausal women. HPD presumably plays a further role only after a longer period than 12 weeks or at a higher performance level. The increase in SMM is even in line with those of elite athletes [57,58]. Consequently, hypertrophy effects can be also achieved with a similar effect to those of young athletes in postmenopausal women with RT. Accordingly, it can be assumed that these signaling cascades are not significantly influenced by the menopausal transition in women, unlike the concentrations of sex hormones such as estradiol and progesterone. this study also has some limitations. One aspect is the current lack of standardization of ultrasound measurements in sports medicine contexts. Even though there are already initial position papers on the implementation of ultrasound measure- ments in clinical examinations [9,29,66,75] these can still be subjectively influenced. Furthermore, the ultrasound results should only be used in correlation with other methods for muscle thickness and hypertrophy to confirm potential effects. Another factor is the self- documentation of the diet. Like other nutritional studies, the actual energy intake and macronutrient distribution cannot be clearly traced. during and after the intervention to identify possible side effects as quickly as possible. 5. Conclusion This study investigated the effects of RT with free weights and an HPD. The results indicate that RT with free weights is a safe method for postmenopausal women and that strength capacity and SMM could be significantly increased. It was also shown that an HPD has a significant effect on strength capacity without training but noadditive effect could be observed with RT. Furthermore,

effect could be observed with RT. Furthermore, increased liver activity was observed due to an increase in GOT concentration because of HPD. The long-term effects of a HPD in postmenopausal women cannot currently be answered. Further studies on HPD in postmenopausal and older people on liver and kidney activity are therefore necessary to identify potential side effects. Introduction Taxifolin (dihydroquercetin) is a representative natural compound from the polyphenol class, belonging to the flavonoid group (Bobrysheva et al., 2023; Fatkullin et al., 2023; Singla et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021). In contemporary nutritional science, polyphenols are classified as minor bioactive compounds. They play a significant role in human metabolism and must be included in the nutriome, which refers to the formulation of optimal nutrition (Tutelyan et al., 2020).

of optimal nutrition (Tutelyan et al., 2020). Polyphenols, including TXL, are among the most extensively studied and safest compounds (Das et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Turck et al., 2017), renowned for their broad spectrum of biological activities. As a result, they have long been of considerable interest to the scientific community as potential agents for the enrichment of food products (Bobrysheva et al., 2023; Fujitaka et al., 2019). The primary focus on polyphenols stems from their

The primary focus on polyphenols stems from their interaction with antioxidant mechanisms in the human body, which is attributed to the presence of multiple hydroxyl groups in their molecular structure (Singla et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2019). This has been convincingly demonstrated by numerous studies (Choi et al., 2009; Fraga et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2018; Ying et al., 2021). It has been estab­ lished that the inclusion of TXL in the diet of mice exerts an inhibitory effect on the overgrowth of proteobacteria induced by an obesity- promoting diet and, in general, improves the diversity of the gut microbiota (Su et al., 2022). The diverse range of favourable physiological effects exerted by polyphenols has generated considerable interest in

has generated considerable interest in these compounds as valuable dietary ingredients. However, polyphenols are typically pre­ sent in small quantities in most natural sources and are concentrated in plant by-products, such as oilcake from olive oil production, grape skins and seeds from winemaking, and citrus peel and membranes from juice production (Caballero et al., 2022). Polyphenol-rich foods often possess a characteristic tart or astringent taste – such as strong tea or coffee, bitter

taste – such as strong tea or coffee, bitter chocolate, citrus fruits, and persimmons. These organoleptic properties can limit the potential for artificially enriching products with phenolic compounds. Free polyphenols, by interacting with salivary mucin, diminish its ‘shielding’ effect on taste receptors, thereby inten­ sifying the perception of astringency. Furthermore, polyphenols are known to exhibit poor absorption in the gastrointestinal tract in their natural form. Their low

tract in their natural form. Their low bioavailability is largely attributed to their poor solubility and chemical instability (Crespy et al., 1999; Fatkullin et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2003; Marín et al., 2015). These challenges underscore the need to explore technological so­ lutions for creating polyphenol-enriched products that can deliver them to the targeted areas of the gastrointestinal tract. One such solution is encapsulation, which is increasingly employed in the development of food

increasingly employed in the development of food products and delivery systems for bioactive substances within the food industry (Caballero et al., 2022). Encapsulation not only masks the undesirable taste of polyphenols but also enhances their stability against external factors (Maqsoudlou et al., 2020; Maqsoudlou et al., 2022), preserves their beneficial physiological effects, and improves their bioavailability (Caballero et al., 2022; Choi & McClements, 2020; Fat­ kullin et al., 2023;

& McClements, 2020; Fat­ kullin et al., 2023; Steiner et al., 2019). Both natural and synthetic biodegradable high-molecular-weight compounds serve as encapsulating materials, with various proteins being widely utilised (Bilia et al., 2014). Whey proteins, in particular, are recognised for their excellent technological properties and nutritional value (De Wit, 1998; Khramtsov et al., 2021). They can interact with polyphenols to improve their sta­ bility during metabolic breakdown under

sta­ bility during metabolic breakdown under digestive conditions, thereby enhancing their antioxidant activity (Chavoshpour-Natanzi & Sahihi, 2019; Cutrim & Cortez, 2018; Kanakis et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015). This highlights the importance of continued research into the use of whey proteins in encapsulation technology. Thermomechanical mixing and spray drying are among the most straightforward methods for implementing the encapsulation process in the food industry. Thermomechanical mixing

in the food industry. Thermomechanical mixing equipment is extensively used in the production of a wide range of food products, enabling reduced energy consumption by integrating multiple technological processes (Zhao et al., 2011). Spray drying systems, renowned for their high efficiency and capacity, are currently the most widely employed equipment for producing a diverse array of dry food products and in­ gredients (Banjare et al., 2019; Castro-L´opez et al., 2021). The aim of this study was to assess the efficiency and identify the optimal process conditions for encapsulating taxifolin (TXL) into whey proteins using thermomechanical mixing and spray drying. Conclusions The results of computer modeling enabled the prediction of the possibility of TXL encapsulation into whey proteins and revealed the intermolecular mechanisms underlying the formation of these com­ plexes. A stable interaction between the TXL molecule model and the amino acid residues of the hydrophobic barrel of the β-Lg molecule, as well as residues Phe31, His32, Leu110,

as well as residues Phe31, His32, Leu110, and Trp118 within a small depression on the surface of the α-LA molecule, was established. The thermomechanical stirring method used for encapsulation of TXL into liquid WPC at 80 ± 2 ◦C did not result in the formation of equimolar protein–polyphenol complexes. Instead, aggregates of protein molecules up to 160 μm in size were formed, which completely or partially encapsulated large TXL crystals. These complexes did not provide high encapsulation

complexes did not provide high encapsulation efficiency, which was found to be 63 ± 3 % according to spectrophotometric analysis, and they did not completely mask the bitterness of TXL. When TXL was encapsulated in whey proteins using spray drying, the maximum encapsulation efficiency of 71 ± 2 % was achieved, as confirmed by Folin-Ciocalteu assay and fluorescence emission spec­ trometry. This was achieved with an inlet air temperature of 150 ◦C in the drying chamber. The size of the resulting

in the drying chamber. The size of the resulting WPC microcapsules ranged from 3 to 30 μm and showed little variation depending on the drying temperature regime used. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that the protein microcapsules had an irregular spherical shape, and no visible TXL crystals were found on their surface. These spray-dried mi­ crocapsules were characterised by the complete absence of the bitterness typically associated with TXL. Regarding the antioxidant activity of

with TXL. Regarding the antioxidant activity of encapsulated TXL, a decrease in its activity was observed after encapsulation by spray drying. The in­ hibition of ABTS●+ decreased from 12.93 ± 1.15 % to 8.47 ± 0.88 %. This reduction is likely due to the shielding of active centres of the polyphenol molecules as they form complexes with whey proteins. 20 min, the antioxidant activity of TXL showed a reversal in its dynamics. The level of ABTS●+ inhibition increased to 11.50 ± 0.95 %. This suggests that ethanol exposure dis­ rupts the WPC microcapsules, releasing the bound polyphenol mole­ cules. This finding indicates that when such WPC microcapsules are ingested with food, the antioxidant activity of TXL could be fully realised in the intestine after the breakdown of the protein structure. Thus, spray drying can be regarded as a promising method for the encapsulation of TXL in whey proteins. This approach ensures the micronization of the interacting substances, provides a sufficiently high stability of the resulting complexes, offers protection for the antioxidant properties of the polyphenol against aggressive environmental condi­ tions, and effectively masks its bitter taste. ABSTRACT Ulcerative colitis (UC), a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), presents therapeutic challenges due to the limitations and side effects of current treatments, creating a need for safer and more effective alternatives. Despite several studies on the health benefits of donkey milk, its specific impact on UC remains unsolved. This study investigates the therapeutic potential of donkey whey protein (DWP), a bioactive-rich functional food, in alleviating UC symptoms in a mouse model of

in alleviating UC symptoms in a mouse model of dextran sodium sulfate–induced colitis. The DWP was processed using thermal and nonthermal techniques, including high-temperature long-time (HTLT) pasteurization, ultrasonic processing (300 W), and UV irradiation, to evaluate the impact of processing methods on its thera- peutic efficacy. The results demonstrated that when pro- cessed nonthermally, DWP mitigated colitis symptoms such as weight loss, diarrhea, and colon shortening. His- tological

diarrhea, and colon shortening. His- tological analysis revealed improved mucosal integrity and reduced inflammation in the colon, with nonthermal treatments showing superior effects. The DWP treatment enhanced antioxidant activity, suppressed proinflamma- tory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), and modulated the gut microbiota, promoting microbial diversity and restor- ing microbial balance. Nonthermal treatments were par- ticularly effective in preserving the bioactivity of DWP, highlighting

preserving the bioactivity of DWP, highlighting their potential in enhancing the functional properties of whey proteins. These findings suggest that DWP, particularly when processed through nonthermal methods, holds potential as a natural and effective alter- native for managing UC and other chronic inflammatory diseases. Introduction According to the World Health Organization (WHO), menopause is defined as a woman's last natural

menopause is defined as a woman's last natural menstruation resulting from the cessation of ovarian function. This condition is confirmed if at least 12 months have passed since the woman's last menstrual period, and no other causes are responsible for this state. Menopause is a period in which the production of female hormones (estrogens and progesterone) gradually decreases, leading to the cessation of menstrual cycles and the loss of reproductive capability. This period begins around the age

capability. This period begins around the age of 40 and lasts until the age of 60–65. Menopause usually occurs around the age of 49 and is diagnosed when a woman has not had a period for twelve months (Gonçalves et al., 2016). During menopause, many women experience a variety of signs and symptoms, including reduced cognitive functions. It can be a nuisance and reduce the quality of life (Hayashi et al., 2022). Hypoestrogenism resulting from menopause is cited as a major cause of disease,

menopause is cited as a major cause of disease, vasomotor status, and genitourinary changes, and contributes to the health and high mortality of women over 50. Women who go through menopause early may have a higher mortality rate, and later from cardiovascular causes (Wu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019). As for cognitive abilities in the postmenopausal period, they tended to be lower than in the pre-and perimenopausal periods, especially long- term verbal memory and executive functions (Weber

term verbal memory and executive functions (Weber et al., 2014), which include cognitive domains considered to be more sensitive to changes in oestrogen levels (Luine, 2014). The Study of Women's Health Across the Nation examined 2362 American women through repeated neuropsy­ chological testing over four years. Women's long-term and short-term memory scores in early and late perimenopause did not improve with repeated testing. However, the pattern seen before menopause was reverted to in the

seen before menopause was reverted to in the postmenopausal period, with incremental changes in scores being normalized. (Greendale et al., 2009). Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) belongs to the neuro­ trophin family, which are peptide growth factors that have been discovered in the last 50 years

that have been discovered in the last 50 years (Hohn et al., 1990; Kowia´nski et al., 2018a; Zhang et al., 2007). BDNF is a protein produced mainly in the central nervous system of the brain (Fletcher et al., 2018). Early in life, the effects of BDNF on the development and addition of neurons were noted, while during the course of life, involvement in processes such as synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity that occurred in the course of cognitive functions was considered (Kowia´nski et

cognitive functions was considered (Kowia´nski et al., 2018b). Scientific research supports the proposition that BDNF is associated with cognitive dysfunction (Alessi et al., 2022), and higher BDNF with improvements (Miranda et al., 2019). It has been shown that BDNF freely crosses the blood-brain barrier in both directions, and the direction of flow depends on its concentration gradient (Trushina et al., 2022). Research suggests that the level of circulating BDNF in the blood may reflect its

of circulating BDNF in the blood may reflect its level in the brain (Li et al., 2020). It has been found that the level of BDNF in human serum, both at rest and during physical exertion, is of 70–80 % of brain origin. The level of BDNF decreases with age (Gait´an et al., 2021). A pro­ ductive diet change can be an effective way to influence BDNF levels, thereby preserving and improving cognitive and active health. It seems that dietary components may act on cognition via pathways related to

may act on cognition via pathways related to energy metabolism and synaptic plasticity (Hoscheidt et al., 2022), where BDNF may occur. There is also a possibility that BDNF support affects the operation of the active module and assembly (van Praag et al., 2014). Although there are studies in the literature showing that diet affects cognitive ability and BDNF levels (Hoscheidt et al., 2022; Key and Szabo-Reed, 2023), there is still a need for more detailed studies to further evaluate nutritional

detailed studies to further evaluate nutritional interventions to increase BDNF, especially in terms of the relationship between peripheral and central effects (Gravesteijn et al., 2022). 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Participants and ethical aspects Seventy-two Caucasian women aged 55–73 years participated in the study. Post-menopausal women from the Lubuskie Voivodship (Poland) were recruited for the study through newspapers and social media, as well as through the “business partner” of the

as well as through the “business partner” of the “Smaczna Dieta” project in 2020. None of the women included in the study suffered from burden­ some chronic diseases, diagnosed cognitive disorders, or other abnor­ malities that could have affected the course of the study. Additionally, all women were in good health. All the women were non-smokers, and naturally post-menopausal, meaning women without menstruation for at least twelve months. Participants who reported an unnatural menopause (as a

who reported an unnatural menopause (as a result of surgery or radiotherapy for cervical cancer) or who were using hormone replacement therapy (HRT) were excluded. Two groups were formed among the women: the Normal BMI group, which included 23 normal- weight women (mean age ± standard deviation (SD) = 60.52 ± 4.61), and the Ov/Ob group, which consisted of 49 women who were over­ weight or obese (mean age ± 61.49 ± 4.40). All procedures of the study were conducted in accordance with the ethical

were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Helsinki Declaration of 1975 and were reviewed and approved by the Bioethics Committee at Pozna´n University of Medical Sciences (decision number 989/18 of 11.10.2018). The research was carried out at the Department of Dietetics, Faculty of Physical Culture in Gorzow Wielkopolski, Pozna´n University of Physical Education, Estkowskiego 13, 66–400, Gorz´ow Wielkopolski, Poland. All women gave their informed consent for inclusion

women gave their informed consent for inclusion before participating in the study. 2.2. Anthropometric measurement Anthropometric assessments and body composition assessments provided important information on women's nutritional status. Anthropometric measurements determined body height, body weight, fatness, leanness and waist circumference (WC). All measurements were taken after a 12-hour fast. Women's body weight was measured using a medical scale, with an accuracy of 0.1 cm. Height was

scale, with an accuracy of 0.1 cm. Height was measured with a medical altimeter with an accuracy of 0.1 cm. Based on the data, the patient's body mass index (BMI) was calculated. Overweight and obesity were classified on BMI. In adults, according to the World Health Orga­ nization (WHO), a BMI in the range of 25.0–29.9 is responsible for overweight, while a BMI over 30.0 is responses for obesity. Data on BMI for adults can be found on the WHO website at http://www.who.int/

found on the WHO website at http://www.who.int/ tools/growth-reference-data-for-5to19-years/indicators/bmi-for-age (accessed on 21 December 2022). Body mass components of body mass (body-fat percentage (FAT %), fat-free mass (FFM), and total body water (TBW) levels) were evaluated using the electrical bioimpedance method (BIA) and the TANITA 780 MC analyzer. Detailed information has been provided elsewhere. 2.3. Nutritional evaluation The eating habits of the participants were evaluated by a

habits of the participants were evaluated by a registered dietitian (K.M.) using the “three-day food record” method (Gronowska- Senger, 2013) where the participants were asked to record the amounts of all meals consumed and food products used to prepare them. The patient, in this method, records the food products needed to prepare the meals and the amount of all meals eaten. After each meal, the participants completed the food record for two days a week, with one day off, totaling three days.

a week, with one day off, totaling three days. An album of photos of the products and dishes was provided to assist in assessing portion size (Szponar et al., 2000). Daily food rations' energy and nutritional value were calculated using the Cambridge Diagnostics computer program “Aliant”. The daily food intake of all participants was compared with their current indi­ vidual daily nutritional and energy requirements, taking into account standard losses due to technical and culinary treatment.

losses due to technical and culinary treatment. The energy and nutritional requirements of each patient were determined based on the Human Nutrition Standards of the National Food and Nutrition Institute at the recommended level (Jarosz et al., 2020). The procedure for nutritional evaluation has previously been described in detail (Mizgier et al., 2020). 2.4. tests made it possible to assess the mental state and motor functions of the women examined. The emotional state and the possibility of depression were assessed using the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). This scale consist of 30 questions to be answered yes or no. A score above 20 points indicates deep depression, and above 10 points – slight depression (Park and Lee, 2021; Park, 2022). The Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) test assessed the K. To assess motor speed, the women were asked to

To assess motor speed, the women were asked to touch the first two fingers of their non-dominant hand as widely and as quickly as possible, with the result being the number of clicks achieved in 5 s. The subjects were asked to perform specific movements with their non-dominant hand to assess psychomotor speed. The movements included clenching the hand into a fist on a flat surface, placing the palm flat on the surface with the palm down, and placing the hand perpen­ dicular to the flat surface

the hand perpen­ dicular to the flat surface with the little finger on its side. The subjects were shown how to perform the sequence of movements, and were allowed to perform the exercises twice. Within 10 s, the number of correctly repeated complete sequences was recorded as the result. 2.5. Publications indicate that BDNF plays an important role in the regulation of energy homeostasis by controlling eating patterns and physical activity, as well as modulating glucose metabolism in peripheral tissues. By stimulating glucose transport and mitochondrial biogenesis, the

transport and mitochondrial biogenesis, the neurotrophic factor of brain origin pro­ tects neurons against damage and diseases, as well as affecting the strengthening of cellular bioenergetics. Acting in the brain and on the periphery, it increases insulin sensitivity and parasympathetic tone (Marosi and Mattson, 2014; Iu and Chan, 2022; Di Rosa et al., 2021). neurotrophic factor a very important as well as an essential regulator of cellular processes underlying cognition and other complex behaviours. INTRODUCTION Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) are anthropogenic chemi­ cals that remain for extremely long periods in the environment and accumulate in flora and fauna around the planet, entering the food chain and contaminating food and water supplies. Within this group of pollutants, we can find polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). PCBs include 209 con­ geners that were

(PFAS). PCBs include 209 con­ geners that were manufactured since the 1930s for several industrial applications and electronic devices. OCPs were exten­ sively used in agriculture and public health campaigns to prevent vector-borne diseases until they were restricted or banned in the 1980s due to their high toxicity, persistence, and bioaccumula­ tion. PFAS are used in industry for obtaining non-stick and waterproof coatings. The list of POPs in the United Nations En­ vironment Program’s

in the United Nations En­ vironment Program’s Stockholm Convention, aimed at taking measures to eliminate or reduce the release of POPs into the en­ vironment by participating countries, includes several of these pollutants. OCPs and PCBs were added in 2001, while perfluor­ ooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) were added in 2019.1 Despite regulation attempts, virtually all humans are still ex­ posed to POPs due to its high persistence in the organism. In this regard,

In this regard, human biomonitoring is a key tool in the assessment of the body burden of pollutants, taking into account that internal levels of pollutants represent all exposure routes simultaneously, as well as their potential health implications.2 Human adipose tis­ sue, where many POPs accumulate due to their lipophilicity, gives meaningful information about the long-term accumulation of some of these chemicals and also plays a fundamental role in the

and also plays a fundamental role in the production and regulation of certain hormones,3 specifically sex steroids.4 In addition, sex hormones regulate adipose tissue activity in a sex-specific way.5 In fact, men and women differ in the amount and type of fat in their bodies, with women generally having a higher fat proportion and less visceral adipose tissue than men. and estrogens—are associated with metabolic and cardiovascular diseases.17 In addition, dysre­ gulation in follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hor­ mone (LH), could lead to infertility18 and, specifically for FSH, in­ creased inflammation, insulin resistance, and atherosclerosis.19 Based on the aforementioned knowledge gaps regarding the hormonal implications of long-term exposure to POPs, this study aimed to explore the associations of OCP, PCB, and PFAS expo­ sure with sex

MATERIALS AND METHODS This manuscript was prepared in close adherence to the STROBE guidelines.20 Study design and population This study is a cross-sectional research conducted within the GraMo adult co­ hort (Granada, Southern Spain), for which an extensive description of popula­ tion characteristics and pollutant exposure levels has been published elsewhere.21–26

levels has been published elsewhere.21–26 The province of Granada encompasses rural, semi-rural, and urban areas, with a total population of over 915,000 inhabitants spread across an area of 12,531 km2. The characteristics of GraMo cohort and enrollment procedure have been thoroughly described elsewhere.24 Briefly, recruitment was performed during 2003 and 2004 in two public hospitals: Clı´nico San Cecilio University Hospital in Granada city (inland urban area) and Santa Ana Hospital in the

(inland urban area) and Santa Ana Hospital in the town of Motril (semi-rural area in the Mediterranean coast). The cohort included patients undergoing non-cancer-related surgery, namely hernias (41%), gallbladder diseases (21%), varicose veins (12%), and other conditions (26%). As described in Figure 1, from a first set of 409 individuals contacted, 387 accepted the invitation to participate. The inclusion criteria were: aged older than 16 years, not having received hormone therapy and having

not having received hormone therapy and having resided in the study areas for at least 10 years before recruitment. Patients with cancer and those with a hormonal disease related to the hypothalamic axis were ex­ cluded. A final group of 253 participants was included in the study, as they pro­ vided samples for hormone assessment and some sample for POP measure­ ment. 234 of them provided sufficient adipose tissue sample for OCP and PCB analyses (Subgroup 1), while 99 had enough sample volume

(Subgroup 1), while 99 had enough sample volume for PFAS quanti­ fication in serum (Subgroup 2). A total of 80 individuals had both serum and adipose tissue analyses. Women who had menstruated at least once in the last 12 months were included in the premenopausal women group. not adjusted for multiple comparisons to enhance sensitivity in detecting potential associations, despite the in­ creased risk of false positives.102,103 Based on the aforemen­ tioned considerations, these findings strongly warrant further confirmation in larger and more diverse populations. Conclusions We observed individual and mixture associations between POP exposure and

and mixture associations between POP exposure and sex hormone levels, with effects differing by sex and menopausal status. The associations were more pro­ nounced in premenopausal women. If confirmed, these findings could have significant public health implications, as human ex­ posure to these pollutants remains widespread, and disturban­ ces in sex hormone levels are highly prevalent in contemporary society. However, this meta-analysis aims to address the relationship between central obesity and risk of pre and postmenopausal breast cancer regardless of the age. Method: A full electronic search of the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, Excerpta Medicine Database (Embase), PubMed, Google Scholar, MESH Medline, and Cancer Literature databases was conducted from 2016 to 2023. The study followed the PRISMA Statement for

2023. The study followed the PRISMA Statement for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses protocol. The relevant cohort and case-control studies were screened by two reviewers independently. The data were extracted using Microsoft Excel and analyzed using STATA version 17. Publication bias was detected using a funnel plot, with a p value <0.05 indicate potential publication bias. The I2 test was used to assess the heterogeneity of the studies. The overall estimates with a 95% confidence interval

overall estimates with a 95% confidence interval were estimated using a random effect model analysis. Results: A total of eight studies with 135,876 women participants were included in this study. The heterogeneity of the studies I2 test was 87.1%. The overall pooled results, women who presented with central obesity was 2.4 times more likely to develop breast cancer than those who had no history of central obesity (AOR=2.4, 95% CI; 1.35-4.27). Conclusion: This study revealed that central obesity is a risk factor of breast cancer. Interventions should be implement to reduce progression of breast cancer through lifestyle change. among women due to its high morbidity and mortality rates [1]. It is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality [2] among women. Worldwide; 2.3 million new diagnoses of breast cancer in women, which represents 11.7% of all new cancer cases in the world[3]. The global fatality rate was account for 6.9% [4]. It accounts for 685,000 fatalities each year, and it is the fifth leading cause of death among different cancers, accounting for 16%, or 1 in every 6 cancer deaths in women [5]. BC is

or 1 in every 6 cancer deaths in women [5]. BC is usually called a group of diseases (>100) due to the presence of various biological subtypes reflecting distinct molecular profiles and clinic-pathological features [5, 6].Environmental variables, including smoking, alcohol drinking, unhealthy food and eating habits, physical inactivity, obesity, excessive sun exposure, and infection with certain viruses and bacteria, have a significant influence on the development of BC in females [7]. on the development of BC in females [7]. Recent trend revealed a significant increase in the incidence of BC worldwide, with postmenopausal women experiencing a greater increase than premenopausal women [8]. One explanation for this rise could be a shifting pattern of lifestyle features as a result of rapid economic change and aging [9]. During the last two decades, physical activity levels have decreased, and eating patterns have changed, resulting in a rise average population body mass index

in a rise average population body mass index (BMI), which is indicative of obesity[10]. Central obesity has been associated with increased risk factors for numerous malignancies and chronic illnesses, including BC in postmenopausal women [6]. A study in South Asia, India, revealed that a higher waist-to-hip-ratio (WHR) and waist circumference (WC) were associated with a threefold increase in the risk of premenopausal and postmenopausal BC[11], but its effect on premenopausal BC seems to vary

but its effect on premenopausal BC seems to vary according to ethnic status [12-14]. Many researchers have investigated the association between central obesity and the development of BC in women, but there are inconsistent related studies [15, 16]. Numerous observational studies have shown that obesity increases the chance of developing BC both before and after menopause [17-19]. According to the findings of certain studies, obesity has a preventive effect on cancer development during the

effect on cancer development during the premenopausal stage but poses a risk during the postmenopausal stage [16, 20]. Premenopausal central obesity in European and American women has been reported to decrease the risk of BC [21], while a positive association between premenopausal obesity and BC incidence in Asian populations has been reported across studies [22, 23]. Although different systematic reviews and meta-analyses have been conducted on central obesity and BC risk outcomes, their

on central obesity and BC risk outcomes, their results and associated factors are different and inconsistent. In addition, there is a lack of evidence on the overall impact of central obesity on BC risk in recent studies. Similarly, the associations between central obesity and BC risk and unfavourable BC status are not well established. Thus, this meta-analysis aimed to determine the association between central obesity and BC worldwide. Methods Source of information and searching strategy This

Source of information and searching strategy This study followed the PRISMA statement protocol for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. A full electronic search was conducted with a bibliographic searching strategy to identify important published studies on the relationship between central obesity and BC. 8 from Embase, 15 from the Cochrane Library, 326 from Google Scholar, and 16 from other electronic databases published from 2016 until 24th August 2023. In addition, a manual searching procedure was used to retrieve unpublished research and gray literature from different sources of database repositories in Ethiopian universities. 3366 ABSTRACT Whey protein phospholipid concentrate (WPPC) is a co-product generated during the manufacture of whey protein isolate. Whey protein phospholipid concentrate is depleted of simple sugars but contains numerous glyco- conjugates embedded in the milk fat globule membrane, suggesting this fraction may serve as a carbon source for growth of bifidobacteria commonly enriched in breastfed infants. In this work, we demonstrate that WPPC can serve as a sole carbon source for the growth of

serve as a sole carbon source for the growth of Bifidobac- terium bifidum, a species common to the breastfed infant and routinely used as a probiotic. Growth on WPPC frac- tions resulted in expression of key extracellular glycosyl hydrolases in B. bifidum associated with the catabolism of glycoproteins. Interestingly, this included induction of fucosidase genes in B. bifidum linked to catabolism of fucosylated human milk oligosaccharides even though the WPPC glycan possesses little fucose.

though the WPPC glycan possesses little fucose. Additional growth studies revealed that WPPC-glycan components N-acetylglucosamine or N-acetylgalactosamine were required for pre-activation of B. bifidum toward rapid growth on fucosylated human milk oligosaccharides. Growth on WPPC fractions also resulted in expression of extracellular sialidases in B. bifidum which promoted a consistent release of sialic acid, a well-known component of bovine milk oligosaccharides and glycoconjugates with

milk oligosaccharides and glycoconjugates with potential effects on gut microbial ecology and host cognition. These studies suggest WPPC may serve as a promising bioactive component to facilitate probiotic activity for use in infant formulas and other synbiotic applications. Key words: Bifidobacterium, milk fat globule membrane, sialic acid, glycoconjugates INTRODUCTION Milk has evolved to meet the nutritional requirements of the neonate supplying key components; protein, fat, carbohydrates,

key components; protein, fat, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals, among others (Zivkovic et al., 2011). Milk also contains various bio- active components known to affect the maturation of gut-associated lymphoid tissues (Ebringer et al., 2008), shape the intestinal microbiota (Maga et al., 2013), in- hibit pathogenic bacteria from attaching to the gut muco- sal layer (Morrin et al., 2021), and promote gut integrity (Tong et al., 2023). Some of these bioactive compounds have a common

Some of these bioactive compounds have a common structural theme: They are glycoconju- gates. Glycans in human milk can be present as free oligo- saccharides or glycoconjugates, the latter represented by glycosylated proteins and lipids. Lactose is the major free disaccharide and can be digested by the host enzymes. The other free oligosaccharides, termed human milk oligosaccharides (HMO), are composed of monomers galactose (Gal), fucose (Fuc), N-acetylneuraminic acid (sialic acid [SA]),

N-acetylneuraminic acid (sialic acid [SA]), N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc), and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) via various linkages. Human milk oligosaccharides are a prominent factor influencing bacterial colonization of the large intestine of breastfed neonates and, notably, they facilitate Bifi- dobacterium species to predominate in the early life gut microbiota (Heiss et al., 2021; Button et al., 2022) using an array of specific enzymes to degrade HMO (Sakanaka et al., 2019). Some

to degrade HMO (Sakanaka et al., 2019). Some Bifidobacterium species are known to grow directly on glycoconjugates, including mucin (Ashida et al., 2009), milk glycoproteins (Kirmiz et al., 2018), and milk glycolipids (Lee et al., 2014). Although milk glycoproteins are considered important components of glycan metabolism by the gastrointestinal microbiome (Gong et al., 2020; Hernell et al., 2020), their catabolism by the microbiota is poorly understood due, in part, to the difficulty in

understood due, in part, to the difficulty in analytically defining these complex milk glycoconjugates. Bifidobacterium bifidum possesses glycosyl hydrolase (GH) family GH95 and GH29 enzymes for degrading fucosylated termini and GH33 for sialylated termini; GH2 and GH110 are expressed for degrading galactosyl residues and GH20, GH84, and GH89 for hexosamine residues in complex glycans (Ashida et al., 2009; Kata- yama et al., 2004; Wada et al., 2008; Miwa et al., 2010; Kiyohara et al., 2011; Wakinaka et al., 2013;
