However, these studies targeted to O-glycosylation on mucin or free oligosaccha- rides in milk and few studies have examined the precise mechanisms by which bifidobacteria consume bovine milk glycoconjugates (Karav et al., 2016; O’Riordan et al., 2018; Karav et al., 2019; Arzamasov and Osterman, 2022). Milk glycoconjugates, including glycomacropeptide, lactoferrin, and osteopontin, as well as ingredients

and osteopontin, as well as ingredients en- riched in milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) are in- creasingly examined as supplements to infant formula and studies have shown their effect on functions ranging from beneficial modulation of the gut microbiome, to improved immune benefits, to increased cognitive func- tion (West et al., 2017; Córdova-Dávalos et al., 2019; Raza et al., 2021; Mohamed et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024). However, the pleiotropic effects of these glycoconju- gates make it hard

effects of these glycoconju- gates make it hard to define which activities are linked to microbial catabolism (along with modulation of the gut microbiome) and which are more direct effects on the host by the glycoconjugates themselves. To help resolve this, a deeper understanding of the microbial catabolism of milk glycoconjugates is required. One target molecule derived from these glycoconju- gates and implicated in bioactivities in both the gut and brain is SA. This unusual sugar, commonly

gut and brain is SA. This unusual sugar, commonly present on human and bovine milk glycans, is involved in cross- feeding interactions among intestinal bacteria (be they beneficial or detrimental; Egan et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2015; Morozumi et al., 2023), and it has been linked to cognitive function in neonates due to its role in brain myelination (Chung et al., 2020). Recently, we characterized whey protein phospholipid concentrate (WPPC), an underused dairy ingredient obtained from the

an underused dairy ingredient obtained from the production of whey protein isolates, which is presently primarily used in animal nutrition (Ozturk et al., 2022). This study revealed the wealth of glycosylated MFGM proteins (~20% of the total) and a SA abundance up to 2% of total dry weight of the ingre- dient. We hypothesized that this fraction would serve as a suitable growth substrate for infant-borne bifidobacteria, notably B. bifidum. This study characterizes the glycan- driven metabolism

study characterizes the glycan- driven metabolism of B. bifidum on WPPC and its de- rivative fractions, showing both the release of SA and the potential for synbiotic applications of B. bifidum and WPPC in future gut health studies. DISCUSSION The sugars that comprise milk glycans are

The sugars that comprise milk glycans are present in 2 distinct forms, either as free oligosaccharides or as conjugates attached to proteins or lipids. These glycans are key bioactive components that perform numerous functions in situ, including facilitating the establishment of the neonatal gut microbiome (Kirmiz et al., 2018), deflecting pathogens (Newburg et al., 2005), and directly affecting host gut barrier and immune functions (Quinn et al., 2020). In addition, numerous studies have

et al., 2020). In addition, numerous studies have linked milk glycans to neonatal brain development (Dallas et al., 2011). Interactions of milk oligosaccharides and the gut mi- crobiome have advanced greatly in the last 10 yr, perhaps culminating in the commercial production of numerous HMO for use in infant formula (Bührer et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022) and more recently as prebiotic supplements for adults (Lodge et al., 2021; Schalich et al., 2024). How- ever, a general understanding of the

2024). How- ever, a general understanding of the interaction between gut microbes and complex milk glycoconjugates lags far behind that of milk oligosaccharides. This is partly due to the complex structure of milk glycans. They are com- posed of several building block monosaccharides linked via specific glycosidic bonds, many, but not all, of which are also present in milk oligosaccharides (Bhattacharya et al., 2019). Via advances in analytical glycomics, the structures of glycans connected

glycomics, the structures of glycans connected with glycoconjugates are revealed which, in turn, enables research on their me- tabolism by gut bacteria (Wilson et al., 2008; Karav et al., 2016). In this work, we defined how B. bifidum, a well-known consumer of mucin and HMO, also readily consumes the milk glycoconjugate pool represented in WPPC, a fraction generated from whey protein manu- facture. In general, the suite of GH used by B. bifidum to consume WPPC has been previously characterized

to consume WPPC has been previously characterized for interaction with mucin or HMO (Turroni et al., 2010; Garrido et al., 2015). Notably, the release of SA from WPPC by B. bifidum may facilitate transfer systemically and benefit the host brain development (Liu et al., 2023). This is because SA is thought to sustain brain myelina- tion in early life by serving as a precursor to gangliosides and cerebrosides that make up the myelin sheath (Chung et al., 2020). Cultivation of B. bifidum in WPPC activates the en- zymes for catabolism of fucosylated HMO (Figure 4B) suggesting WPPC may facilitate pre-activation of bifi- dobacteria toward overall HMO consumption. Among the monosaccharides that comprise the WPPC glycans, GlcNAc and GalNAc both exhibited pre-activation to- ward 2’FL, suggesting these sugars drive a specific HMO regulon in B. bifidum. In a previous study, Arzamasov et al. (2022) reported that NagR in B. bifidum PRL2010

(2022) reported that NagR in B. bifidum PRL2010 (BBPR_0565) regulates the enzymes related to external HMO or mucin O-glycan degradation. In that model, NagR, when bound by GlcNAc, derepresses expression of genes involved in mucin degradation. Bifidobacterium bifidum YK1043 contains an identical NagR homolog (8082051987) suggesting this regulator performs same role in B. bifidum YK1043 and is likely linked to pre- activation of HMO consumption shown in Figure 7. with SA, and B. bifidum YK1043, as well as other B. bifidum strains, likely releases this sugar in the gut. In infants, thanks to a higher permeability of the gut barrier, SA could be absorbed by the intestinal cells, transported into the bloodstream and eventually reach the brain (Chung et al., 2020). In the brain, SA plays a critical role in the formation of gangliosides and glycoproteins, which are essential for neural development and function. These molecules are especially concentrated in

These molecules are especially concentrated in the myelin and synaptosomal fraction of brain tissue, highlighting their importance in brain activity and cognitive function (Lis-Kuberka and Orczyk-Pawiłowicz, 2019). Although further research is needed, supplementation of milk glycoconjugates with appropriate gut bifidobacteria that release SA may influence neonatal brain development (Bian et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2022). Plas Gogerddan, Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, SY23 3EE, UK c Volac Whey Nutrition Ltd, 50 Fishers Lane, Orwell, Royston, Hertfordshire, SG8 5QX, UK A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Whey protein Polysaccharides Lubrication Tribology Sensory A B S T R A C T For older adults, whey protein is associated with negative sensory attributes, including undesirable mouthfeel qualities, that limit consumption and acceptance. Previous work suggests that increased lubrication may have the ability to reduce whey

lubrication may have the ability to reduce whey protein-associated mouthdrying, a driver for disliking, by limiting interactions of whey protein with salivary proteins and mucin. This was investigated in the current study by co-spray drying whey protein with combinations of maltodextrin, xanthan gum and/or guar gum; the resulting powders were used to make 10% suspensions. The particle size, zeta potential, rheological and tribological profiles of these suspensions were measured. It was shown

of these suspensions were measured. It was shown that co-spray drying whey protein with guar gum led to a reduction in instrumental friction, irrespective of changes in viscosity. These samples were perceived as significantly more mouthcoating and smooth when assessed by a trained sensory panel. Contrastingly, suspensions containing xanthan gum showed increased viscosity and enhanced shear thinning compared with whey protein, but no change in instrumental friction at higher sliding speeds. friction at higher sliding speeds. This may be a result of a larger particle size, representing increased aggregation in samples containing xanthan gum. There was no significant difference in mouthdrying or slip­ periness perception between the suspensions. These findings suggest that the incorporation of guar gum has the capacity to reduce oral friction and impact mouthfeel in whey protein model beverages. This should be taken forward into temporal sensory trials to further investigate the

sensory trials to further investigate the effects of additional lubrication. 1. Introduction 1.1. The need for additional lubrication of whey protein Adequate protein intake is important in maintaining the health of older adults by enhancing immune function and reducing the risk of fracture, frailty, cognitive decline, and sarcopenia development (Smith, Clegg, & Methven, 2022). In the UK, the reference nutrient intake for older adults is the same as the general population at 0.75 g/kg/day

same as the general population at 0.75 g/kg/day (Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition, 2011). However, the Eu­ ropean Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) suggest that 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day may be more appropriate for older adults (Deutz et al., 2014). It has been reported that older adults repeatedly fall short of these guidelines: in a UK study of 256 older adults, 35.6% consumed less than 0.75 g/kg/day of protein and 81.6% consumed less than the ESPEN recommendation (Morris

less than the ESPEN recommendation (Morris et al., 2020). The reasons for the reduced protein intake in this demographic are multifactorial; these are best described in the recent review by Walker- Clarke, Walasek and Meyer (2022). This low protein intake contributes towards the development of sarcopenia: . Sarcopenia significantly in­ creases the risk of falls (Lim & Kong, 2022), frailty (Woo et al., 2015), morbidity and mortality (Sobestiansky et al., 2019). Sarcopenia pro­ gression can be

Sarcopenia pro­ gression can be reduced through adequate nutrition in combination with exercise (Colonetti et al., 2023; Hern´andez-Lepe et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2019; Nasimi et al., 2023). Our previous review (Giles et al., 2024) highlighted the positive effect of protein supplementation and fortifi­ cation on muscle mass. Such a protein supplement, whey protein, has been shown to be a beneficial protein source for fortification due to its high leucine content (Etzel, 2004),

Despite the nutritional benefits of whey protein, it has some sensory attributes with negative associations, limiting its acceptance and con­ sumption. A key driver for disliking of whey protein-based supplements is mouthdrying (Zhang et al., 2020). The mechanism responsible for whey protein-associated mouthdrying is not fully understood; current

mouthdrying is not fully understood; current theories were summarised in the authors’ recent review (Giles et al., 2024). In this review, mouthdrying was attributed to a combination of interactions of whey protein with salivary proteins and the oral mucosa. Increased oral friction is a common pathway to these mechanisms, meaning the addition of polysaccharides as lubricants may reduce these interactions. It was proposed this may be a result of lubricants competitively binding to the oral

of lubricants competitively binding to the oral mucosa, binding to whey protein, and/or increasing the rate of oral clearance. 1.2. Justification of selected polysaccharides to increase lubrication Polysaccharides have been investigated previously for their intrinsic lubrication properties. Xanthan gum (XG) and guar gum (GG), commonly used to modulate viscosity, have contrasting conformations: GG has a random coil conformation whereas XG has a rigid rod conformation. Li et al. (2022)

XG has a rigid rod conformation. Li et al. (2022) investigated the impact of additional lubrication of WPI using XG, where it was shown that the addition of XG led to a reduction in friction in the lower boundary regimes, due to the brush effect of the polysaccharide interacting with the WPI particle. In agreement with this, when comparing the two in aqueous solutions, Ji et al. (2022) found that XG had higher lubricating capacity at lower sliding speeds, compared with GG, but that this

sliding speeds, compared with GG, but that this relationship was reversed at higher speeds (<20 mm/s). The mouth experiences a wide range of sliding speeds during oral processing, so it is unclear which of these is likely to correlate with sensory perception. Ji et al. (2023) investigated the use of XG, GG and carboxymethyl cellulose in combi­ nation with whey protein in an oil-in-water emulsion: the study reported that the addition of 0.2% XG led to instability and induced oil droplet

XG led to instability and induced oil droplet aggregation, whereas the uncharged GG (added at 0.235%) did not (Ji et al., 2023). GG decreased the friction coefficient of the whey protein-oil emulsion more than XG which the authors attributed to the lower particle size and aggregation levels (Ji et al., 2023). However, the omission of a non-polysaccharide control means these results can only be compared with each other and not with a whey-oil emulsion. The study also omits to include an aqueous

The study also omits to include an aqueous suspension of whey, meaning all whey samples are an oil-in-water emulsion, so the effect of poly­ saccharides on whey protein alone cannot be elucidated. When using a trained sensory panel, a correlation was reported between the degree of shear thinning and creamy, thick and fatty sensations (Ji et al., 2023). However, the study did not report significant differences in mouthdrying or slipperiness perception using an untrained panel (Ji et al., 2023).

Previous work in other models has shown that the use of a hydrocolloid thickener led to a reduction in mouthdrying perception (Rossetti et al., 2009), meaning it is unclear if this is an intrinsic property of whey protein or due an investigative limitation. Whilst previous research has investigated the ability of XG and GG to act as lubricants in isolation (Ji et al., 2023), research into their effect in combination is limited. It was previously shown

combination is limited. It was previously shown that when GG and lo­ cust bean gum were applied in combination, they produced a different rheological profile than the one shown by either gum alone (Garrec & Norton, 2012). Our review suggested that whey protein-associated mouthdrying is a result of multiple mechanisms (Giles et al., 2024); therefore, using polysaccharides with different properties may address different causes of mouthdrying, leading to a greater reduction of the mouthdrying

leading to a greater reduction of the mouthdrying sensation. The use of other polysaccharides as lubricants has also been inves­ tigated: maltodextrin is a good potential lubricant for whey protein due to its high emulsifying properties and sweet taste (Akhtar & Dickinson, 2007). Increasing sweetness in protein-beverages has been shown to decrease mouthdrying through a cognitive pathway (Methven et al., 2010); thus, maltodextrin has the potential to ameliorate mouthdrying both physically and

to ameliorate mouthdrying both physically and cognitively. Blok et al. (2020) investigated the sensory impact of the addition of maltodextrin to iced coffees and showed that maltodextrin levels correlated with creaminess and slip­ periness perception. This was supported instrumentally, where the friction coefficient reduced upon addition of maltodextrin (Blok et al., 2020). However, older adults have reported excessive sweetness as a common reason for rejection of oral nutritional supplements

for rejection of oral nutritional supplements (Zhang et al., 2020), so this should be added with caution. 1.3. Co-spray drying whey protein with polysaccharides to increase lubrication Spray drying is part of the commercial production process of whey protein isolate (WPI), but has not been fully utilised in combination with polysaccharides for the modification of WPI’s sensory properties. It is hypothesised that the drying process could be optimised to increase lubrication through the inclusion

to increase lubrication through the inclusion of a second stage of drying of WPI with additional ingredients using a fluidised-bed agglomerate system (co- spray drying). To the authors’ knowledge no work exists investigating the effect of co-spray drying WPI with polysaccharides (XG, GG, maltodextrin) on mouthdrying perception; therefore, this methodology may be an unutilised opportunity to modify the mouthfeel of WPI. Previous work has focused on adding polysaccharides to an existing whey

on adding polysaccharides to an existing whey protein-fortified product (Ji et al., 2023), rather than using them to coat whey particles before addition into products, with the aim of reducing interactions between whey protein and components of the oral cavity. The previous studies used the addition of high levels of poly­ saccharides, leading to large changes in viscosity and physical structure, meaning the impact of lubrication alone cannot be elucidated. It is also possible that these levels

elucidated. It is also possible that these levels would impact flavour and consumer accep­ tance, which has been omitted from some previous work (Li et al., 2022). The authors propose that co-spray drying has the potential to increase lubrication and impact mouthdrying with lower levels of polysaccharides. Spray-drying may have the capacity to improve taste: encapsulations have been previously shown to reduce the bitterness perception of whey protein hydrolysates (Ma et al. 2014; Yang et al.

protein hydrolysates (Ma et al. 2014; Yang et al. 2012). These flavour-focused results indicate that this approach could reduce in­ teractions between whey proteins and taste receptors and influence the sensory profile differently to simply mixing the ingredients. Previous research has investigated the capacity of spray drying to improve solubility: Ji et al. Whilst this study did not look at the sensory impacts of encapsulation, it sup­ ports its use as a potential mitigation strategy for mouthdrying by reducing interactions between whey proteins and the oral mucosa and saliva. No studies to the authors knowledge have investigated the effect of this technique on mouthfeel

the effect of this technique on mouthfeel properties, leading to the need for further investigation. 1.4. Research hypothesis Although previous work has investigated mixing WPI with poly­ saccharides or co-spray drying of whey protein with other materials, to the authors knowledge, studies have not used co-spray drying of WPI and polysaccharides to investigate the impact on lubrication and mouthfeel. This study bridges the gap between the ability of co-spray drying to increase lubrication and

of co-spray drying to increase lubrication and the subsequent impact on sensory perception. It is also noted that in the literature, researchers use high levels of polysaccharides, leading to large changes in the viscosity of the product and the subsequent nutritional content of WPI as an ingredient. This study, using low levels of polysaccharides to maintain the high H. Giles et al. Food Hydrocolloids 160 (2025) 110778 2 protein content (>90%) of WPI, hypothesises that co-spray drying WPI with

WPI, hypothesises that co-spray drying WPI with maltodextrin, XG and/or GG would significantly decrease instru­ mental friction. Materials Whey protein isolate (WPI) was provided by Volac Whey Nutrition Ltd (Hertfordshire, UK). This contains 92% protein (calculated by ni­ trogen content) and is instantized with a sunflower lecithin inclusion (E322). Maltodextrin, XG and GG were sourced from Special Ingredients (Chesterfield, UK). 2.2. Powder preparation Coated samples were prepared with a

preparation Coated samples were prepared with a fluidised bed spray dryer using 5 kg batch agglomeration and microencapsulation (LZL Engineering, Owatonna, US): 3 kg of WPI powder was fluidised and heated to 35 ◦C. When at temperature, the WPI powder was sprayed with water from a top-nozzle spray for 7 min before replacing this feed with poly­ saccharides dissolved in warm water to allow for optimum substance coating (see Table 1). XG and GG were prepared as solutions in 500 mL of warm water;

prepared as solutions in 500 mL of warm water; the amounts used were the upper limit of solubility whilst mixing with a magnetic stirrer (ThermoFisher, UK; setting 3), corresponding to 0.3 and 0.5% w/v respectively. The level of malto­ dextrin used (4.76% w/v) was based on both initial sensory tastings (data not shown) to ensure no perceptible increase in sweetness and to ensure the thickness of the suspension was suitable for top-nozzle spray drying. The speed of spraying was manually

spray drying. The speed of spraying was manually manipulated (15–40 rpm) to control humidity inside the bed. During spraying, the inlet and outlet temperature ranged from 50 ◦C–67 ◦C and 25 ◦C–36 ◦C respectively. After addition of ingredients, the powder was dried to 45 ◦C to achieve the desired moisture content in the final powder of 5% w/w (±1%), and then immediately cooled to 35 ◦C before collection. Powders were stored in airtight containers at room temperature (19 ± 2 ◦C) until required

at room temperature (19 ± 2 ◦C) until required and used within 8 months. 2.3. Powder analysis 2.3.1. Conclusion WPI is a key ingredient used within oral nutritional supplements; a common reason for disliking these products is whey protein-associated mouthdrying. The authors’ previous review suggested that additional lubrication may have the capacity to reduce this mouthdrying (Giles et al., 2024). Earlier research has incorporated high levels of poly­ saccharides for this purpose; the current study

saccharides for this purpose; the current study aimed to use lower levels to increase lubrication whilst maintaining a high protein content and having a minimal impact on the sweetness of a model WPI beverage. Introduction Despite challenges during the menopausal transition (e.g., weight gain prevalence), some women maintain a healthy weight, often attributed to healthier behaviors and lifestyles, enhancing overall health and life expectancy [1,2]. Middle-aged women often struggle with weight management, even if they achieve a healthy

weight management, even if they achieve a healthy weight [3,4]. The National Weight Control Registry identifies effective strategies, including daily breakfast, regular weight monitoring, increased physical activity, frequent vegetable consumption, and a healthy diet [5]. Spe­ cifically for middle-aged women, successful strategies include dietary plan adherence, social support, problem-solving skills, planning content (plan types of food/physical activity in advance of performing behavior), and

activity in advance of performing behavior), and impulse management: acceptance (responding to im­ pulses through acceptance of the feeling) [1,2,6]. Current literature primarily addresses weight management strategies in specific groups, mainly young adults and individuals maintaining weight loss, which may not directly apply to older populations [3,7]. Research on weight-related behaviors in menopausal women is a pri­ ority, given the knowledge gaps, limited data, and therapeutic ap­ proaches

gaps, limited data, and therapeutic ap­ proaches requiring a culturally appropriate perspective [6,8]. Discussion Our study demonstrated that Portuguese postmenopausal women who maintain a healthy weight during the menopausal transition employ several cognitive-behavioral weight management strategies. While most of these strategies align with the OxFAB Taxonomy, our research identified five new strategies that should be

identified five new strategies that should be considered in future studies. 4.1. Successful weight management strategies in postmenopausal women Our study confirms that during the menopausal transition, women employ strategies such as energy compensation, content planning, in­ formation seeking, regulation (involving restrictions, permissions, and rule-setting), restraint, self-monitoring, stimulus control, and weight management aids, and seek support from family and friends. Microflora refers to a group of micro-organisms including bacteria and fungi. Supplemental microflora protein products have recently become commercially available and have been marketed as environ­ mentally friendly animal-free proteins that are identical in amino acid (AA) composition as dairy proteins. Hence, microflora protein is sug­ gested to represent a promising innovative source of dietary protein to closely mimic the AA composition of high-quality proteins, whilst potentially mitigating some environmental (e.g., carbon-emissions) and ethical (e.g., animal welfare) consequences associated with large-scale intensive animal agriculture. This protein source is manufactured by providing microflora with sugars containing an exact copy of the genome

sugars containing an exact copy of the genome corresponding to whey protein (considered one of the highest quality dietary proteins), as published by the Bovine Genome Sequencing and Analysis Consortium (Elsik et al., 2009; Tellam et al., 2009). The microflora cells incorporate the foreign DNA to repair breaks in its own DNA through homologous recombination (Kowalczykowski, 2015). Following fermentation and several purification and filtering steps, an ‘animal-free dairyprotein’ is produced and

an ‘animal-free dairyprotein’ is produced and is claimed to be identical to whey protein derived from cows’ milk. However, the ability for microflora to replicate the AA composition of whey, as well as the efficacy of these products in supporting skeletal muscle health remains untested. Skeletal muscle mass is regulated by variations in rates of muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and muscle protein breakdown (Atherton & Smith, 2012; Kumar et al., 2009). The MPS response and subsequent muscle remodelling is driven by exercise (predominantly resistance exercise) and in part, by the availability of AA into circulation following consumption of protein-rich foods which likely explains some of the superiority of animal proteins for MPS and skeletal muscle remodelling (Atherton & Smith, 2012; Kumar et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2021; Witard et al., 2016). In addition, intracellular signalling pathways, such as the mammalian target of rapamycin

such as the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) cascade, are responsible for upregulating the MPS response to dietary protein ingestion and acute resistance exercise (Hodson & Philp, 2019; Matsakas & Patel, 2009). protein dose of MIC on postprandial plasma AA concentrations and intracellular anabolic signalling path­ ways compared with WHEY in healthy adults following a single bout of resistance exercise. Participants Twelve healthy young active (sex: M = 6, F = 6; age: 21.1 ± 3.0 years; body mass index: 24.6 ± 4.4 kg m−2; body fat: 21.1 ± 7.3%; fasting glucose: 4.3 ± 0.4 mmol L−1) adults participated in the present study. did not assess the menstrual status of our female partici­ pants as menstrual cycle phase does not seem to influence MPS or whole- body myofibrillar proteolysis in response to resistance exercise (Colenso Semple et al., 2024). 2.2. Study design Following screening and consent, and in a randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced, cross-over design, participants completed two exper­ imental test days involving an identical bout of resistance exercise, with WHEY or MIC consumption post-exercise. Randomisation was per­ formed by an independent person using a computerised randomiser. Prior to each visit, participants were asked to complete a 3-d diet diary, with the final 24 h replicated

a 3-d diet diary, with the final 24 h replicated for the subsequent visit. Dietary intake was assessed by nutrition software (Nutritics©, Dublin, Ireland) and can be viewed in Supplementary Table 1. Participants were advised to avoid vigorous activity in the 24 h prior to trials and to replicate physical activity patterns before their subsequent visit. to arrive at the laboratory in an overnight fasted state, as verified on arrival. Test days were separated by ~7-d to allow partici­ pants to re-establish habitual dietary patterns and recover from the resistance exercise. 2.6. Discussion The present study demonstrates, for the first time, that the AA composition of microflora protein manufactured based on the genome of whey protein presents a similar pattern to that of a high-quality con­ ventional animal-based whey protein. In addition, the consumption of microflora protein after resistance exercise resulted in a similar

after resistance exercise resulted in a similar increase in postprandial plasma TAA, BCAA, EAA concentrations, and stimula­ tion of anabolic intramuscular signalling pathways compared with whey protein in healthy, young adults. However, and in direct contrast to our hypothesis, a favourable increase in postprandial leucine (a particularly anabolic AA important for stimulation of MPS and as a substrate for skeletal muscle remodelling (Churchward-Venne et al., 2014; Devries et al., 2018;

et al., 2014; Devries et al., 2018; Phillips, 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2013)) concentrations was observed with microflora protein, in accordance with the higher leucine content of the microflora protein supplement. Collectively, these data support the potential of microflora protein as an alternative animal-free protein source for supporting skeletal muscle remodelling in healthy and active young adult populations. 4.1. Amino acid composition There is rapidly growing interest in alternative

There is rapidly growing interest in alternative protein sources to reduce the intake of animal foods (Morgan et al., 2025; van der Heijden et al., 2023). However, plant-based proteins are typically, albeit not al­ ways (Monteyne et al., 2023; van Vliet et al., 2015), less potent in stimulating MPS compared with animal proteins (Berrazaga et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2021; Pinckaers et al., 2021; van Vliet et al., 2015), which is assumed to be attributable to their ‘lower quality’ (Morgan et

attributable to their ‘lower quality’ (Morgan et al., 2021; Pinckaers et al., 2021; van Vliet et al., 2015) and highlights the need to identify higher-quality alternative protein sources at a lower environmental cost. Herein, and in contrast with our primary hypothe­ sis, we found comparable pattern of AA composition between microflora and conventional whey protein (Table 1), which was largely compatible with human skeletal muscle protein AA content (with potentially important implications for

(with potentially important implications for EAA requirements for human skeletal muscle, see Gorissen et al., 2018). Indeed, the AA composition of the microflora protein represents a typical profile of a high-quality protein (Gorissen et al., 2018). Importantly, leucine content was ~17% higher in the microflora protein vs. whey condition (9.13g vs. 7.80g per 100g) which may be considered important given the anabolic potency of leucine (Churchward-Venne et al., 2014; Devries et al., 2018;

et al., 2014; Devries et al., 2018; Phillips, 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2013). In addition, lysine content was similar between sources (7.66g vs. 7.78g per 100g), which is notable given that many non-animal proteins lack this EAA (Young & Pellett, 1994). Taken together, these data indicate microflora protein is an alternative animal-free protein source which closely mimics the AA composition of traditional high-quality dairy protein, and theoretically could mitigate some of the environmental

could mitigate some of the environmental (i.e., carbon-emissions) and ethical (i.e., animal welfare) consequences associated with large-scale intensive an­ imal agriculture. 4.2. Skeletal muscle anabolism Skeletal muscle hypertrophy is regulated by multiple mechanisms but is underpinned by a positive net protein balance due to an increased stimulation of MPS (Cermak et al., 2012; McGlory et al., 2019; Morton et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2023). However, in the absence of a sufficient exogenous

However, in the absence of a sufficient exogenous supply of all EAAs (i.e., failing to achieve a well-balanced EAA profile), the muscle remodelling process will be limited as all EAAs are required to synthesise skeletal muscle (Wolfe, 2017). Although the AA composition of microflora protein was broadly comparable to that of whey protein, this may not translate to equal bioavailability and anabolic potency (Church et al., 2024), and it was therefore important to also assess the anabolic effects

important to also assess the anabolic effects of microflora protein in vivo. Perhaps the most notable differences in the AA composition were that leucine and methionine content, as key EAA supporting the postexercise MPS response (van der Heijden et al., 2023), were ~17% and ~26% higher in microflora compared with whey protein. Therefore, microflora protein appears to potentially offer a favourable profile of AA composition for supporting skeletal muscle remodelling. This notion is supported by

muscle remodelling. This notion is supported by our postprandial AA data showing that microflora protein ingestion elicited a significant increase in TAA, EAA, and BCAA plasma concentrations which was not significantly different with that of whey protein. In addition, a more favourable increase in plasma leucine concentrations was observed with microflora protein ingestion, likely a consequence of the higher leucine content in this supplement. The postprandial AA response to microflora protein

postprandial AA response to microflora protein ingestion following resistance exercise supports its use as an alternative, novel, animal-free protein source that may support skeletal muscle remodelling to a similar extent to high-quality conventional whey protein. In accordance with the comparable AA response between supplements, both microflora and whey protein supplementation upregulated intra­ muscular anabolic signalling (i.e., p-mTOR, p-4E-BP1, p-Akt, p-RPS6) to a similar degree (Fig. 4), despite the higher content and plasma avail­ ability of leucine in MIC. Whilst we might expect a dietary protein source with higher leucine content

Therefore, our findings indicate that inges­ tion of microflora protein following a bout of

Experimental considerations and future directions Our findings should be interpreted with several important J. Pratt et al. The Journal of Nutritional Physiology 1

et al. The Journal of Nutritional Physiology 1 (2025) 100001 8 considerations in mind. First, we focussed on healthy young adults and hence the generalisability of our findings to other populations such as older adults remain to be established. This consideration is particularly important in the context of populations associated with impaired nutrient digestion and absorption (e.g., ageing). In this regard, it is noteworthy that the fibre content of microflora is relatively high (7.0g vs. 4.5 g

of microflora is relatively high (7.0g vs. 4.5 g per 100 g protein) compared to conventional whey protein. Whilst postprandial AA availability did not seem to be affected by this in the present study of young healthy adults, a reduced digestibility and absorption of nutrients is possible in populations with compromised digestive health. Future studies are also warranted to explore the long- term health effects of microflora ingestion, which remains unknown. This is particularly relevant

remains unknown. This is particularly relevant considering the higher carbohydrate con­ tent of microflora protein, which was associated with statistically sig­ nificant elevations in postprandial glucose concentrations in the present study, and has potentially important implications for metabolic health (Blaak et al., 2012). In addition, it is pertinent to note that we did not assess the effects of the protein supplements in fed-only compared with exercise and fed-states and were unable to

with exercise and fed-states and were unable to differentiate between the independent effects of the exercise and protein sources. Although we assessed the content of several phosphorylated proteins involved in anabolic signalling pathways, whose quantitative association with MPS is equivocal (Hodson et al., 2019; Mitchell et al., 2014), we did not assess muscle protein turnover directly and therefore cannot comment on the impact of microflora protein on MPS following resistance exer­ cise.

Given that cellular signalling pathways are dynamic, the use of stable isotopes to measure changes in MPS would have provided greater insight into the effects of microflora protein on muscle protein turnover. Nevertheless, acute molecular responses to exercise and dietary provi­ sion can be informative for understanding alterations to MPS and skel­ etal muscle adaptation (Egan & Sharples, 2023). The reason for this notably lower leucine (as well as methionine and other EAAs) content in whey is difficult to reconcile but may reflect typical variance observed with nutritional supplements due to different manufacturing processes and warrants further attention (Nyakayiru et al., 2020). and as such, the effects of the product when integrated as part of a whole-food diet remain to be elucidated. With a broader view, the scalability of microflora protein production, together with product cost, consumer acceptance and pre­ cise estimates of environmental impact compared with other emerging alternatives (e.g., insect, algae), will be key determining factors of its feasibility for widespread use amongst the general population. Indeed, whilst the palatability and acceptability of

whilst the palatability and acceptability of the microflora supplement in this study was high, microflora proteins are associated with their own GMO (i.e., genetically modified organism) considerations, which may influence dietary choices independent of findings on human health. Nonetheless, while it should be acknowledged that complementary blending of plant protein sources, as well as alterations in food pro­ cessing, have gained credence as a strategy to potentially overcome the barriers

a strategy to potentially overcome the barriers associated with the typically unfavourable profile of AA composition of plant proteins (Nichele et al., 2022; Pinckaers et al., 2021; van der Heijden et al., 2024a,b), our findings demonstrate how an alternative approach, based upon genome replication of high-quality proteins, may provide another strategy for overcoming the anabolic inferiority of lower-quality dietary proteins. 5. Conclusion We show that the AA composition of microflora protein,

that the AA composition of microflora protein, manufac­ tured based on the genome of whey protein, was comparable to that of a high-quality conventional animal-based whey protein. The consumption of microflora protein after resistance exercise resulted in a similar in­ crease in postprandial AA concentrations in healthy young adults, including a favourable increase in leucine, and comparable stimulation of anabolic intramuscular signalling pathways compared with high- quality animal-based whey

compared with high- quality animal-based whey protein. Collectively, these data support the potential of microflora protein as an alternative animal-free protein source for supporting muscle anabolism in heathy young adults. Introduction Anthocyanins (ACNs) are plant secondary metabolites that are widely distributed in the flowers and fruits.

are widely distributed in the flowers and fruits. Their molecular structure, characterized by a unique C6-C3-C6 carbon skeleton, is formed through a glycosidic bond between anthocyanidins and sugars. The physico­ chemical properties of ACNs depend on the number and position of hydroxyl groups, degree of methylation, as well as the structure and position of the bound sugar groups (de Mejia et al., 2020; Rodriguez Amaya, 2018). ACNs exhibit various biological activities, including

exhibit various biological activities, including anti-inflammatory, anticancer properties and the regulation of lipid metabolism (Yang, Guo, et al., 2022). The bioavailability of ACNs is closely related to their degradation during gastrointestinal digestion (Mansour et al., 2020). The roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa), a tropical and subtropical economic crop, has been widely cultivated in Guangxi, Fujian, Guangdong, Yunnan provinces in China (Yang, Li, et al., 2022). Its calyx is globally used in

Li, et al., 2022). Its calyx is globally used in the food and pharmaceutical industries (Jeffery & Richardson, 2021). It is abundant in ACNs, primarily delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside, which contribute to its distinctive color. However, ACNs are highly susceptible to degradation caused by various environmental factors, such as pH, light exposure, temperature, etc., significantly limiting their develop­ ment and utilization (Tang et al., 2023). The stability and

(Tang et al., 2023). The stability and functional properties of ACNs can be improved through interactions with food components, such as polysaccharides, proteins, and polyphenols (Cheng et al., 2023). Apple pectin (AP) as an anionic polysaccharide is extensively utilized in the food industry due to its multifunctional properties as a gelling agent, stabilizer, emulsifier, and thickener. The main chain of apple pectin consists of α-(1,4)-linked D-galactosonic acid residues, along with other

D-galactosonic acid residues, along with other natural sugars such as D-galactose, D-arabinose, and L-rhamnose. Previous study reported that the degree of methylesterification (DM) is approximately 34.90 % (Hu et al., 2024). Its interaction with ACNs has been reported to enhance the stability and functional characteristics of ACNs, attracting significant research attention in recent years. Both whey protein and bovine serum albumin were also found to exert a protective effect on the stability of ACNs during storage or in vitro digestion (Chung et al., 2015). Whey protein isolate (WPI) has been utilized as a natural carrier for bioactive components in multiple delivery

for bioactive components in multiple delivery systems (Hu et al., 2019). The stability of ACNs can be improved through interacting with WPI via hydrogen bonds and van der Waals (Gong et al., 2021). This ACNs-loaded WPI complex has been successfully applied in solid food systems. However, the surface charge and hydrophobicity of protein-based materials make them susceptible to environmental factors such as pH, ionic strength, and temperature. The combinations of natural biological macromolecules

Compared to ACNs-AP and ACNs-WPI complexes, the incorporation of WPI and AP significantly raised the encapsulation efficiency of ACNs. The utilization of WPI and AP in the formulation resulted in a smaller particle size and PDI, indicating improved stability of this nanocomplex. The increase of ΔH suggested

of this nanocomplex. The increase of ΔH suggested an improvement in the thermal stability of roselle ACNs after interacting with WPI or/and AP. Morphological im­ ages further verified the particle size results of these nanocomplexes and illustrated the smooth surface and uniform distribution of the ternary complex. CD data demonstrated that the addition of AP induced a more compact three-dimensional conformation of ACNs-loaded nanocomplex. FTIR analysis revealed that the characteristic

FTIR analysis revealed that the characteristic absorption peaks at 1741 cm−1 of ACNs disappeared after being encapsulated by WPI and AP, providing evidence for the formation of a bilayer embedding structure. Furthermore, the stability of ACNs, particularly through the double embedding by WPI and AP, was significantly enhanced during in vitro simulated digestion. Hence, the construction of roselle ACNs-loaded ternary nanocomplex could be employed as a potential delivery sys­ tem to expand the

as a potential delivery sys­ tem to expand the application of anthocyanins in functional foods or pharmaceutical fields. Introduction The human body harbors trillions of microorganisms that are essential for various aspects of human physiology and health main- tenance. This rich community of microorganisms is termed the microbiota, which includes bacteria, yeast, fungi, protozoa, archaea, and viruses. The human microbiome is crucial for maintaining healthy aging and preventing diseases (Ghosh et al., 2022), and a large subset of microbes colonizing the human oral cavity, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and genital

cavity, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, and genital tract has a mutualistic relationship with the host (Singh et al., 2019). The oral cavity contains one of the most diverse microbiota (Human Microbiome Project, 2012; Li et al., 2012), and a perturbation in the microbial composition can lead to multiple oral diseases, including periodontitis and dental caries (Almstahl et al., 2010; Dewhirst et al., 2010). As the direct route to both the respira- tory and digestive systems, the oral cavity

tory and digestive systems, the oral cavity inﬂuences activity at other body sites. Dysbiosis of the oral microbiome is related to several malignant tumors (Farrell et al., 2012; Kostic et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2015; Peters et al., 2017; Wolf et al., 2017; Ganly et al., 2019; Karpinski, 2019) and many systemic diseases (Ren et al., 2024), such as cardiovascular diseases (Takeshita et al., 2016; Malla et al., 2018), stroke (Joshipura et al., 2003), and diabetes (Genco et al., 2005; Mealey et

and diabetes (Genco et al., 2005; Mealey et al., 2006). In addition, more than 1014 bacteria colonize the GI tract, the majority of which reside in the lumen and mucus of the ileum and colon (Lampe et al., 1998; Aldunate et al., 2015). The oral and gut microbiota in women of reproductive age have been extensively discussed, while the transition to the speciﬁc period of menopause has been somewhat

the speciﬁc period of menopause has been somewhat overlooked (Graham et al., 2021). In our previous review, we synthesized several aspects of ovary-microbiota crosstalk in female healthy aging and summarized some gut bacterial groups that are related to ovarian aging (Huang et al., 2024a). The host-microbiome interplay is involved in age-related diseases throughout women’s later years (Graham et al., 2021; Barrea et al., 2023). The changes in oral microbiota may also play an important role in

microbiota may also play an important role in the pathogenesis of menopause-related diseases (Hernandez-Vigueras et al., 2016; Barrea et al., 2023). Menopause, as a natural part of female aging, is characterized by the cessation of menstruation for one year and represents the per- manent loss of ovarian follicle activity (Edwards and Li, 2013). Menopause usually occurs between the ages of 45 and 55 (Brotman et al., 2014). The years around menopause that begin from a rising variance in menstrual

that begin from a rising variance in menstrual cycle length and ﬁnish a whole year after the ﬁnal menstrual period (FMP) are termed perimenopause (Harlow et al., 2012). The menopausal transition is a time of extreme ﬂuctuations in hormonal levels. At early postmenopause, follicle-stimulating hor- mone (FSH) continues to rise, whereas estradiol continues to decrease until approximately two years following the FMP; at this time, stabilization of elevated FSH levels and reduced estradiol values

elevated FSH levels and reduced estradiol values occurs (Burger et al., 2007; Harlow et al., 2012). Some signiﬁcant pathophysiological changes may occur during the menopausal tran- sition and early postmenopause (Santoro et al., 2021), making these two periods important stages for the transformation of female health. A series of medical conditions including obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease (CVD), osteoporosis, anxiety, depression, dementia, and cancer, may

anxiety, depression, dementia, and cancer, may occur after meno- pause (Lobo and Gompel, 2022). Because the world population is rapidly aging and women tend to live longer than men (Ji et al., 2024b; Su et al., 2024), menopause can persist for approximately 30 years in some women (Brotman et al., 2014). Therefore, the management of menopause is highly important for healthy aging in females. Changes in the levels of female sex hormones play essential roles in modulating the microbiota, and the

roles in modulating the microbiota, and the microbiota interacts with sex hormones and is relevant to healthy aging in menopausal women. Over the last decade, the interaction between the vaginal microbiota and female healthy aging has been widely discussed. The vaginal microbiota is intimately related to vaginal health and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) (Geng et al., 2020; Łaniewski and Herbst-Kralovetz, 2022) and vaginal microbiota dysbiosis increases the susceptibility of women to

increases the susceptibility of women to atrophic vaginitis, bacterial vaginosis, and endometrial cancer (Lev-Sagie et al., 2019; Graham et al., 2021; France et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024). However, the relationships between the oral and gut microbiomes and menopause in healthy female individuals are often overlooked. Therefore, this review highlights the current insight into the role of the microbiome in menopause, focusing on alterations in the oral and gut microbiomes and microbial

in the oral and gut microbiomes and microbial crosstalk, and discusses associations between the microbiome and diseases related to menopause. The use of microbiome-targeting therapies for the precaution or treatment of diseases is also discussed. We aim to enhance the current comprehension of the interactions among the microbiota, female hormones, and healthy aging in women to facilitate the development of strategies for maintaining a healthy microbial community and promoting resilience in

microbial community and promoting resilience in older women. Oral microbiota and menopause Sex steroid hormones inﬂuence oral health through regulating oral host cells and the oral mucosa. The oral mucosa and salivary glands are sensitive to estrogen, and estrogen receptor-beta is observed in the oral cavity and gingiva, primarily in keratinocytes and salivary gland acinar and ductal cells (Valimaa et al., 2004). Age-related al- terations have also been observed in the buccal mucosal cells of

also been observed in the buccal mucosal cells of women, with a decrease in the nuclear diameter and cell diameter of mucosal cells in the 45e60-year age group (Donald et al., 2013) (Fig. 1A). Estrogen deﬁciency also impacts the maturation of the oral mucosal epithelium, which can lead to thinning and atrophy, increasing susceptibility to local injuries (Leimola-Virtanen et al., 1997; Meurman et al., 2009; Suri and Suri, 2014). Moreover, the salivary ﬂow rate is signiﬁcantly lower in

the salivary ﬂow rate is signiﬁcantly lower in postmenopausal women than in menstruating women (Mahesh et al., 2014). The above ﬁnd- ings provide clinical evidence for oral complaints, such as dry mouth and burning mouth, in postmenopausal women (Meurman et al., 2009; Mahesh et al., 2014). The teeth and gums are extremely sus- ceptible to any hormonal changes (Dutt et al., 2013). Fluctuations in sex hormone levels may increase the sensitivity of gums to plaque, thus causing changes in

of gums to plaque, thus causing changes in periodontal status (Mascarenhas et al., 2003; Suresh and Radfar, 2004). Along with alterations in hormone levels, concomitant osteoporosis in menopausal women may also be a risk factor for missing teeth and periodontitis (Esfahanian et al., 2012; Hernandez-Vigueras et al., 2016). Therefore, periodontitis is frequently observed in women during menopause (Hernandez- Vigueras et al., 2016). In addition to alterations in oral host cells and the oral mucosa

in oral host cells and the oral mucosa during menopause, the composition and behavior of the oral microbiome are remodeled (Cornejo Ulloa et al., 2021). Studies show that the incidences of some oral infectious diseases are higher in postmenopausal women than in premenopausal women, such as oral lichen planus (Mohan et al., 2017) and periodontitis (Agrawal et al., 2021; Ciesielska et al., 2021). The major etiological agents of the above diseases are oral pathogens, which indicates the potential

are oral pathogens, which indicates the potential relationship between estrogen and the oral microbiome. Alterations in hormone levels during menopause may favor the growth of peri- odontal pathogens, and certain Gram-negative bacteria, such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Tannerella forsythia, are the main pathogens responsible for periodontitis in postmenopausal women (Brennan et al., 2007a; Haas et al., 2009). Several early studies have examined certain periodontal pathogens from subgingival

certain periodontal pathogens from subgingival bioﬁlms and revealed some trends, such as increasing levels of Porphyr- omonas gingivalis with age (Rodenburg et al., 1990; Slots et al., 1990; Savitt and Kent, 1991). Recent cross-sectional studies have exam- ined the oral microbial composition of postmenopausal women (Brennan et al., 2007b; Hernandez-Vigueras et al., 2016) and have identiﬁed several periodontal pathogens, including Campylobacter rectus, Tannerella forsythia, Fusobacterium

rectus, Tannerella forsythia, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and Por- phyromonas gingivalis. Among postmenopausal women, measures of clinical periodontal disease have been found to be correlated with taxonomic differences in the diversity and composition of the sub- gingival microbiome (Genco et al., 2019), providing evidence of the pathogenesis of the periodontal microbiota. In addition to changes in the periodontal microbiota, the composition and behavior of other oral microbiota are altered during

of other oral microbiota are altered during menopause, but the impact on human health remains unknown. A decrease in the salivary ﬂow rate during menopause may disturb the homeostasis of the oral micro- biome (Nasidze et al., 2009, 2011; Belstrom et al., 2014), hence impacting oral health. A recent study of 117 postmenopausal women has revealed numerous correlations between the presence and quantity of several oral taxa and particular estrogens and estrogen metabolites (Wu et al., 2023);

and estrogen metabolites (Wu et al., 2023); however, further conﬁrmation is required to better understand the underlying mechanisms. Conclusions and perspectives The incidence of several chronic diseases increases after meno- pause, which impacts women’s quality of life. It is critical to fully understand the characteristics of the microbiota in healthy aging individuals to develop strategies for microbial modulation. The oral and gut microbiomes of women of reproductive age have been studied for decades; however, the menopausal phase has been understudied. Human studies have acknowledged the aging transi- tion of the oral

acknowledged the aging transi- tion of the oral and gut microbiomes during menopause, but small sample sizes and different detection methods impact the consis- tency of conclusions among studies. In addition, most studies on the microbiome and menopause have been performed among Cauca- sian populations. As geography, ethnicity, and social status all contribute to the diversity of the human microbiome, future studies need to enroll women from different backgrounds. Furthermore, no published

different backgrounds. Furthermore, no published research has focused on longitudinal individual trends in the oral and gut microbiomes during the menopausal transition, which may reduce interpersonal variations and help researchers examine whether alterations in microbial composition are expedited during the menopausal transition. The interplay between female sex hormones and the gut micro- biota is bidirectional and inﬂuences the health of women. The gut microbiome regulates circulating

women. The gut microbiome regulates circulating estrogens through the estro- bolome, and estrogen modulates the microbiome of the oral cavity and gut in return. The details of the gut-oral axis and its role during menopause need to be further explored. Few studies have collected samples from multiple sites; hence, there are gaps in understanding the crosstalk between the oral and gut microbiomes during meno- pause. Future studies need to investigate how this crosstalk affects the health of

how this crosstalk affects the health of women. Finally, MHT is not effective for all menopausal women; although there are a limited number of human intervention studies, probiotics, and prebiotics have shown positive effects on bone, cardiovascular system, adipose tissue, mental health, and breast. Therefore, these treatments represent convenient and safe management strategies for menopause-related diseases. Oral probiotics containing Lacto- bacillus ssp. plantarum, rhamnosus, and reuteri, as

ssp. plantarum, rhamnosus, and reuteri, as well as prebiotics containing isoﬂavones, have shown beneﬁcial effects on health, and they can be used alone or in combination with MHT as a therapeutic strategy. Dysbiosis of the oral ecosystem is related to a series of oral diseases, such as caries and periodontal disease during menopause, and it also interacts with the gut microbiota and contributes to sys- temic diseases. and proper eating habits in maintaining the homeostasis of the oral microbiota has been understudied in menopausal women, and the oral microbiome may be a potential therapeutic target for enhancing menopausal health. While microbiome-targeting therapies have shown potential beneﬁts for menopausal women, additional work should be done to promote the use of probiotics and prebiotics. Introduction Diabetes mellitus (DM) affects approximately 451 million in­ dividuals worldwide, with a steadily increasing prevalence across countries of various income levels [1]. Chronic exposure to blood glucose excess has been

Chronic exposure to blood glucose excess has been traditionally associated to adverse outcomes, including macrovascular (e.g., peripheral vascular diseases, coronary heart disease, stroke) and microvascular conditions (e.g. diabetic kidney disease, neuropathy and retinopathy) [2] as well as increased suscepti­ bility to infectious diseases [3]. Particularly, numerous studies have demonstrated remarkable links between DM and genitourinary infections (g-UTI), mainly among postmenopausal women.

(g-UTI), mainly among postmenopausal women. Indeed, hy­ perglycemia is thought to be a driver of infections among women affected by DM, representing one of major cause of functional disability. Consequently, quality of life and sexual health in these patients may be severely impaired [4]. The mechanistic pathways associated to the greater susceptibility to infections include a reduced T cell and neutrophil function and the impaired humoral immunity. A diminished production of interleukins

immunity. A diminished production of interleukins released by T cells, as IL1 and IL6, might be also implicated in the poor response to infections observed in diabetic patients [5]. Indeed, ovarian ageing is characterized by a progressive and

ageing is characterized by a progressive and sub­ stantial decline in estrogens production and a relative and slowly emerging androgens excess, thus resulting in the loss of estrogen pro­ tection against cardiometabolic disease. As hormonal rearrangement of menopause occurs, the rate of visceral fat deposition increases, while the lean mass and insulin sensitivity are reduced. These dynamics can trigger DM development [9]. Additionally, the menopausal transition is associated with genitourinary symptoms, such as vaginal dryness and atrophy, vulvar burning and recurrent g-UTI due to estrogen/androgen deficiency [8]. As part of the vaginal ecosystem, these bacteria may contribute to genitourinary complications, despite not reaching the 10^5 CFUs/mL threshold. Recent advances in microbial analysis through 16S rRNA sequencing have better clarified the substantial diversity that inhabits the female urinary tract. This complex biosystem, known as vaginal microbiome,

complex biosystem, known as vaginal microbiome, includes microorganisms, their genomes, and the surrounding environ­ ment [11]. With the occurrence of DM, the critical balance of vaginal ecosystem can be disrupted, as observed by its altered composition and pH levels, resulting in increased susceptibility to infections and inflammatory conditions [12]. Additionally, postmenopausal women affected by DM often experience sexual dysfunction due to various adverse factors such as the occurrence of

various adverse factors such as the occurrence of g-UTI, neurovascular diseases and psychological disorders. These complications contribute to decreased libido and dys­ pareunia, inadequate vaginal lubrication, arousal and orgasmic dysfunction, with detrimental effects on female sexual health [4]. Ulti­ mately, sexual dysfunction in women, as for men, can represent the clinical precocious expression of an increased cardiovascular disease [13]. This niche is commonly domi­ nated by a limited number of species of lactic acid bacteria (LAB), which vary at different life stages [11,14]. These LAB species significantly contribute to vaginal health through 1) a close adherence to the specialized epithelium, 2) the production of lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide, thereby regulating pH levels in response to menstrual and age- related estrogen fluctuations. This ensures a balance among resident species which collectively act as primary

species which collectively act as primary defense mechanism, promoting gynecological wellness [11,14]. Impaired sexual functioning is frequently accompanied by stress-induced comorbidities, including general anxiety and depression [62]. However, intensive lifestyle intervention and management of comorbidities can ameliorate sexuality in one-third of diabetic women by improving FSFI scores [63]. obesity and FSD requires an interdisciplinary approach that accounts for the complex interplay of metabolic, psychological, and social factors. Introduction Menopause is a critical biological and psychological transition in a woman's life, marked by the permanent cessation of

life, marked by the permanent cessation of menstruation. The average global age of menopause onset is 48.8 years, with regional variations inﬂuenced by genetic, socio-economic, and cultural factors. In Bangladesh, studies indicate a median menopausal age of 47.4 years in the eastern region and 46 years in the western region [1,2]. With increasing life expectancy, Bangladeshi women are spending a substantial portion of their lives in the postmenopausal phase, necessitating focused attention on

phase, necessitating focused attention on their health and well-being [3]. A growing body of global evidence highlights that menopausal women are at an increased risk of depressive symptoms [4].The prevalence of depressive symptoms during menopause varies across populations, inﬂuenced by ethnicity, socio-economic status, and lifestyle factors [5,6]. In Bangladesh, particularly in rural and low-income settings, limited healthcare access, socio-economic disadvantages, and poor nutritional

disadvantages, and poor nutritional awareness may exacerbate the risk of depression among menopausal women [7]. Diets rich in omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and B vitamins are associated with lower depressive symptoms, whereas those high in trans fats, reﬁned carbohydrates, and deﬁcient in essential nutrients are linked to increased depression risk [8,9]. However, while extensive global research supports these associations, studies speciﬁcally investigating the relationship between dietary

investigating the relationship between dietary intake and depressive symptoms in menopausal women within low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Bangladesh, remain limited [10]. Existing research in Bangladesh has primarily focused on menopausal symptom prevalence and overall nutritional status without adequately addressing dietary intake's impact on mental health during menopause [11,12]. To address this gap, this study was designed to determine the association between dietary

to determine the association between dietary patterns and depressive symptoms among menopausal women in Bangladesh. For this study, dietary intake is operationally deﬁned based on nutrient composition and food group consumption patterns, while depressive symptoms are assessed using standardized psychometric tools. Socio-economic status is categorized based on household income, education, and occupational status. We hypothesize that inadequate dietary intake signiﬁcantly contributes to

dietary intake signiﬁcantly contributes to depressive symptoms in menopausal women. The study objectives include assessing dietary patterns and socio-demographic factors and deter- mining their associations with depressive symptoms. Methodology Study design and settings This study employed a descriptive cross-sectional design to identify the association between dietary patterns and depressive symptoms among menopausal women. in two urban settings in Dhaka City: Mirpur-2 Jhilpar slum and Boshoti housing society during July 2024 to October 2024. Sample size and sampling technique The required sample size of 310 respondents was determined using the formula n ¼ z2pq/d2, where the prevalence (p) of menopausal women in Bangladesh was estimated at 23%, based on data from the Bangladesh Demographic Health Survey (BDHS) 2011 and 2014. A 95% conﬁdence interval and a 5% margin of error were applied to ensure statistical robustness. Systematic random sampling was employed to select participants, ensuring

was employed to select participants, ensuring equal representation from both study locations. The sam- pling interval (K) was determined by dividing the estimated number of eligible menopausal women in each study site by the required sample size for that area. In Mirpur Jhilpar slum, approximately 1,200 menopausal women were estimated, resulting in an interval of every 4th eligible woman being selected. In Boshoti housing society, with an estimated 800 menopausal women, an interval of every 3rd

800 menopausal women, an interval of every 3rd eligible woman was used. A random starting point was chosen in each area to ensure unbiased selection. Women residing in housing societies exhibited better nutritional habits, including higher consumption of fruits, dairy, and protein-rich foods. This dietary pattern may contribute to their lower levels of depressive symptoms. In contrast, slum

These ﬁndings align with global research demonstrating that nutrient-rich diets, particularly those high in omega-3 fatty acids, anti- oxidants, and essential vitamins, play a protective role against depression by reducing inﬂammation, oxidative stress, and neurotransmitter dysregulation [13,14]. Menopausal transition and mental health risks The menopausal transition itself did not differ signiﬁcantly between groups in terms of the average age of menopause. The biological underpinnings of menopause-related depression warrant further investigation, particularly in the context of socio- economic and lifestyle differences. Study limitations and future directions The cross-sectional design prevents us from establishing causal relationships between dietary intake, physical activity, and depressive symptoms. Future longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal dynamics of these associations.

the temporal dynamics of these associations. Additionally, the reliance on self-reported dietary data in- troduces the possibility of recall bias, which may affect the accuracy of our ﬁndings. Furthermore, this study did not account for genetic or hormonal inﬂuences, both of which play critical roles in depression during menopause. Incorporating biological markers alongside lifestyle factors in future research could offer a more comprehensive understanding of their interactions. Depression in

of their interactions. Depression in menopausal women is also shaped by a complex interplay of sociocultural, economic, and medical factors, including social stigma, limited healthcare access, ﬁnancial instability, and pre-existing medical conditions. To capture these nuanced inﬂuences, future studies should incorporate qualitative methodologies to explore the lived experiences of menopausal women. Such insights could inform the development of culturally sensitive dietary and mental health

of culturally sensitive dietary and mental health interventions tailored to their speciﬁc needs. The study primarily focused on women from a speciﬁc socioeconomic background. Expanding research to include higher-income groups could provide a more holistic understanding of the rela- tionship between socioeconomic status and depression in menopausal women. Lastly, body compo- sition was assessed using BMI, which, while commonly used, does not fully capture obesity-related risks. Future studies

capture obesity-related risks. Future studies should integrate additional anthropometric measures, such as body fat percentage and waist-to-hip ratio, to enhance our understanding of obesity's impact on mental health during menopause. Conclusion This study underscores the strong association between dietary intake, socioeconomic status, and depressive symptoms among menopausal women in Bangladesh. The stark disparities in nutrition and mental health outcomes between socioeconomic groups

health outcomes between socioeconomic groups highlight the urgent need for targeted in- terventions. Strategies such as dietary education programs, improved access to affordable nutrient-rich foods, and culturally adapted mental health services could signiﬁcantly improve the well-being of menopausal women, particularly those in underserved communities. Study design: This study was conducted on 1814 postmenopausal women from the population-based Rotterdam Study. Main outcome measures: Dietary patterns were identified using reduced rank regression. Response variables included bone mineral density, body composition parameters, lipid profile markers, insulin resistance, systolic blood

markers, insulin resistance, systolic blood pressure, cognitive function, depression, and sleep quality. The associations with risk of mortality were assessed using Cox proportional hazard models. Results: The first dietary pattern, characterized by higher intake of vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, coffee, tea, alcoholic beverages, and cheese, explained 2.95 % of the variation in responses, accounted for 12.11 % of the variation in general cognitive function captured by G-factor, 5.62 %

cognitive function captured by G-factor, 5.62 % in systolic blood pressure, and 4.13 % in bone mineral density, and was correlated with less adiposity, lower blood pressure, lipid markers, and insulin resistance. The second dietary pattern, characterized by higher intakes of processed meat, unprocessed red meat, poultry, eggs, and coffee, and lower intakes of sweets and tea, explained 1.54 % of the variation in responses, accounted for 5.45 % of variation in fat mass percentage, 3.47 % in lean

variation in fat mass percentage, 3.47 % in lean mass index, and 3.29 % in bone mineral density, and was correlated with higher adiposity, insulin resistance, and lipid markers. No as­ sociations with mortality risk were identified after adjusting for confounders such as demographics, socioeco­ nomic status, lifestyle, disease history, and medication use. Introduction Women's health is influenced by distinct life phases, such as preg­ nancy and menopause. Menopause is an important event, leading to hormonal and metabolic alterations affecting overall health [1,2]. Because of

affecting overall health [1,2]. Because of these changes, menopausal period is associated with higher prevalence and risk of several chronic diseases, including increased risk of dyslipidemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, dementia, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases (CVD) [1,3,4]. Additionally, several chronic conditions such as depression and dementia occur more in post­ menopausal women compared to men or women in premenopausal stage [5–9]. Lifestyle factors such as diet have a

[5–9]. Lifestyle factors such as diet have a fundamental role in maintaining health, and several studies have documented their role in improving menopausal health [10]. Also in postmenopausal stage, studies have shown the positive effect of several dietary components, such as lignans, phytoestrogen rich foods, protein, and plant oils on adiposity, glucose homeostasis, and blood lipids [11–14]. Given that nutrients or food items are not consumed isolated and there are potential synergistic and

isolated and there are potential synergistic and antagonistic effects between them [15,16], dietary pattern analysis might give more insight in optimal diets. Dietary patterns [17] involves two main approaches: hypothesis-driven scores (a priori) and explor­ atory patterns (a posteriori). A posteriori-derived patterns are identified in a specific study population, accounting for variations in response vari­ ables [17,18]. Using an a posteriori approach and consequently involving factors

approach and consequently involving factors important for the health status of postmenopausal women as responses, one can identify dietary patterns that might offer the maximum benefits to women during the postmenopausal stage, which in turn can be used for more targeted dietary recommendations. While some prior studies in postmenopausal women have explored the effects of dietary patterns on health outcomes, such as mortality and cardio­ vascular risk factors [19–22], the majority focused on

risk factors [19–22], the majority focused on known dietary patterns. Notably, none specifically identified patterns based on the health conditions of this population, taking into account the diverse health challenges individuals may encounter concurrently. In our current study, we integrated various factors that reflect major health issues related to postmenopausal women in identifying dietary patterns. These factors included bone mineral density, body composition parameters, lipid profile

body composition parameters, lipid profile markers, insulin resistance, blood pressure, cognitive function, depression, and sleep quality. Subsequently, we investigated whether the identified dietary patterns are associated with the risk of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. 2. Rotterdam Study incorporates three cohorts that were established in 1989, 2000, 2006, and 2015. 2.1. Study population Menopausal status was evaluated using a home interview question­ naire. We included all postmenopausal women with data on dietary intake and response variables of fifth visit of the first cohort (I-5, 2009–2011), third visit of the second cohort (II-3, 2011–2012), and first visit of the third cohort (III-1, 2006–2008). This FFQ

food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). This FFQ includes questions about the frequency and amount of con­ sumption of 389 food items per day, week or month in the previous year and was filled out at home. For the estimation of the portion sizes in grams, standardized household measures were applied. Dietary intake levels estimated from FFQ data were evaluated by comparison with di­ etary records and dietary histories in other Dutch study populations. These validation studies used earlier versions

These validation studies used earlier versions of the FFQ, developed using the same foundational methodology. Validation against three 3- day dietary records within a subgroup of a Dutch diet-cancer cohort [28] showed crude Pearson's correlation coefficients ranging from 0.40 to 0.86 for macronutrients and micronutrients. Another validation, against dietary histories covering the past four weeks [29], demon­ strated comparable results. These findings indicate that the FFQ has adequate to good

indicate that the FFQ has adequate to good ability to rank individuals by their intake levels. For the purpose of the dietary pattern analyses, all food items were categorized into 25 pre-defined food groups to reduce the complexity of dietary data [30–32], which were based on similarities in food source/ type (for example different of fats and oils), product composition (for example refined-grain and whole-grain products) or culinary use (for example ready meals). 2.3. Bone mineral density (gram/cm2), total lean mass (gram), and total fat mass (gram) were measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) using Lunar Prodigy densitometer (Rotterdam Study II-3 and III- 1) and Lunar iDXA densitometer (Rotterdam Study I-5). wore light clothes and no shoes. Total fat mass percentage was calculated by dividing total fat mass (kg) to weight (kg) multiplied by 100. Lean mass index was calculated dividing total lean mass by the square of height (kg/m2). A non-stretchable tape was used to measure waist circumference over the unclothed abdomen at the narrowest point between the lowest rib and the iliac crest. Fasting blood samples were obtained from all participants. Serum lipids and glucose were measured using automatic

lipids and glucose were measured using automatic enzyme procedures (Roche Diagnostic GmbH, Man­ nheim, DE). Insulin concentration was evaluated by an automatic immunoassay. HOMA-IR was calculated based on fasting blood glucose (mmol/L) × fasting insulin (mU/L) divided by 22.5 [38]. Blood pressure (mm Hg) was assessed by a random sphygmomanometer on the right arm after 5 min of rest when participants were in the seated mode. Systolic blood pressure were calculated as the mean of the two consec­

were calculated as the mean of the two consec­ utive measurements. For global cognition function, we summarized five tests, the 15-word learning test, the Stroop task, the letter-digit substi­ tution test, a word fluency test, the Purdue pegboard test, into s single score known as G-factor, which is the first component of a principal component analysis [39] and explained 50.6 % of the variance among the cognition tests.
