Data-analysis procedure To identify the dietary patterns, we applied the reduced rank regression approach to identify linear functions of predictors that simultaneously explain as much variation in the response variables as possible [17,48]. We used the intake of 25 food groups (gram/day) as predictors and TC/HDL,

food groups (gram/day) as predictors and TC/HDL, triglyceride, HOMA-IR, systolic blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, lean mass index, total fat mass percentage, bone mineral density, PSQI, G-factor, and CESD as response. Thus, we calculated linear functions of food group intakes (dietary patterns) that explain as much variation in the factors reflecting the major health issue in postmenopausal women. We used log-transformed triglyceride and HOMA-IR and the square root of PSQI and CESD scores to

and the square root of PSQI and CESD scores to normalize their distributions. Factor loadings represent the coefficients that indi­ cate the strength and direction of the relationship between each food group and the identified dietary pattern. For the interpretation of the identified patterns, we characterized and described the dietary patterns based on food groups with factor loadings ≥0.2 or ≤−0.2, as reported in previous studies [49–53]. However, to ensure transparency, the factor loadings

to ensure transparency, the factor loadings for all food groups are reported in Table 2. We used Pearson's correlation coefficients to assess the relation between the dietary pattern scores and response variables. The number of extracted dietary patterns using reduced rank regression is equal to the number of response variables [17]. Since the first few identified dietary patterns are optimal in the sense that no other linear function of predictors explains more response variation than them,

explains more response variation than them, the first two dietary patterns were retained for subsequent anal­ ysis in this study, as reported in previous studies [54–60]. Additionally, according the visual inspection of the rank trace plot, the first two di­ etary patterns accounted for the most amount of explained variation while maintaining relatively low model complexity (Fig. S1). We investigated the associations between adherence to these two dietary patterns and risk of all-cause and CVD

dietary patterns and risk of all-cause and CVD mortality using Cox proportional hazard models (per standard deviation increase and ter­ tiles). In model 1, associations were adjusted for age, energy intake, and sub-cohorts of the Rotterdam Study. Model 2 was additionally adjusted for physical activity, smoking status, education level and employment status. Model 3 was additionally adjusted for body mass index, intake of lipid lowering medication, anti-hypertensive medication, and anti- diabetic

anti-hypertensive medication, and anti- diabetic medication, and prevalence of CVD at baseline. Missing data on covariates were imputed using multivariate impu­ tation by chained equations (mice) with 5 imputations and 20 iterations. The proportion of missing values in the variables was as follows: 7.17 % for physical activity, 1.43 % for education, 1.27 % for coronary heart disease, and <1 % for heart failure, employee status, and medication use. Analyses were performed on each imputed dataset

Analyses were performed on each imputed dataset and the results are presented as pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with 95 % confidence in­ tervals (95 % CI). A two-sided p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed in RStudio software [61], version 1.3.1056 (R version: 4.0.5) using packages “rrr” [62], “mice” [63] and “survival” [64]. 3. Discussion We identified dietary patterns that accounted for the variation in factors related to major health conditions in postmenopausal women, including bone mineral density, body composition, lipid profile, insulin resistance, systolic blood pressure, cognitive function, depression, and sleep

cognitive function, depression, and sleep quality. While these patterns explained up to 12.1 % of the vari­ ation in individual health factors, their collective explanation for the combined health factors was <5 %. The subsequent analysis on adher­ ence to these patterns showed no association with the risk of cardio­ vascular and all-cause mortality. As women transition into the postmenopausal phase, there is a notable decline in estrogen production by the ovaries and increase in iron levels.

by the ovaries and increase in iron levels. This shift may lead to a higher susceptibility in post­ menopausal women to heart diseases, osteoporosis, and dyslipidemia [3,66–68]. At postmenopausal stage, women also experience a redistribution of body fat that favors an increase in abdominal fat [69] compared to premenopausal women [70]. Furthermore, post­ menopausal women are more susceptible to depression, cognitive impairment, osteoporosis, and sleep disturbances compared to age- matched men

sleep disturbances compared to age- matched men or women at younger ages [5–8,71–74]. So, this popula­ tion may require and get most benefit from dietary recommendations targeted at these health conditions. This study is the first to identify dietary patterns in postmenopausal women using a holistic approach, taking into account various health conditions within this population, rather than focusing on a single outcome. This approach acknowledges that individuals may experience multiple health

that individuals may experience multiple health conditions simultaneously. We derived the dietary pat­ terns using reduced rank regression as a posteriori approach. Unlike a priori dietary patterns based on existing knowledge, this method helps identify dietary patterns, incorporating health-related factors within the population. The identified dietary patterns shared some similarities with a pos­ teriori patterns in other populations of postmenopausal women, that were derived based on

postmenopausal women, that were derived based on variation in food intake rather than health fac­ tors, using principal component or factor analysis. Our first identified pattern shares similarities with a more Prudent pattern, including higher intake of vegetables, whole grain, and legumes; while the higher factor loadings of unprocessed red meat and processed meat in the second identified pattern make it more similar to a Western dietary pattern [75–77]. Conclusion We identified dietary patterns integrating multiple factors related to postmenopausal health. The first pattern, predominantly featured higher intake of whole grains, vegetables, nuts, and beverages, while the second one was characterized by elevated

the second one was characterized by elevated consumption of processed and unprocessed red meat, poultry, and coffee, with lower tea and sweets intake. While these patterns showed moderate explanatory power for certain individual response variables, the combined explained variation was low. No association of the dietary patterns with the risk of prema­ ture mortality was found in our study population. This suggests that the identified patterns might be more predictive of specific health risks

might be more predictive of specific health risks among postmenopausal women. Future studies should delve into whether these identified dietary patterns could mitigate risk of diseases and enhance overall postmenopausal health. Introduction Proteins and polyphenols are key components in the food system. They contribute to the nutritional quality and functional properties of food products. Protein-polyphenol complexes, formed via non-covalent and/or covalent interactions, occur naturally and can be designed to enhance the stability, functionality,

designed to enhance the stability, functionality, and bioactivity of these compo­ nents. These interactions influence protein structure, polyphenol sta­ bility, and the overall quality of food products, with factors such as temperature, pH, and the physicochemical properties of proteins and polyphenols playing critical roles (Khalifa et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021). Vitexin, a polyphenol widely known for its many biological activities including, antioxidant, neuron-protection,

including, antioxidant, neuron-protection, cardio-protection, glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism and liver function, anti-inflammation, anti-cancer, anti-bacterial, and anti-virus from both in vitro and in vivo studies (Peng et al., 2021; Sae-tan et al., 2020). However, vitexin has poor water solubility (37.2 mg/L) and low bioavailability, which lead to the difficulty in food application (Wu et al., 2021). Encapsulation is one of the techniques that has been used to improve solubility,

that has been used to improve solubility, thermal stability, bioaccessibility, and antioxidant activity of target compounds. A recent study reported that vitexin-loaded phytosome nanoparticles had higher bioaccessibility, antioxidant activity, and thermal stability compared to free vitexin (Peanparkdee & Yooying, 2023). However, limited research has explored how encapsulated vitexin interacts with proteins under thermal processing conditions, a key consideration for industrial food

a key consideration for industrial food applications. In a real food system, thermal treatments such as pasteurization and sterilization are important unit operations in food processing. They are essential for food safety and shelf-life extension but can significantly alter the structural and functional properties of proteins and poly­ phenols. Up to date, the information about the effects of thermal treat­ ments on the complexes between proteins and polyphenols is limited and inconclusive.

and polyphenols is limited and inconclusive. Some studies showed that thermal treatment pro­ moted the oxidation of polyphenols and reduced antioxidant activity (Quan et al., 2019). On the contrary, some studies showed that higher temperatures strengthened the interaction between proteins and poly­ phenols, which could stabilize the bioactivity and bioavailability of polyphenols (Condict et al., 2019a; He et al., 2016b). * Corresponding author. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the effects of thermal treatments (pasteurization and sterilization) on the structural and functional properties of soy protein isolate (SPI) and whey protein isolate (WPI) when combined with vitexin or vitexin-loaded phytosomes. These proteins were chosen in this study due to their widespread use in food products. The concentration of vitexin in the study corresponded to the Thai recommended daily intake for

to the Thai recommended daily intake for poly­ phenols (500–1500 mg/day) (Bureau of Nutrition, 2020). This study focuses on key physicochemical parameters (particle size, PDI, ζ-po­ tential, and protein structure) and biofunctional properties (antioxidant activity, bioaccessibility, and protein digestibility) before and after digestion. The findings of this study aim to clarify the role of thermal treat­ ments in modulating protein-polyphenol interactions and their impli­ cations for functional

and their impli­ cations for functional food design. By highlighting the interplay between processing, digestion, and biofunctional properties, this work provides foundational insights for developing thermally stable functional foods enriched with proteins and polyphenols. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Chemicals and reagents Soy protein isolate (SPI) and whey protein isolate (WPI) (90 %w/w of protein) were kindly provided by Nutrition SC Co., Ltd. (Nakhonpa­ thom, Thailand). Free vitexin

Ltd. (Nakhonpa­ thom, Thailand). Free vitexin (commercial grade) was purchased from Chengdu Biopurify Phytochemicals Ltd., (Chengdu, China). Vitexin (HPLC grade) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Other reagents and chemicals used in the study were of analytical grade. 2.2. Vitexin-loaded phytosome nanoparticles (V-PHN) preparation V-PHN were prepared according to the previous study (Peanparkdee & Yooying, 2023). Briefly, 43.24 mg of free vitexin (commercial grade) and 78.61

mg of free vitexin (commercial grade) and 78.61 mg of phosphatidylcholine (PC) were dissolved separately in 50 mL of methanol and stirred for 5 min. Then, vitexin and PC solutions were mixed and stirred for 30 min. The mixed solution was kept at 4 ◦C for 18 h. After incubation, the mixed solution was evaporated at 50 ◦C in a rotary evaporator (Buchi R300, Flawil, Switzerland) until thin dry films were formed. HPLC-grade vitexin was used to quantify the con­ centration of vitexin in free vitexin

the con­ centration of vitexin in free vitexin and vitexin-loaded phytosome nanoparticles. 2.3. Sample preparation The samples were prepared by dispersing 5 % w/v of SPI or WPI in distilled (DI) water to achieve S or W. Free vitexin particles were added to S or W at the concentration 104 mg/100 mL to achieve SV or WV. Vitexin-loaded phytosome nanoparticles were added to S or W at the concentration 510.2 mg/100 mL to achieve SV-PHN or WV-PHN. The final concentrations of vitexin in the SV, WV,

final concentrations of vitexin in the SV, WV, SV-PHN, and WV-PHN were equal and based on the recommended daily intake for Thais (Nutrition, 2020). S, SV, SV-PHN, W, WV, and WV-PHN were prepared and shaken well for 5 min at room temperature before thermal treatments. 2.4. Thermal processes All six samples (S, SV, SV-PHN, W, WV, and WV-PHN) were sub­ jected to a non-thermal process (25 ◦C), pasteurization process (65 ◦C for 30 min in a water bath), and sterilization process (121 ◦C for 15 min in

and sterilization process (121 ◦C for 15 min in a pressure steam sterilizer). After thermal processing, the samples were quickly cooled to room temperature and stored at −20 ◦C until analyzed. The frozen samples were thawed at room temperature (25 ◦C) for 10–15 min before analysis. 2.5. Particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and ζ-potential Particle size, PDI, and ζ-potential were determined using Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments Co. Ltd., Worcestershire, UK). Samples were diluted 100

Worcestershire, UK). Samples were diluted 100 times and the measurements were conducted at 25 ◦C. 2.6. Circular dichroism (CD) spectrum measurement The secondary structure changes of protein were determined using a CD spectrometer (Jasco J-815, Jasco Corp., Tokyo, Japan) between 190 and 260 nm with 3 replications. The samples were diluted with DI water to achieve 0.1 mg/mL protein concentration and DI water was used as the blank for all samples. The scan rate was 50 nm/min, with a band­ width

The scan rate was 50 nm/min, with a band­ width of 1 nm at 25 ◦C. The BeStSel was used to determine the per­ centage of secondary structure content. 2.7. Intrinsic emission fluorescence spectrum measurement The fluorescence spectra were recorded using a spectrofluorometer (Jasco FP-6200, Japan Spectroscopic Co., Tokyo, Japan). A quartz cuvette with a 1 cm optical path was used. The excitation wavelength was 285 nm. Both the excitation and emission slit widths were 5 nm. The spectra were

emission slit widths were 5 nm. The spectra were recorded between 300 and 490 nm. The background fluorescence was calibrated using DI water. 2.8. Introduction Ageing is linked to an increased risk of developing long-term con­ ditions including dementia and cognitive decline (Daviglus et al., 2010). According to estimates, there are over 50 million cases of dementia worldwide, and by 2030, that number is predicted to rise to ~82 million cases (World Health Organisation, 2019). These conditions have far- reaching effects on people's lives and finances,

reaching effects on people's lives and finances, including decreased ca­ pacity for daily living (Giebel et al., 2015), shorter life expectancies (Mooldijk et al., 2022), and a greater financial and emotional strain on families and carers (Kasper et al., 2015). Meta-analyses suggest that age- related cognitive impairment may be linked to sarcopenia (Chang et al., 2016; Cipolli et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2020), the decline in skeletal muscle mass (SMM), strength, and physical function with age

(SMM), strength, and physical function with age (Cruz- Jentoft et al., 2019). This association may be explained by common pathologies of both conditions, which include decreases in growth hormones, insulin resistance, and chronic systemic inflammation (Chang et al., 2016). Accordingly, strategies that curb sarcopenia may also assist in mitigating age-related declines in cognitive function. Resistance exercise (RE) is well established as a strategy for reducing the progression and associated

for reducing the progression and associated effects of sarcopenia (Phillips and Mar­ tinson, 2019). Several studies have also reported improvements in cognitive function following RE, including enhanced executive function (Anderson-Hanley et al., 2010; Best et al., 2015; Ikudome et al., 2017; Liu-Ambrose et al., 2010; Yoon et al., 2018), memory (Best et al., 2015; Cassilhas et al., 2007; Coelho-Júnior et al., 2020; Ikudome et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2019), and global cognitive function

et al., 2019), and global cognitive function (Coelho-Júnior et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2014; Smolarek et al., 2016). Increases in circulating concentrations of different neurobiological markers, such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as well as decreased cortisol secretion and inflammation, are thought to be associated with exercise-induced improvements in cognitive function (Ahlskog et al., 2011; Cassilhas et al., 2007; Erickson et al.,

2011; Cassilhas et al., 2007; Erickson et al., 2011; Liu-Ambrose et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2014, 2015; Walsh et al., 2016). In addition to RE, in order to prevent sarcopenia, it is advised that older adults consume higher amounts of dietary protein (Phillips and Martinson, 2019). Research also indicates that consuming more dietary protein may help to postpone the cognitive deterioration that comes with ageing (Coelho-Júnior et al., 2021; van de Rest et al., 2013; Yeh et al., 2022). Rest et al., 2013; Yeh et al., 2022). Increased dietary protein intake in older adults has been reported to acutely improve memory (Kaplan et al., 2001) and in the long-term, improve reaction time, memory, and emotion identification (Charlton et al., 2016; Kita et al., 2019; Lefferts et al., 2020; van der Zwaluw et al., 2014). Protein-induced improvements in cognition are thought to be caused by elevated brain insulin receptor signalling stimulation (Frazier et al., 2019), reduced inflammation

(Frazier et al., 2019), reduced inflammation and increased IGF-1 (Bordoni et al., 2017; Journel et al., 2012), and increased avail­ ability of brain neurotransmitters (van de Rest et al., 2013). Recent randomised-controlled trials suggest that RE and increased dietary protein intake may interact to suppress age-related cognitive decline, whilst synergistically improving reaction time, executive func­ tion, memory, and processing speed compared to RE alone (Bell et al., 2019; Rondanelli et al.,

RE alone (Bell et al., 2019; Rondanelli et al., 2020). Conversely, others have not observed augmented effects (Formica et al., 2020; Mundell et al., 2022; van de Rest et al., 2014); though, van de Rest et al. (2014) did report a syner­ gistic effect on information processing speed compared to protein sup­ plementation alone. The observed inconsistencies may be attributed to the participants' habitual protein intake, variations in daily dosage, and deviations in dietary protein intake from

and deviations in dietary protein intake from baseline. In studies that re­ ported null findings (Formica et al., 2020; Mundell et al., 2022; van de Rest et al., 2014), habitual protein intake was sufficient (1.0–1.3 g/kg/ d) according to consensus groups (Bauer et al., 2013; Deutz et al., 2014) and was increased during the intervention period by ≤0.3 g/kg/d. Contrastingly, whilst Rondanelli et al. (2020) increased dietary protein intake by a similar magnitude to these studies (0.3 g/kg/d),

and to investigate the individual and combined effects on neurobiological, inflammatory and insulin sensitivity biomarkers, and diurnal salivary cortisol, to explore mecha­ nisms of action. Discussion This study investigated the individual and combined effects of 12 weeks of RE and whey protein supplementation on cognitive function in older men and explored potential mechanisms of action. The main findings were: i) whey protein supplementation significantly improved executive function compared to a carbohydrate control; ii) RE did not improve any domain of cognitive function compared to no exercise, with processing speed (incongruency

no exercise, with processing speed (incongruency cost) worsening; iii) no synergistic ef­ fects of RE combined with whey protein supplementation were observed; iv) outcomes related to sarcopenia (muscle strength and physical function) positively correlated with several cognitive function domains at baseline; however, only changes in SMI and episodic memory correlated at 12 weeks; and v) whilst RE significantly reduced systemic inflammation, no significant between-group changes in other

no significant between-group changes in other biomarkers occurred and changes did not correlate with changes in cognitive function. 4.1. Whey protein supplementation Whey protein supplementation significantly improved executive function compared to a carbohydrate control. The improvement in ex­ ecutive function following increased dietary protein intake agrees with previous work (Muth and Park, 2021). Whilst no significant between- group differences were observed for working memory or global

were observed for working memory or global cogni­ tive function, clinically relevant (>0.5 SD (Crichton et al., 2012)) within-group increases were observed in the whey protein supplemen­ tation group, suggesting that although not statistically significant compared to a carbohydrate control, these improvements may be clin­ ically meaningful. Previous acute (Kaplan et al., 2001) and longitudinal studies (Charlton et al., 2016; Kita et al., 2019; Lefferts et al., 2020; van der Zwaluw et al., 2014)

et al., 2020; van der Zwaluw et al., 2014) are consistent with the clinically significant improvement in working memory; however, cognitive benefits have not been observed by others (Bell et al., 2019; Moran et al., 2018; Zajac et al., 2019). Inconsistencies may be explained by variations in the particular study groups, the length of the intervention, and the protein dosage utilised. In support, two studies (Bell et al., 2019; Zajac et al., 2019) that did not find benefits from higher dietary

that did not find benefits from higher dietary protein intake examined the effects over a period of 6–8 weeks, which, according to earlier research, was probably insufficient to stimulate longitudinal changes in cognitive function (Vellas et al., 2008). Furthermore, only 8 g of whey protein was present in the multi-ingredient supplement that Moran et al. (2018) examined, whilst dietary intake data from study participants by van der Zwaluw et al. (2014) showed an increase in protein intake of

The dose of protein supplemented in these studies may therefore have been insufficient to yield changes in cognitive function; though, no dose-response study has yet to be con­ ducted to determine the optimal daily intake of protein to improve cognitive function in older adults. Mechanisms of action Potential mechanisms through which RE and increased dietary pro­ tein intake are purported to improve cognitive function include, but are not limited to, increases in various growth and

not limited to, increases in various growth and neurotrophic factors, decreases in inflammation and cortisol secretion, and improved insulin sensitivity (Ahlskog et al., 2011; Camfield et al., 2011; Liu-Ambrose et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2016). Meta-analyses also suggest a relationship between sarcopenia outcomes (SMM, strength and function) and cognitive function (Chang et al., 2016; Cipolli et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2020), likely explained by common pathologies of both

likely explained by common pathologies of both conditions. Interestingly, baseline correlation data from the present study coincides with these meta-analyses, with significant correlations observed between muscle strength and physical function outcomes and domains of cognitive function. However, whilst fat-free mass, muscle strength and physical function outcomes were improved in this cohort, particularly following RE but also gait speed following whey protein supplementation, as previously

whey protein supplementation, as previously reported (Griffen et al., 2022a), changes in most of these outcomes did not correlate with changes in cognitive function domain scores, and only a significant positive correlation was observed between changes in SMI and episodic memory. This finding highlights the importance of maintenance of SMM for cognitive health. Furthermore, whilst systemic inflammation decreased (Griffen et al., 2022a) and insulin sensitivity (derived from QUICKI) increased

sensitivity (derived from QUICKI) increased (Griffen et al., 2023b) following RE and whey protein supplementation, respec­ tively, RE failed to improve cognitive function and whilst whey protein supplementation did improve executive function, no changes in bio­ markers correlated with cognitive function domains. No between-group differences in fasting BDNF or IGF-1, or salivary cortisol indicies also occurred, and in fact, BDNF decreased over the 12-week intervention period following both RE

the 12-week intervention period following both RE and whey protein supplementation. Conse­ quently, the findings of this study imply mechanistic changes in cogni­ tive function in this cohort were not due to changes in the aforementioned purported mechanisms. Instead, as amplified brain in­ sulin receptor signalling stimulation (Frazier et al., 2019) and increased brain neurotransmitter availability (van de Rest et al., 2013) have been purported to contribute to protein-induced improvements in

to contribute to protein-induced improvements in cognitive function, we cannot rule out these mechanisms contributed to improved cognitive function following whey protein supplementation. However, due to not measuring these outcomes in this study, this cannot be confirmed. Analysis of these outcomes should therefore be prioritised in future work. 4.5. Strengths and limitations Our study has several strengths, including the comprehensive assessment of multiple domains of cognitive function under

of multiple domains of cognitive function under highly controlled conditions in a population of older men and measurement of a wide array of biomarkers to explore potential mechanisms of action, including the comprehensive measurement of the acute-chronic-acute effects on BDNF, which, to our knowledge, has not been investigated previously following RE and whey protein supplementation. Due to the robustness of our methods, the results presented in this study reliably add to the current evidence

this study reliably add to the current evidence base. Limitations of this study include investigation of relatively healthy participants who already had high levels of physical and cognitive functioning prior to recruitment and were generally well educated. Further limitations include the use of pooled data for the main analyses, which may have impacted the indi­ vidual effects of RE and whey protein supplementation; the small sample size to determine between-group cognitive effects,

Theoretical and practical implications, applications, and recommendations for future research The results of this study have important theoretical and practical implications and applications. From a theoretical

implications and applications. From a theoretical perspective, the results further build the evidence base for a role of dietary protein intake (at a dose of ~1.6 g/kg/d incorporating high-quality protein sources such as whey protein) as a nutritional strategy to slow cognitive decline with ageing. Consequently, the findings provide preliminary evidence to allow researchers to investigate such an intervention on a larger scale which may have a significant impact on future dietary guidelines.

significant impact on future dietary guidelines. Additionally, as the mechanisms of action for improved cognitive function following whey protein supplementation could not be confirmed in the present study, this study highlights a research gap to allow researchers to investigate to further build the evidence base. As no effect of high intensity RE on cognitive function was observed in the present study, hypothesised to be due to reduced habitual physical ac­ tivity, this contributes

habitual physical ac­ tivity, this contributes significantly to the literature that there may be a fine balance of RE intensity to maximise overall health in older age (e.g., physical and cognitive function), which should be examined in future work. From a practical perspective, these findings provide evidence to healthcare professionals and the general population that consuming a high protein diet (~1.6 g/kg/d), focussing on increased intakes at breakfast and lunch where intake is suboptimal

at breakfast and lunch where intake is suboptimal in older adults (Griffen et al., 2022a), is feasible in healthy older adults and may promote improved cognitive health, particularly executive functioning. There­ fore, such an intervention, or recommendations to increase protein in­ takes at these meals, should be promoted and may be a beneficial strategy to curb cognitive decline with age. To further build the evidence base, additional research is warranted including a larger sample size over

is warranted including a larger sample size over a longer duration of ≥6 months with an emphasis on dose to determine optimum thresholds of RE and whey protein supplementation to provide improved cognitive outcomes. As previously mentioned, additional research to determine mechanisms of action is also warranted. Moreover, over recent years, there has been a rapidly increasing global interest in reducing animal-derived products and increasing plant-based food consumption, for various reasons,

food consumption, for various reasons, including sustainability, religious/cultural, animal welfare, health, and personal preference reasons (Delsoglio et al., 2023; Griffen et al., 2023a, 2023c). However, whilst the effects of plant-based proteins on cognitive function are beginning to be investigated, the effects are relatively unexplored and further research is warranted. 5. Conclusion Twice daily ingestion of whey protein supplementation for 12 weeks is an effective stimulus to elicit

for 12 weeks is an effective stimulus to elicit improvements in cognitive function, specifically executive function. This data reinforces the importance of dietary protein to support healthy ageing. Twice weekly RE, at an in­ tensity of 80 % 1RM, had no positive effects on cognitive function and no synergistic effects occurred. Finally, changes in cognitive function do­ mains did not correlate with changes in neurobiological, inflammatory, or insulin sensitivity markers but change in SMI

or insulin sensitivity markers but change in SMI correlated with change in episodic memory. This emphasises the importance of maintenance of SMM with age. Introduction Curdlan is a microbial, high-molecular-weight carbohydrate poly­ mer consisting of glucose monomers linked by β-1,3-glycosidic bonds (Chaudhari et al., 2021). This exopolysaccharide was first obtained in the 1960s, and it is still of great interest in the food industry, environ­ mental protection, pharmacy, and medicine (Ganie, Rather, & Li, 2022).

and medicine (Ganie, Rather, & Li, 2022). Curdlan owes its popularity thanks to its rheological, biological, and gel- forming properties (Aquinas, Bhat, & Selvaraj, 2022; Chen & Wang, 2020). The most commonly used gels are those obtained by thermal incubation of its aqueous suspension above 90 ◦C. These colourless, odourless, and non-toxic hydrogels have been successfully applied as a component of food products, drug carriers (Klimek, Benko, Pałka, Lud­ wiczuk, & Ginalska, 2019; Tong et al.,

Lud­ wiczuk, & Ginalska, 2019; Tong et al., 2020; Zhang & Edgar, 2014) or biomaterials for applications in regenerative medicine (Belcarz et al., 2013; Przekora et al., 2017; Wojcik et al., 2021). However, curdlan- based biomaterials obtained using the thermal method are charac­ terised by relatively poor mechanical properties and low cytocompati­ bility in vitro (Klimek et al., 2017). Conclusions Biomaterials based on curdlan hydrogel, obtained by thermal incu­ bation of its aqueous suspension (especially above 90 ◦C), have great interest among scientists. Therefore, new scientific reports are still being developed. In

scientific reports are still being developed. In this work, we decided to compare the properties of two hydrogels – (i) consisting only of curdlan and (ii) consisting of curdlan with WPI – and determine which of them has a greater biomedical po­ tential. Taking into account all the obtained results, we determined that: 1. The surface of the curdlan hydrogel exhibits hydrophobic properties and adsorbs more proteins but changes their conformation (or to a lesser extent protects them from

(or to a lesser extent protects them from unfavourable changes); 2. The surface of the curdlan/WPI hydrogel exhibits greater roughness and hydrophilicity but also enhances proteins adsorption in their native conformation; 3. The surface of the curdlan hydrogel does not support the growth of human chondrocytes and osteoblasts and also induces a greater in­ flammatory response in human macrophages; 4. The surface of the curdlan/WPI hydrogel not only promotes the growth of human chondrocytes and

promotes the growth of human chondrocytes and osteoblasts but also induces significantly less inflammation in human macrophages; 5. Unlike curdlan hydrogel, curdlan/WPI hydrogel enhances regener­ ative properties in vivo via the promotion of re-growth of the amputated caudal fin of zebrafish larvae; 6. Curdlan/WPI hydrogel has greater biomedical potential as an im­ plantation biomaterial compared to curdlan hydrogel. CRediT authorship contribution statement Katarzyna Klimek: Writing – review &

Background & Aims: The loss of ovarian functions deﬁning menopause leads to profound metabolic changes and heightens the risk of developing metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Although estrogens primarily act on the female liver through estrogen receptor alpha (ERa), the speciﬁc contribution of impaired ERa signaling in triggering MASLD after menopause remains unclear. Methods: To address this gap in knowledge, we compared the liver transcriptomes of sham-operated

the liver transcriptomes of sham-operated (SHAM) and ovariecto- mized (OVX) control and liver ERa knockout (LERKO) female mice by performing RNA-Seq analysis. Results: OVX led to 1426 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the liver of control mice compared to 245 DEGs in LERKO mice. Gene ontology analysis revealed a distinct ovariectomy-induced modulation of the liver transcriptome in LERKO compared with controls, indicating that hepatic ERa is functional and necessary for the complete

ERa is functional and necessary for the complete reprogramming of liver metabolism in response to estrogen depletion. Additionally, we observed an ovariectomy-dependent induction of male-biased genes, especially in the liver of control females, pointing to hepatic ERa involvement in the masculinization of the liver after estrogen loss. To investigate the translational relevance of such ﬁndings, we assessed liver samples from a cohort of 60 severely obese individuals (51 women; 9 men). Notably,

MASLD can progress to severe liver condi- tions and is closely linked with other cardiometabolic dis- eases.1,2 However, after menopause, changes in estrogen levels predispose women to hepatic steatosis, nullifying sex differences in MASLD susceptibility.3,4 Estrogens predominantly exert their effects in the female liver through estrogen receptor alpha (ERa), whose signaling concurs to modulate the hepatic metabolism according to each reproductive stage.5,6 Such

according to each reproductive stage.5,6 Such a regulatory role of hepatic ERa in metabolism and reproduction,5–8 has likely been acquired through evolution,9,10 and contributes to sex differences in MASLD susceptibility. Indeed, when exposed to a diet rich in lipids, fertile female mice exhibit a greater ability, which is largely dependent on hepatic ERa, to limit liver lipid deposition compared with males.11 Nevertheless, estrogen’ deprivation impairs hepatic lipid metabolism and promotes

impairs hepatic lipid metabolism and promotes lipid accumu- lation in mouse models of menopause.5,12 Given its relevance in the regulation of hepatic metabolism, estrogen supplementation has the potential to mitigate dysme- tabolism and prevent liver lipid accumulation in women after menopause.13 Although hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can be beneﬁcial, it cannot be considered a primary approach to counteract MASLD in post-menopausal women. Indeed, the restricted window of opportunity (<10

Indeed, the restricted window of opportunity (<10 years after menopause), the individual beneﬁt:risk ratio, and the low HRT prescription rate and uptake,14 limit this approach. Because women spend more than one-third of their lives in the post-menopausal state15 and the global burden of metabolic diseases and MASLD,16,17 the search for valuable alternative(s) to the classical estrogen-based HRT is of utmost importance for women’s health. Estrogen loss following ovariectomy surpasses the changes observed in the hepatic transcriptome due to the simple lack of hepatic ERa, a ﬁnding not surprising, as estrogen deﬁciency affects the entire organism, including signaling pathways in organs cross-talking with the liver. It could be hypothesized that the absence of hepatic ERa represents an intermediate phenotype between the SHAM and OVX mice, while most of ovariectomy-induced changes in the liver transcriptome may be ascribable

in the liver transcriptome may be ascribable to factors other than ERa in hepatocytes. How- ever, if ovariectomy-induced changes were primarily hepatic ERa-independent, we would expect similar changes in CTRL and LERKO after ovariectomy. Nonetheless, the ovariectomy- induced changes were limited in LERKO mice and exhibited signiﬁcant differences compared with CTRL mice (Fig. 3), arguing against this hypothesis. In our study, ovariectomy led to the over-expression of genes involved in lipid

to the over-expression of genes involved in lipid storage and deposition in the liver of both genotypes. An intriguing hypothesis suggests that he- patic ERa might enhance the transcription of male-biased genes by facilitating the binding of STAT5B and coactivators, like the glucocorticoid receptor (GR), to DNA,35 potentially through an ‘assisted loading’ mechanism.36 Supporting this, some of the male-biased genes (Cyp7b1, Hsd3b5, Mups, Serpin1e) upregulated by OVX in CTRL mice but not or to a lesser extent in LERKO mice are known to be responsive to GR.37,38 In the absence of estrogens, hepatic

to GR.37,38 In the absence of estrogens, hepatic ERa can be activated by various factors and extracellular signals, including AA, growth factors, and cytokines.7,39 The cross-talk between ERa and the insulin signaling pathway (INS) represents one potential mecha- nism involved in this process. Besides classical activation, STAT5B can also be activated through phosphorylation by the insulin receptor (IR) or downstream components of INS.40 Studies in mice treated with agonist/antagonist for GR

In this study, the comparison between OVX and SHAM mice was limited to the estrus phase characterized by low estrogen levels, to speciﬁcally assess the broader impact of long-term es- trogen deﬁciency on hepatic gene expression. We cannot rule out that several other or more marked differences may

that several other or more marked differences may exist during different phases of the estrous cycle, particularly at proestrus when estrogen levels are the highest. It is also possible that the timing and duration of ovariectomy may contribute to some of the observed differences, while other differences may be masked. Considering the role of hepatic ERa in sensing nutritional status, it is plausible to speculate that liver reprogramming may be inﬂu- enced by various nutritional conditions.

Despite all these limitations, it is most noteworthy that liver transcriptomics conﬁrmed that MASLD in obese women was associated with a similar shift toward a male- like metabolic proﬁle in key genes. These results are concordant with several clinical observations that have reported sexual hor- mone abnormalities and dysfunctions, including masculinization/ defeminization, in women with liver diseases.43–45

in women with liver diseases.43–45 To our knowl- edge, however, this is the ﬁrst study reporting a masculinization of liver transcriptome in obese women with MASLD. Since the Liver Biopsy Cohort did not include information on the hormonal status of participants, we utilized the age of 51 years as a cutoff to distinguish between pre- or post- menopausal stages, following guidelines from the Endocrine Society. We observed a masculinization of the liver tran- scriptome speciﬁcally in women with

liver tran- scriptome speciﬁcally in women with MASLD, particularly pronounced in those aged >−51 years. Notably, obese women JHEP Reports, October 2024. vol. 6 j 101143 9 Research article <51 years without MASLD did not exhibit liver masculinization. In our experimental mouse model, the complete liver mascu- linization was due to estrogen loss and relies on hepatic ERa. Consequently, our ﬁndings suggest that, besides obesity, the impairment of hepatic ERa signaling following menopause may

of hepatic ERa signaling following menopause may serve as a primary factor driving liver masculinization and the development of MASLD in women. In summary, this study unravels the peculiar role of hepatic ERa signaling in fully mediating the reprogramming of the fe- male liver following estrogen loss toward a male-like proﬁle, modelling MASLD development in women after menopause and, thereby, pointing to hepatic ERa as a valuable target for precision pharmacological therapy approach for post-

Introduction Human milk (HM) is the primary source of nutrition for newborns and is essential for their growth and development. The World Health Organization advocates for HM as the sole source of nutrition for infants up to the first six months after birth and recommends continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods for at least two years (World Health Organization (WHO),

least two years (World Health Organization (WHO), 2023). Thanks to its unique composition of nutritional elements, immune and anti-infective factors, and enzymes, HM covers the crucial developmental needs of early life. HM contains various proteins with physiological functions, such as providing nutrition, antibacterial properties, immune regulation, and promoting digestion and absorption. These proteins can be categorized into three main groups based on their composition: casein, whey pro­

based on their composition: casein, whey pro­ teins, and milk fat globule membrane proteins. Whey proteins, which comprise approximately 60 %–80 % of the total protein content in HM, are the most abundant protein component in HM (Meng et al., 2021). Structurally, whey proteins in HM are characterized by small, tightly packed spherical formations with strong hydrating ability and high dispersibility. These proteins are present in HM as high-molecular- weight protein solutions and can easily

weight protein solutions and can easily dissolve in acidic environ­ ments, facilitating absorption in infants (Zhao et al., 2022). Whey pro­ teins are also rich in essential amino acids, particularly branched-chain amino acids, which play a crucial role in protein regulation, glucose balance, and lipid metabolism (Wang & Guo, 2013). Whey proteins have various health benefits, including antioxidative, antimicrobial, anti­ cancer, antitumor, immunomodulatory, gut-barrier protective, and gut

immunomodulatory, gut-barrier protective, and gut health-promoting effects (Ahmed et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2024). With the rapid advancements in early-life nutrition, HM continues to be a subject of interest in various research fields. As an indispensable protein component of HM, whey proteins, not only directly influence infant physical development but also play a crucial role in establishing and maturing the infant’s immune system. Currently, research on the functions of HM whey protein may

research on the functions of HM whey protein may be predominantly focused on some well-known aspects, such as common functions like nutrient supply and immunomodulation. Nevertheless, HM whey protein also possesses several potential functions. Main components of HM whey proteins and their functions The whey-to-casein ratios in HM vary throughout the lactation period. Specifically, the proportion of whey protein diminishes from approximately 90 % during the colostrum stage (0–5 days postpartum) to around 65 % during the transition milk stage (6–15 days postpartum),

the transition milk stage (6–15 days postpartum), and subsequently stabilizes at approximately 60 % (L¨onnerdal et al., 2017). The key components of whey proteins in HM include alpha- lactalbumin (α-lactalbumin), lactoferrin (LF), secretory IgA (sIgA), osteopontin (OPN), lysozyme (Lyz), and growth factors (Fig. 1). 2.1. α-Lactalbumin α-Lactalbumin in HM weighs approximately 14.1 kDa and comprises 123 amino acids and four disulfide bonds. As the predominant protein in HM, α-lactalbumin

As the predominant protein in HM, α-lactalbumin constitutes 41 % of whey proteins and 28 % of total proteins. Structurally, α-lactalbumin is a major calcium-binding milk protein, with strong calcium-binding sites capable of interacting not only with Ca2+ but also with other divalent metal ions such as Mg2+, Sr2+, Zn2+, and Cu2+, thereby aiding the absorption of essential min­ erals. Concurrently, the interaction between α-lactalbumin and metal ions alters the intrinsic characteristics of the

ions alters the intrinsic characteristics of the α-lactalbumin structure, function, and stability (Permyakov, 2020). Furthermore, α-lactalbumin contains some essential amino acids that are crucial for meeting the developmental needs of infants. For example, tryptophan in α-lactal­ bumin can enhance infant sleep and affect neurobehavioral develop­ ment (Layman et al., 2018). Functionally, α-lactalbumin is a component of the lactose synthase complex and acts as a regulator of galactosyl­

complex and acts as a regulator of galactosyl­ transferase, thereby regulating lactose synthesis (Permyakov, 2020). Furthermore, the enzymatic hydrolysates of α-lactalbumin exhibit antibacterial properties and effectively inhibit the biological activity of pathogenic bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Salmonella, thereby effectively preventing invasive bacterial infections in the gastrointes­ tinal tract of newborns (Brück et al., 2006). Factors affecting whey proteins in HM Breastfeeding plays an important role in neonatal health and growth. HM composition is subject to various influences, such as maternal diet, lifestyle, physical condition changes, and infant development. These factors collectively shape the nutritional composition of HM, ensuring that it meets the evolving needs of newborns. Variations in the

the evolving needs of newborns. Variations in the nutrient content and composition of HM can adapt to the needs of infants at various stages, thus offering them optimal nutrition and protection. The composition of whey proteins, as critical nutritional components of HM, is influenced by various factors, including maternal, infant, temporal, and spatial factors (Table A.1; Fig. 2). Studies on the influence of maternal factors on whey protein composition have mainly focused on the mother’s

composition have mainly focused on the mother’s physical condition during pregnancy, age at childbirth, mode of delivery, parity, and postpartum weight loss. Infant factors include gestational age, sex, and weight changes. Moreover, the lacta­ tion period, geographical location, and living environment also signifi­ cantly affect HM whey protein content. Understanding these factors and taking appropriate measures to enhance the stability of HM quality and production is of paramount importance

quality and production is of paramount importance for ensuring the newborns’ health and growth. 3.1. Maternal factors 3.1.1. Anthropometric indicators The characteristics of HM are closely linked to the status of its pro­ vider, i.e., the lactating mother. Every mother is a unique individual, with variations in age, height, and weight, among other parameters. In recent years, a trend of delayed childbirth has been observed, resulting in decreased childbirth rates in younger women and increased

childbirth rates in younger women and increased childbirth rates in older women. Maternal age is one of the main factors affecting HM protein content. The total protein concentration in the colostrum of women aged ≥30 is relatively low but increases in mature milk content (Zhang et al., 2021). Furthermore, as maternal age rises, OPN concen­ tration in HM also increases (Zhang et al., 2021), whereas sIgA con­ centration decreases (Groer et al., 2004). Firstly, whey protein exerts a positive facilitating effect on the brain development of infants. Nevertheless, the specific mechanism underlying this positive impact remains ambiguous. Whey protein occupies a crucial position in

Whey protein occupies a crucial position in the regulation of the intestinal microbiota. However, the question of whether whey protein can influence brain development by modulating gut microbiota is still awaiting further research and exploration. Sec­ ondly, there are still no clear patterns regarding the impact of maternal individual differences, physical conditions, and dietary habits on HM whey protein. Further in-depth research by investigators is required, especially research on the

is required, especially research on the influence of diet, to provide a scientific basis for mothers to better feed infants. Meanwhile, current research on the differences in the composition and function of HM whey protein among different races and regions is still incomplete. In view of this, more HM samples from various regions and races should be widely collected to conduct systematic research on the differences in whey protein. Through in-depth analysis of the unique properties of HM whey

analysis of the unique properties of HM whey protein of mothers from different races and regions, more targeted and scientifi­ cally based suggestions for infant feeding can be provided to meet the diverse demands of infant feeding. Finally, in light of the fact that other milk sources have relatively low production capacities and are thus unable to meet the market demands, their high prices have dampened consumers’ purchasing desires. Consequently, bovine milk remains the principal raw

bovine milk remains the principal raw material for infant formula. Hence, the most crucial research direction on how to process bovine milk whey protein is currently to reduce the allergenicity of bovine milk and enhance its digestibility. Based on the distinctive attributes of whey proteins from milk sources other than bovine milk, researchers can conduct in-depth exploration and exploitation of their superiority to engineer infant for­ mula that more precisely complies with specific

mula that more precisely complies with specific requisites. This is conducive to providing infants with more optimal immune protection and growth support, while simultaneously addressing the knowledge gap in the current infant formula market related to special needs conditions. MENOPAUSE HORMONE THERAPY MHT is currently indicated for the treatment of VMS, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, the preven- tion of bone loss and reduction of fracture risk. MHT consists of oral, transdermal, and vaginal formula- tions (which include both systemic and low-dose vaginal preparations). Women with an intact uterus should not receive estrogen therapy alone as this

should not receive estrogen therapy alone as this in- creases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and can- cer. Instead, their MHT should also include a progestin or a SERM (selective-estrogen receptor modulator) with antagonist effects on the endome- trium. Because of ﬁrst pass hepatic metabolism, oral formulations are associated with an increased risk of hypertriglyceridemia, VTE, and elevated high- sensitivity C-reactive protein. Transdermal and vaginal estrogen, by contrast, circumvents

and vaginal estrogen, by contrast, circumvents hepatic metabolism. While no large-scale randomized trials have assessed the relative safety of transdermal compared to oral estrogens, available evidence and observational studies suggest that transdermal op- tions may pose less risk of VTE and stroke than oral estrogens.74-76 The consideration of transdermal route of delivery for those with moderate risk for CVD is recommended by current MHT position statements. CONCLUSIONS The MT is a time of accelerated CVD risk that is often underdiagnosed and undertreated. It is important to recognize the cardiometabolic shifts and accelerated biological aging along with the multi-organ, social, and psychological changes that converge during this time. This is an important part of clinical competency during cardiovascular, internal medicine, obstetrics and

cardiovascular, internal medicine, obstetrics and gynecology, sleep medicine, and psychiatry training and is often not addressed during medical school, residency and fellowship training, or in formalized curricula for allied health care pro- fessionals. Given most medical specialties will encounter women undergoing this universal life transition, a baseline awareness and basic compe- tency in timely recognition, prompt diagnosis, and early referral to subspecialties when needed is important.

to subspecialties when needed is important. This manuscript can serve as a guide for any clinician participating in the care of a menopause patient. The management of the MT should not fall solely on gynecologists, and a multidisciplinary team- based, patient-centered approach is needed to address the optimal care that women deserve. treatments. 1. Introduction Heat treatment is an essential process to ensure the safety of milk products and is broadly divided into low-temperature and high- temperature methods (Dash et al., 2022). Low-temperature treatments (below 100 ◦C), commonly used to produce pasteurized milk, are traditionally believed to preserve the best nutritional and flavor quali- ties (Liu et al., 2020). In contrast, high-temperature treatments (above 100 ◦C), such as ultra-high temperature (UHT, 135–150 ◦C) and

as ultra-high temperature (UHT, 135–150 ◦C) and spray- drying temperature (SDT, above 150 ◦C), are more commonly employed in milk processing. These methods can eliminate virtually all microorganisms, including heat-resistant bacteria and spores in milk, thereby significantly extending the shelf-life of dairy products. Howev- er, such heat treatment can induce various changes in the physico- chemical properties of milk constituents (Liao, Liu, & Ku, 2017; Moatsou, 2023), including the

Liu, & Ku, 2017; Moatsou, 2023), including the denaturation of proteins, interactions between the denatured proteins and the casein micelles, non-enzymatic browning, and the conversions of soluble calcium, magnesium and phosphate to the colloidal state (Tarhan & Kaya, 2021). These alter- ations can reduce the milk’s nutritional and functional qualities. Despite these impacts, few studies have focused on the composition and function of whey proteins through high-temperature treatments. Milk

through high-temperature treatments. Milk mainly contains two types of proteins: casein (80%) and whey protein (20%) (Tarhan & Kaya, 2021; Goulding, Fox, & O’Mahony, 2020). Casein is a heat-stable protein group that does not aggregate during or after heating; in contrast, whey protein, which includes active components like β-lactoglobulin, α-lactalbumin, and immunoglobulins, is heat-sensitive (Donato & Fanny Guyomarc’h., 2009). Upon exposure to high temperatures, whey proteins irreversibly

to high temperatures, whey proteins irreversibly denature and coagulate. Although whey proteins comprise a smaller proportion of milk proteins, they are crucial in enhancing immune functions, promoting gut health, and possessing insulin -otropic and glucose-lowering properties (ˇCurlej et al., 2022). Furthermore, the peptides and amino acids generated from the digestion of whey protein in the gastrointestinal tract stimulated the release of several gut hormones, such as cholecystokinin, peptide

gut hormones, such as cholecystokinin, peptide Y⋅Y, the incretins gastric inhibitory peptide, and glucagon-like peptide one that potentiate the secretion of insulin from β-cells associated with regulation of food intake (Duca, Waise, Peppler, & Lam, 2021). Despite the prevalence of high-temperature processed milk products like UHT milk and milk powder, there is a gap in research regarding the thermal stability of whey proteins derived from milk, especially goat milk (Ali et al., 2021). Discussion Milk proteins are susceptible to temperature treatments, whether above or below zero. (Regardless of whether the temperature is above or below zero). Notably, protein denaturation caused by heat treatment is more complex, including gathering, glycosylation,

more complex, including gathering, glycosylation, and hydrolysis. The present SDS-PAGE analysis indicated that SDT treatment almost completely damaged all the macromolecules in whey protein compared to the control and UHTIS treatment. This is consistent with previous findings on cheese whey from goat milk treated at 65 ◦C for 30 min, 80 ◦C for 5 min, or 90 ◦C for 5 min (Huang et al., 2023), also consistent with another previous research on the soluble proteins in reconstituted milk exposed to

soluble proteins in reconstituted milk exposed to at 75 ◦C or 85 ◦C or 90 ◦C for 20 min (Hamouda et al., 2022; Moatsou, 2023; Zhang, Wang, Lu, Kong and Ge, 2023), suggesting that both SDT and low-temperature treatments could initiate the hy- drolysis of milk proteins, meanwhile all of which could lead to the destruction of most active proteins in both whey and milk powders. Furtherly, the present work showed that treatment lowered the con- centration of whey protein; this could be ascribed to

of whey protein; this could be ascribed to the hydrolysis of the part of whey proteins. Further, the current Venn analysis demonstrated that UHTIS treat- ment caused a certain degree of damage (roughly 6%) to whey protein. Still, most did not change, similar to the previous work on whey proteins (Zhang et al., 2024; Akhlaghi, 2024; Krishna et al., 2021). Meanwhile, the current work of the tree graph of samples clustering showed the same group shared with almost identical protein patterns,

shared with almost identical protein patterns, suggesting UHTIS treatment indeed affected the composition of whey protein, consistently with the previous works (Rosendo-Silva, Viana, Carvalho, Reis, & Matafome, 2023; Zhang, Hao, et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023). Meanwhile, the present work showed that the content of the whey protein marked decreased in UHTIS treatment group. So, it concluded that UHTIS treatment altered the profile of whey protein because of the hydrolysis of some whey

protein because of the hydrolysis of some whey proteins. Though the UHTIS treatment had a light impact on the whey proteins from goat milk, it could affect some metabolic pathways human body, similar to a study on the role of proteins playing in health and disease (Wang et al., 2023; Gobena, Admassu, Kinde, & Gessese, 2024). These changes of metabolic pathways may be caused by the essential amino acids, including valine, leucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, methionine,

tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine, and histidine, as well as the whey proteins themselves and their degraded peptides. The present results showed that the diameter of whey protein par- ticles treated with UHTIS and SDTIS increased, consistent with previous works on heat-treated protein (Gobena et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023); this may be due to whey protein aggregation and gelation. Aggregation and gelation of globular proteins are readily induced by heating that renders

are readily induced by heating that renders the peptide chain, especially in the beta-sheets more mobile, allowing amino acids to interact with and bind to other proteins (Saguer, Alvarez, Sedman, & Ismail, 2013; Nicolai, 2019; Sabbagh, Muhamad, Niazmand, Dikshit, & Kim, 2022; Yan et al., 2023). Therefore, UHT liquid dairy products should be homogenized after heat treatment to prevent protein from precipitation during shelf-time. Lactose, a unique carbohydrate in human and mammalian milk, is a

carbohydrate in human and mammalian milk, is a disaccharide composed of glucose and galactose. Based on the reduc- ibility of glucose, glycation of whey protein during heating should be considered (Han et al., 2024; Ozturk et al., 2024). The molecular docking results indicated that the carbonyl ammonia reaction between whey protein and lactose may occur. Dairy products subject to high- temperature treatment, especially for a long time, may produce a certain amount of protein glycosylation,

a certain amount of protein glycosylation, which may cause allergic re- actions in some human bodies (Beck et al., 2015). Consequently, the optimal combination of temperature and time for milk processing has been extensively studied to maximize the preservation of milk’s inherent components, such as using high temperatures for short durations. 5. Conclusion Whey protein contains many immune-active proteins and is sensitive to heat treatment. Both UHTIS and SDTIS treatments cause the whey

Both UHTIS and SDTIS treatments cause the whey protein particles to enlarge due to partial agglomeration, with SDT treatment notably leading to significant degradation of macromolecular whey proteins. After UHTIS treatment, Pfam annotations identified 426 proteins, including 386 common proteins and 16 unique proteins in the UHTIS-treated group and 24 in the control group, respectively. The UHTIS treatment increased the levels of 55 whey proteins and decreased 98 whey proteins, with nearly half

and decreased 98 whey proteins, with nearly half of the whey proteins experiencing changes in concentration in the UHTIS-treated group. Additionally, UHTIS-treated whey proteins may influence three metabolic pathways positively while negatively impacting one. scale epidemiological studies3 several of the main risk factors for CVD, such as low cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), arterial hypertension, obesity, and hypercholesterolemia are substantiated to increase during the menopause transition. Finally, sarcopenia and altered muscle metabolism may additionally occur in women at midlife.4 Exercise-training (ET) is a cornerstone in the pre­ vention and treatment of CVD,5 however, long-term studies based on real-life manageable conditions are not only

on real-life manageable conditions are not only lacking but fully absent. However, these studies are required to reach the highest level of evi­ dence for the recommendations of exercise as medicine.6 Soccer training can be described as a motivating, fun and social multicomponent ET form with broadspectrum fitness and health effects for untrained adults across the lifespan as well as for specific patients’ groups.7–10 Recreational soccer training performed for an hour twice weekly for 12–16

performed for an hour twice weekly for 12–16 weeks has at meta-analysis level been substantiated to induce clinically relevant improvements in CRF,11,12 arterial blood pressure (BP), body composition and blood lipid profile.13 Moreover, soccer training has been demonstrated to markedly upregulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial function in middle-aged women.14 Finally, a recent meta-analysis on 81 randomized controlled trials (RCTs)15 con­ cludes that multicomponent complex ET appears to be

that multicomponent complex ET appears to be superior to con­ ventional endurance, resistance or high intensity interval ET alone in improving cardiometabolic health. However, the majority of the RCT’s used in the meta-analyses mentioned above are short-term trials, and do not exhibit the long-term impact of complex ET modes in women entering menopause. A few long-term ET trials have been conducted using multicompo­ nent complex training approaches. Recently 75-year-old males partici­ pated in

Recently 75-year-old males partici­ pated in floorball training for a five-year period with an ET <2 times weekly with improvements in exercise performance and body fat con­ tent compared to inactive controls.16 Moreover, men aged 71 years diagnosed with prostate cancer did improve bone mineralization and functional capacity compared to inactive controls, but did not improve VO2max, BP and blood lipid profile after five years of soccer training.17 These types of long-term trials are limited or

These types of long-term trials are limited or to our knowledge non- existing in women. In 2013 on the Faroe Islands, an archipelago in the North Atlantic with ~55,000 inhabitants, middle-aged sedentary women with mild hypertension were recruited to a four-arm RCT, evaluating the broad- spectrum health effects of 15-weeks of soccer or two swim-in­ terventions.18 The soccer intervention was extended to 1 years of ET, and since the original cohort has been training continuously for 9 consecutive

has been training continuously for 9 consecutive years, a 9-year follow-up study was planned. Since the participant group were premenopausal and around 45 years old when the baseline measurements were done, nearly all of them have now entered menopause, which provides an opportunity to study the effect of multicomponent complex ET on CV health with increasing age as well as during the transition into menopause. Thus, the principal purpose of the study was to test the hypothesis that regular and

study was to test the hypothesis that regular and consistent multicomponent ET maintains car­ diometabolic health profile during a 9-year period in middle-aged women with mild hypertension. A secondary exploratory aim was to evaluate the hypothesis that cardiometabolic health can be preserved with regular ET with increasing age and during the transition into menopause. Methods Participants Middle-aged women (n = 25) participated in this 9-year long follow- up RCT. Originally, in 2013, 85

long follow- up RCT. Originally, in 2013, 85 sedentary premenopausal women with moderate hypertension were recruited. This original cohort was selected among 262 volunteers based on training history, medication, BP and body mass index (BMI) after a detailed screening.19,20 Of the 85 participants, which all meet the inclusion criteria, forty-four were randomly assigned to two different swimming groups as part of another study,20 while 41 took part in a soccer training study lasting 15 weeks (19)

in a soccer training study lasting 15 weeks (19) with a follow-up after 1 year.21 The 41 participants were originally randomized into a soccer training group (EX, n = 21) and a control group (CON, n = 20), and the participants in each of these groups remained in the same groups and are also part of the present study (CON, n = 20). Of the 41 initial participants, 25 were included in the present study (EX: n = 12 and CON: n = 13; Table 1). The twelve participants in the SOC-group have since

twelve participants in the SOC-group have since March–April 2013 to March–April 2022 participated in regular soccer-training session, while the CON-group had not been taken part in regular ET over the 9-yr long intervention period, which was evident in questionnaires (data not shown). Originally, the sample size was chosen based on the ET responses observed in the pri­ mary end points (arterial blood pressure and body composition) in similar training studies. studies. experimental procedures and associated risks, all participants gave their written consent to take part in the study both in 2013 and in 2022. Experimental design The study is a follow-up RCT where the original selection criteria were: Sedentary lifestyle for the last 2 years (no participation in regular ET or physical activity); mild hypertension [mean arterial pressure (MAP) > 95 mmHg]; and BMI >25 kg/m2. Randomization was done by card drawing first selecting four groups and thereafter

first selecting four groups and thereafter randomizing the groups to the different interventions. The original 41 participants were randomized into two groups in 2013, i.e. a soccer training group con­ ducting multicomponent exercise training (EX) and an inactive control group (CON). EX (n = 12) took part in the long-term recreational soccer training as well as pre- and post-testing. Throughout the 9-year inter­ vention period, four weekly 1-h training sessions were organized tar­ geting a

training sessions were organized tar­ geting a minimum of 2 weekly ET sessions for each of the participants. ET attendance was recorded during the entire 9-yr period. The partici­ pants in CON did not take part in regular physical training during the 9- yr period, which was shown in questionaries conducted during the follow-up testing. From the original EX-sample two participants dropped out during the first year, while six others dropped out during the next eight years, while one participant,

the next eight years, while one participant, who still is playing, did not volunteer to the 9-yr follow-up testing resulting in a final sample of twelve par­ ticipants. The entire original CON-group was invited to take part in the 9-yr follow-up and thirteen out of original twenty volunteered. In EX 11 out of 12 entered menopause during the intervention period, while in CON this was the case in 11 out of 13 participants. All the participants performed an intermittent endurance test with heart

an intermittent endurance test with heart rate recordings and had their BP, body composition and blood profile assessed, and a muscle biopsy taken at baseline and at the 9-year follow-up time-point. The primary endpoints were arterial BP, blood lipid profile and body fat content, while the secondary end points were lean body mass, skeletal muscle oxidative capacity, fasting blood glucose, resting and submaxi­ mal heart rates, as well as CRF. Training intervention EX performed an average of 1.7

intervention EX performed an average of 1.7 ± 0.6 (±SD) (range: 0.8–2.7) 1-h small-sided soccer training sessions per week during the 9-yr interven­ tion period, corresponding to a total of 796 ± 275 (range: 374–1264) 1- h small-sided soccer training sessions during the 9-yr intervention period. Training sessions were organized during the entire year including holiday periods. Four sessions were held each week (three on M. Mohr et al. Progress in Cardiovascular Diseases 85 (2024) 54–62 56

in Cardiovascular Diseases 85 (2024) 54–62 56 weekdays and one at the weekend). Each session lasted 1 h and consisted of a 10-min warm-up period followed by 4 × 12 min of small-sided soccer games (4v4–8v8), as previously described.19 A trained soccer coach was present during all ET sessions to control the duration of the training, ensure competitive games and record training attendance during the first year of training. During the remaining eight years two players were made responsible for

eight years two players were made responsible for training every week and training attendance was registered. Mean and peak heart rate during a training session after 9 years were 140 ± 13 and 164 ± 10 bpm corresponding to 81.1 ± 10.1 and 95.7 ± 9.7% HRmax, respectively. Relative heart rate loading was the same as training during the monitored sessions in the initial period of training and in a session 9 years later.19 Total distance covered, high intensity running distance and sprinting during

intensity running distance and sprinting during training were 4309 ± 636, 220 ± 124 and 51 ± 41 m, respectively, while 571 ± 127 and 608 ± 103 ac­ celerations were performed. BP measurements The participants reported at the hospital at 8.00 a.m. after an over­ night fast and rested in a supine position for 2 h. Systolic BP (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) were measured according to standard procedures using an automatic BP monitor (HEM-709; OMRON, IL, US) once every 30 min over the 2-h resting

IL, US) once every 30 min over the 2-h resting period. The average of the four measure­ ments was used as the test result. MAP was calculated as 1/3 SBP + 2/3 DBP. Resting heart rate (RHR) was measured during the same time in­ tervals as for BP. Resting blood sampling Resting blood was collected under standardized conditions from an antecubital vein between 7 and 8 a.m. after an overnight fast using the venepuncture technique. The blood sample was rapidly centrifuged for 30 s and the plasma was

rapidly centrifuged for 30 s and the plasma was collected and analyzed by an automatic analyzer (Cobas Fara, Roche, City, France) using enzymatic kits (Roche Diagnostics, City, Germany) to determine plasma total cholesterol (TC), low density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high density lipoprotein cholesterol(HDL–C), triglycerides(TG), glucose, vitamin D and c-reac­ tive protein (CRP). body mass (LBM) were evaluated by total- body DXA scanning (Norland XR-800, Norland Corporation, Oslo, Nor­ way). The body was segmented in accordance with standard procedures to evaluate regional tissue distribution and all analyses were performed using Illuminatus DXA software (Norland Corporation, Oslo, Norway). The effective radiation dose was <0.2 mSv per scan. Exercise performance testing The Yo-Yo intermittent endurance test level 1 (Yo-Yo IE1), a marker of cardiorespiratory fitness

Discussion The present trial recruited middle-aged sedentary women with mild hypertension for an exercise intervention in 2013; and after regular weekly multicomponent (soccer) training for 9 consecutive years, a follow-up experiment was performed comparing the cardiometabolic health profile of the ET group with the original

health profile of the ET group with the original controls. The principal findings of this long-term ET intervention were that regular multicom­ ponent training counteracts the detrimental effects of aging around the age of the menopause transition on cardiometabolic health status for hypertensive women. The participants in the soccer group had lower arterial BP compared to the inactive controls, along with a maintenance of body mass, BMI, body fat content in the soccer group compared to marked

content in the soccer group compared to marked increases for the controls. Moreover, 9 years of regular multicomponent exercise training lowered both TC and LDL-C with the inactive controls dis­ playing a diverging significant increase. CRF was additionally improved in the ET group in contrast to a large decline in the controls. LBM was increased in the intervention group only, and fasting plasma glucose was maintained, while a marked increase in fasting plasma glucose occurred in the control

in fasting plasma glucose occurred in the control group over the 9-year period. Finally, both groups pooled together displayed a potentially age-induced change in skeletal muscle metabolic profile. The alterations and diverging patterns between the ET group and the inactive controls occurred over a 9-year period where a vast majority of the women entered menopause, leading us to conclude that the participation in 800 multicomponent training sessions almost Fig. 2. An interesting finding was the opposite change in TC and LDL-C in the intervention group and controls. The ET group demonstrated a decline of 0.4 and 0.5 mmol⋅L−1 in LDL and TC after 9 years of ET, while the control group flaunted an increase of 0.4 and 0.7 mmol⋅L−1, respectively. These finding have clinical value, since dyslipidemia is well-known

clinical value, since dyslipidemia is well-known to be associated with atherosclerotic plaque formation, as well as the inflammatory processes that provoke plaque destabilization resulting in subsequent CVD event, and part of the elevated risk of developing CVD after menopause is likely to be associated with estrogen deficiency and dysregulated lipid metabolism.30,31 Estrogens exert a protective role in the CV system and are mainly synthesized in the ovaries via a process that uses LDL-C as

in the ovaries via a process that uses LDL-C as substrate. However, circulatory LDL cannot be utilized to synthesize estrogen during menopause, thereby resulting in reduced estrogen production.
