Women in these critical life stages have distinct and specific nutritional needs. Not only is adequate nutrition important for the health of women of childbearing age but also

the health of women of childbearing age but also crucial for infants’ neurodevelopment from conception through pregnancy and for the first 2 y of life (8, 25). Key nutrients that support neurodevelopment include zinc, choline, folate, iodine, and vitamins A, D, B-6, and B-12 (25). Adequate intake of DHA is also critical for infants’ brain development during the intrauterine period (26). In addition, WCBA require more iron than do WMENO due to menstrual iron losses in fertile women and increased

iron losses in fertile women and increased blood volume in pregnant women (27). As women age, there is an association between nutritional intakes with ovarian reserve and the timing of menopause (28). For WMENO, the decline in estrogen production and increase in resorption of calcium can increase risk of bone fractures (18). Thus, adequate intakes of calcium and vitamin D are essential for optimal bone health in women at this life stage (18, 29). Given specific nutritional needs for WCBA and

Given specific nutritional needs for WCBA and WMENO, understanding nutritional intakes for women in these life stages is critical to best tailor dietary recommendations for optimal health. Despite dietary guidance, the majority of Americans have inadequate intakes of at least 1 vitamin or mineral in their diet (1–3). Of emphasis, the 2015–2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans identified “shortfall nutrients” with high prevalence of inadequate intakes (1). Analysis of NHANES nutrient intake data

(1). Analysis of NHANES nutrient intake data (2009–2012) showed that ≥25% of adults aged 19–70 y consume (from food only) below the EAR or AI for choline, calcium, magnesium, and vitamins A, C, D, and E (7). Similarly, our data show that WCBA and WMENO are not meeting the dietary recommendations for calcium, magnesium, and vitamins A, C, D, and E. A separate study found that in addition to these shortfall nutrients, a significant number of pregnant women are not meeting nutritional

of pregnant women are not meeting nutritional recommendations for iron (8). Here, we found that more WCBA are at risk for inadequate amounts of iron compared with WMENO. In contrast, we found that as women transitioned from early perimenopause (ages 40–50 y) to postmenopause (ages 51–65 y), nutrient gaps were higher for vitamin B-6 and calcium, suggesting specific guidance is needed for WMENO to meet nutritional needs. Thus, we conclude that women of various ages are not obtaining the vital

women of various ages are not obtaining the vital nutrients they need from their diets alone. The use of dietary supplements has been shown to help increase nutrient intake, reduce inadequacies, and is associated with more favorable health and lifestyle choices (2, 4–6, 30). Indeed, more than half of American adults use dietary supplements (30) to improve and/or maintain overall health (31). Regular supplement usage is associated with higher nutrient intakes and lower inadequacies, particularly

intakes and lower inadequacies, particularly for vitamins A, B-6, B-12, C, D, and E (4–6, 32). Importantly, supplement usage does not substantially increase the risk of nutrient overconsumption (6). Introduction Sarcopenia is the insipid age-related decline in skeletal lean muscle mass and muscle function, increasing the risk of falls, fractures, physical disability, and immobility (Therakomen, Petchlorlian, and Lakananurak 2020). The precise understanding of the etiology of

The precise understanding of the etiology of sarcopenia remains unknown. Physically active individuals do not tend to become sarco­ penic, and inactivity or decreased activity seems to contribute to sar­ copenic muscle loss (DeVito et al. 2022). This muscle disease progresses slowly, beginning as early as the fourth decade of life (Evans 1996; Paddon-Jones and Rasmussen 2009). The disease is potentiated by the inability of anabolic stimuli such as dietary protein to stimulate muscle protein

as dietary protein to stimulate muscle protein synthesis (MPS), a phenomenon termed anabolic resistance (Phillips et al. 2017; Brook et al. 2016; Smeuninx et al. 2017; Mitchell et al. 2017; Moore et al. 2015; Lima et al. 2023). Anabolic resistance may be reversed by inhibiting de novo ceramide synthesis to restore mitochondrial and protein homeostasis in muscle aging (Lima et al. 2023). Other adverse outcomes are strongly linked to sarcopenia, for example, frailty and chronic diseases like

for example, frailty and chronic diseases like type-2 diabetes, further reducing one’s quality of life and leading to premature death (Phillips et al. 2017; Therakomen, Petchlorlian, and Lakananurak 2020; Verreijen et al. 2015b; Lima et al. 2023; Reidy et al. 2020). The age-related loss of muscle mass and function is intrinsic to aging, and the prevalence of sarcopenia is expected to rise, with estimations suggesting it affects ~5-13% of persons aged 60 y and up to 50% of persons aged 80 y (von

aged 60 y and up to 50% of persons aged 80 y (von Haehling, Morley, and Anker 2010). Allied health interventions such as physical therapy, rehabilitative resistance exercise, and nutritional strategies are routine therapeutics to combat sarcopenia (Shi et al. 2023). Ingestion of milk proteins causes aminoacidemia and activates MPS via the mechanistic target of rapamycin signaling pathway in human skeletal muscle (Rennie et al. 2004). Whey protein is acid soluble and digested rapidly, resulting

is acid soluble and digested rapidly, resulting in transient hyperaminoacidemia (Boirie et al. 1997). Discussion Over the past decade, nutritional intervention studies have suggested that a class of WP+LEU are optimal clinical nutrition recipes that pri­ mary healthcare providers could use. The results presented here have indicated that this class of WP+LEU containing suboptimal or near- optimal doses of whey protein for stimulating MPS induces improve­ ments in body composition, strength,

improve­ ments in body composition, strength, and physical function within 8 to 24 weeks of supplementation in individuals diagnosed with sarcopenia (Table 1). Additionally, one study included a follow-up period after 24 weeks of discontinuing the WP+LEU intervention (Mori and Tokuda 2022). The study indicated that muscle mass and strength were main­ tained (Mori and Tokuda 2022). A post-trial follow-up can provide valuable information about medical interventions’ longer-term benefits and risks

interventions’ longer-term benefits and risks (Llewellyn-Bennett et al. 2018). This scoping review shows that commonly used WP+LEU study products typically contain about 20 g of whey and two to three g of free leucine. On average, 25 g of whey contains about three g of leucine, optimal for inducing aminoacidemia and leucinemia and stimulating MPS (Traylor et al. 2019; McKendry et al. 2024). Therefore, these WP+LEU would include approximately four to five g of leucine. Additionally, three of the

to five g of leucine. Additionally, three of the studies reported using suboptimal protein doses ranging from 8.5 g to 11 g of whey, which is 34% to 44% lower than the optimal dose of whey. The total leucine amount for the WP+LEU suboptimal doses would be approximately two to three and a half grams of leucine. Sestrin2, a member of a three-protein family, detects amino acids and acts as a specific leucine sensor (Wolfson and Sabatini 2017). When the intramuscular/intracellular concentrations of

the intramuscular/intracellular concentrations of leucine increase, Sestrin2 can no longer bind to the protein complex GATOR2, thereby stopping the inhibition of MPS (Wolfson et al. 2016). This interaction leads to the stimulation of the mTORC1 pathway and an increase in the rate of MPS (Wolfson et al. 2016). In the present scoping review, the total leucine content and supply of amino acids of the WP+LEU were sufficient for better muscle development in sarcopenic humans. Further research is

in sarcopenic humans. Further research is needed to determine the efficacy of this class of WP+LEU in adults with sarcopenia and other muscle-wasting diseases. The formula was suggested not to pose any adverse events or to negatively impact daily protein intake, kidney function, liver function, vital signs, or calcium and vitamin D metabolism (Hill et al. 2019). Expert-recommended strategies to maintain or improve bone health in older adults include eating a balanced diet rich in high-quality pro­ tein, calcium, and vitamin D (Munoz-Garach, Garcia-Fontana, and Munoz-Torres 2020). Foods such as dairy products, green leafy vegeta­ bles, tofu, orange

Furthermore, medications such as bisphosphonates, hormone replace­ ment therapy, denosumab, and teriparatide can help slow bone loss and can even help increase bone density (Lyu et al. 2019; Wimalawansa 1998). The recommended calcium intake for adults is 1000 milligrams per day for males and females up to 50 y and increases

for males and females up to 50 y and increases to 1200 milli­ grams per day for females above 50 and males over 70 (Plantz and Bittar 2022). Thus, a whey protein + leucine + calcium + vitamin D3 formulation may better promote the maintenance of lean mass and bone in sarcopenic older adults. It remains unclear whether WP+LEU without calcium and vitamin D3 is effective for replenishing bone content, and therefore, future studies are needed to test the efficacy of specific for­ mula(e). a WP+LEU and performed physical therapy focused on gait retraining (Moriwaki et al. 2019). Furthermore, Mori et al. showed that lean mass and strength were maintained for at least 24 weeks following a WP+LEU intervention in sarcopenic older adults (Mori and Tokuda 2022). In contrast, Ama­ sene et al. reported no additional benefits from a WP+LEU combined with a resistance training program in a small sample size of sarcopenic males and females (Amasene et al. 2019). Thus, consuming a high-quality proteinaceous diet, exercise rehabilitation, and WP+LEU seems effec­ tive for combating sarcopenia by improving body composition, physical function, and daily activities, thereby supporting dependent living and protecting skeletal muscle in aging (Fig. 3) (Keys et al. 1986; Bull et al. 2020; Morton et al. 2018). Conclusion The etiology of sarcopenia is complex

Conclusion The etiology of sarcopenia is complex and multifaceted, and the age- related loss of muscle mass and function increases the risk of falling, fractures, disability, age-related chronic diseases, morbidity and mor­ tality, and dependent living. Given the global increase in the aging population, these risks increase in prevalence when consuming inade­ quate protein intakes and reducing physical activity. There is no widely available pharmacologic intervention with suitably low

pharmacologic intervention with suitably low off-target effects D.A. Traylor et al. Archives of Gerontology and Geriatrics Plus 1 (2024) 100058 8 to combat sarcopenia directly. Consuming WP+LEU optimizes the daily protein intake for older people diagnosed with sarcopenia. Data reviewed here show that dosing with different WP+LEU could boost protein-induced enhancements in lean mass and function, reverse sar­ copenia, or prevent the disease from worsening even when consuming large doses of

from worsening even when consuming large doses of protein. Consuming higher-quality proteins and adding more leucine to the diet should also be considered an alternative feeding strategy when combined with exercise. Ingesting a WP+LEU formula can aid in maintaining lean mass in sarcopenic obese individuals on a calorie-restricted weight loss diet. Combined with calcium and vitamin D3, the WP+LEU may effectively maintain bone mass for patients with compromised skeletal bone con­ tent. Future

with compromised skeletal bone con­ tent. Future studies must elucidate the mechanisms associated with body composition, strength, and function improvements due to WP+LEU in sarcopenic adults. Objective: We prospectively examined the associations of 15 urinary metal concentrations and their mixtures with natural menopause in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation Multi-Pollutant Study. Methods: The study population consisted of 1082 premenopausal women from multiple racial/ethnic groups, aged 45–56 years at baseline (1999–2000), with the median follow-up of 4.1 years. Urinary concentrations of 15 metals, including arsenic, barium, cadmium, cobalt, cesium, copper,

Natural menopause was defined as the final bleeding episode prior to at least 12 months of amenorrhea, not due to surgery or hormone therapy. Cox pro­ portional hazards models were used to examine associations between individual metal concentrations and timing of natural menopause. The associations between metal mixtures and natural

associations between metal mixtures and natural menopause were evaluated using elastic net penalized Cox regression, and an environmental risk score (ERS) was computed to represent individual risks of natural menopause related to metal mixtures. Results: The median age at natural menopause was 53.2 years. Using the Cox proportional hazards models, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) (and its 95% confidence interval (CI)) for natural menopause was 1.32 (1.03, 1.67) for arsenic and 1.36 (1.05, 1.76)

(1.03, 1.67) for arsenic and 1.36 (1.05, 1.76) for lead, comparing the highest with the lowest quartiles of metal concentrations. The predicted ages at natural menopause in the highest and lowest quartiles were 52.7 and 53.5 years for arsenic; and 52.9 and 53.8 years for lead. A significant association between ERS and menopause was also observed. Women in the highest vs. the lowest quartiles of ERS had an HR of 1.71 (1.36, 2.15), equivalent to a 1.6 year earlier median time to natural

to a 1.6 year earlier median time to natural menopause. Conclusion: This study suggests that arsenic, lead, and metal mixtures are associated with earlier natural menopause, a risk factor for adverse health outcomes in later life. 1. exposures, alters the hormonal and homeostatic systems that enable the organism to communicate with and respond to its environ­ ment” (Diamanti-Kandarakis et al., 2009). Metals are widely dispersed in the environment, and the general population can be exposed to metals through smoking, dietary sources, drinking water, and ambient air (Wang et al., 2019a). Substantial evidence suggests that arsenic (ATSDR, 2007), cadmium (ATSDR, 2012), mercury (ATSDR, 1999), and particularly lead (ATSDR, 2020; Mendola et al., 2008) alter fertility and reproductive outcomes, and have endocrine-disrupting potential. The final menstrual

potential. The final menstrual period (FMP) indicates the end of a woman’s reproduction capability, or menopause, and is considered a risk marker for age-related morbidity and mortality. Earlier age at menopause has been associated with overall mortality (Jacobsen et al., 2003; Mondul et al., 2005; Ossewaarde et al., 2005), cardiovascular disease (Atsma et al., 2006; Hu et al., 1999), osteoporosis (Kritz-Silverstein and Barrett- Connor, 1993), mental health disorders (de Kruif et al., 2016),

mental health disorders (de Kruif et al., 2016), and other chronic conditions (Shuster et al., 2010). Growing evidence from epidemiologic studies suggests that environmental factors may play a role in determining age at menopause (Ding et al., 2020b; Gore et al., 2011; Grindler et al., 2015; Vabre et al., 2017). However, it is still un­ clear whether exposure to metals is associated with ovarian aging and the timing of menopause. Few epidemiologic studies have examined associations between

studies have examined associations between exposure to metals and age at menopause, and those studies have yiel­ ded inconsistent results (Eum et al., 2014; Mendola et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2020; Popovic et al., 2005; Yunus et al., 2014) Most studies were cross-sectional, and primarily focused on lead exposure (Mendola et al., 2013; Popovic et al., 2005). Associations between other metals and menopause have been largely unexplored. Furthermore, people are generally exposed to multiple metals

people are generally exposed to multiple metals as mixtures (Wang et al., 2019a), yet most studies have narrowly focused on individual metals, possibly due to statistical challenges, given the complex correlations among metal exposures and the lack of well-established statistical methods to evaluate the effects of exposure to metal mixtures (Park et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019b, 2018). To our knowledge, no study has considered multiple metals, except for a recent prospective cohort study,

except for a recent prospective cohort study, which examined 16 metals and their mixtures in toenails from 903 premeno­ pausal women in the Sister Study (White et al., 2020). Individual metals were not associated with the timing of menopause; however, later age at menopause was linked to a quartile increase in metal mixtures (HR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.64, 1.02) (White et al., 2020). We thus examined the associations of 15 urinary metal concentra­ tions with the timing of natural menopause in the

tions with the timing of natural menopause in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN), a multi-site, prospective cohort study of midlife women from multiple racial/ethnic groups. We hypothesized that higher lead concentration would be associated with earlier natural menopause. We also sought to determine associations between other metals and natural menopause as an initial exploratory inquiry of environmental factors related to ovarian aging. Finally, we constructed an

to ovarian aging. Finally, we constructed an environmental risk score (ERS) (Park et al., 2017, 2014; Wang et al., 2020, 2019b, 2018) as a summary measure of the health risk of exposure to multiple metals to evaluate the association between exposure to metal mixtures and natural menopause. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study design and population SWAN is an ongoing, multi-site, community-based prospective study of a cohort of midlife women from multiple racial/ethnic groups, designed to

from multiple racial/ethnic groups, designed to characterize the physiological and psychosocial changes that occur during the menopausal transition and their effects on subse­ quent health endpoints. Study participants were enrolled between 1996 and 1997 from seven study sites; each site recruited White women and Black women were recruited at the Boston, MA, Pittsburgh, PA, south­ east Michigan, MI, and Chicago, IL sites; Hispanic women from the Newark, NJ site; Chinese women from the Oakland,

Newark, NJ site; Chinese women from the Oakland, CA site; and Japa­ nese women from the Los Angeles, CA site (Sowers et al., 2000). To be eligible, women had to be aged 42 to 52 years, have an intact uterus and at least one ovary, have had at least one menstrual period and not taken menopausal hormone therapy (HT) in the past three months, and self- identified with the site’s designated racial/ethnic groups. Participants returned for regular examinations approximately annually. The insti­

examinations approximately annually. The insti­ tutional review board at each participating site approved the study protocol, and all participants provided written, signed informed consent. The SWAN Multi-Pollutant Study (SWAN-MPS) used urine samples from the SWAN Repository collected during the third SWAN follow-up visit (1999–2000) for environmental exposure assessment (Ding et al., 2020a; Wang et al., 2019a). A subset of 1,400 SWAN participants from the five SWAN sites who provided urine

from the five SWAN sites who provided urine samples to the SWAN Re­ pository (Boston, MA; southeast Michigan, MI; Los Angeles, CA; Oak­ land, CA; and Pittsburgh, PA) were assayed for metal concentrations. Women from Chicago and Newark were excluded because urine samples were not collected at these two sites. This subpopulation, by design, included self-identified White, Black, Chinese, and Japanese women but not Hispanic women who were recruited exclusively from Newark. For these analyses, we

exclusively from Newark. For these analyses, we excluded 237 women who had already reached nat­ ural menopause and 48 who had a hysterectomy or oophorectomy at the SWAN-MPS baseline, and 33 who had no information on key covariates, yielding a final analytic sample of 1,082 pre- or early perimenopausal women. These women were followed approximately annually through 2014, with a median follow-up of 4.1 (interquartile range: 2.3, 6.1) years. 2.2. Natural menopause Our primary outcome was age at

Natural menopause Our primary outcome was age at the natural FMP, based upon in­ formation provided in the approximately annual interviews. The natural FMP was defined as 12 months of amenorrhea since the last menstrual period with menstruation cessation not due to other causes (including hysterectomy, bilateral oophorectomy, or HT). Menopausal status and date of the FMP were ascertained prospectively by interviewers at each annual visit. Each annual follow-up interview asks 1) whether the

annual follow-up interview asks 1) whether the woman has had a period in the last year; 2) whether she has had a period in the last three months; and 3) the date of her most recent menstrual period. Discussion In this multi-site, prospective study of a cohort of 1,082 midlife women from multiple racial/ethnic groups, higher urinary arsenic and lead concentrations were associated with earlier natural menopause, after adjusting for sociodemographic variables, lifestyle factors, BMI, and parity. In the mixture analysis, an ERS was calculated to integrate the impacts of metal mixtures on

to integrate the impacts of metal mixtures on natural menopause and capture an individual’s risk based on her combined metal exposure. The association between ERS and natural menopause suggests that exposure to metal mixtures may play a critical role in ovarian aging, with women in the highest ERS quartile having 1.6 years earlier age at menopause than women in the lowest quartile. Even a small advance in the age at natural menopause associated with metal exposures may have substantial public

with metal exposures may have substantial public health consequences, given the widespread nature of metal exposures and the importance of health outcomes related to accelerated ovarian aging. The earlier occurrence of menopause indicates a reduction in the reproductive lifespan and a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (Atsma et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2006; Hu et al., 1999; Løkkegaard et al., 2006), osteoporosis and fracture (Kritz-Silverstein and Barrett-Connor, 1993; Parazzini et al.,

and Barrett-Connor, 1993; Parazzini et al., 1996; Van der Voort et al., 2003), neurological disorders (de Kruif et al., 2016; Georgakis et al., 2016), and psychiatric disease (Bromberger et al., 2001) in later life. For example, for every one year decrease in age at natural menopause, the risk of coronary heart disease has been esti­ mated to increase by 3% (Hu et al., 1999). All-cause mortality has been estimated to increase by 5% (Jacobsen et al., 2003; Mondul et al., 2005; Ossewaarde et al.,

2003; Mondul et al., 2005; Ossewaarde et al., 2005). One robust finding from our analysis was that urinary arsenic was associated with an earlier natural menopause. Epidemiologic studies on arsenic exposure and natural menopause have been limited, and prior findings have been inconsistent. A cross-sectional study of 210 women in Bangladesh with high arsenic exposure reported that having an arsenic skin lesion, a marker of chronic arsenic exposure, was associated with an earlier age at menopause

was associated with an earlier age at menopause (Yunus et al., 2014). In a recent case-control study of 169 primary ovarian insufficiency cases and 209 healthy con­ trols, higher urinary arsenic concentration was observed in patients compared to controls (Pan et al., 2020). In the same study, urinary arsenic was also associated with higher serum levels of follicle- stimulating hormone and lower estradiol and anti-Mullerian hormone levels, supporting the possibility that arsenic exposure has

the possibility that arsenic exposure has adverse reproductive effects that could affect ovarian reserve and timing of menopause (Pan et al., 2020). In contrast, in a recent prospective cohort study, no association between toenail arsenic and age at menopause was found (White et al., 2020). The association between arsenic and earlier natural menopause is biologically plausible. It is known that arsenic exposure can cause oxidative stress through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Arsenic

reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Arsenic may impair ovarian folliculogenesis and disrupt normal function of female reproductive system through oxida­ tive stress. For instance, female rats with an oral administration of 4 ppm arsenic through drinking water for 28 days had increased free-radical productions and induced apoptosis in the uterus (Chatterjee and Chat­ terji, 2017; Chattopadhyay and Ghosh, 2010). Ommati et al. treated parent mice with 0, 0.2, 2, and 20 ppm arsenic through

mice with 0, 0.2, 2, and 20 ppm arsenic through drinking water; and they also found increases in ROS content, decreases in mitochon­ drial dehydrogenase activity, and autophagy in the ovaries of F1-female mice (Ommati et al., 2020). We also found that urinary lead was associated with an earlier nat­ ural menopause. Previous studies on lead and menopause have been cross-sectional, and findings have been mixed. Popovic et al. observed that women who were occupationally exposed to lead from

who were occupationally exposed to lead from smelting had an earlier menopause than similar-aged women without occupational exposure (Popovic et al., 2005). Mendola et al. used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999–2000 and reported a similar association between higher blood lead levels and higher odds of natural menopause (Mendola et al., 2013). In contrast, using cross-sectional data from 434 women participants in the Nurses’ Health Study, no as­ sociation was detected

Health Study, no as­ sociation was detected between patella or blood lead and age at menopause; whereas, higher tibia lead, as an indicator of cumulative lead exposure, were associated with younger age at menopause (Eum et al., 2014). Lead has been found to disrupt the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. A study of rats found that lead treatment upregulated the pro­ duction of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which further triggers the secretion of follicle stimulating hormone, a key indicator of

follicle stimulating hormone, a key indicator of ovarian reserve (Sokol et al., 2002). Lead may also interfere with follicular function. In an in vitro study of human ovarian granulosa cells, lead treatment led to reduced levels of both mRNA and protein levels of cy­ tochrome p450 and estrogen receptor beta (Taupeau et al., 2003). Further, a study of mice also showed that the accumulation of lead in the ovary led to altered folliculogenesis (Taupeau et al., 2001). In this study, inverse

(Taupeau et al., 2001). In this study, inverse associations of essential metals including cop­ per, molybdenum, and zinc with natural menopause were detected in analyses of individual metals, though the associations were not statis­ tically significant. The inverse associations were also retained in the mixture analyses. Existing evidence directly examining the associations between essential metals and age at natural menopause is sparse. In a case-control study of primary ovarian insufficiency,

study of primary ovarian insufficiency, higher serum zinc concentration was associated with lower odds of primary ovarian insufficiency and higher follicle stimulating hormone levels (Kebapcilar et al., 2013). In a United Kingdom cohort study of women aged 40–65 years, dietary intake of legumes, which is one of the primary sources of molybdenum for the general population, was associated with later age at menopause (Dunneram et al., 2018). Another large cross-sectional study in central and

large cross-sectional study in central and eastern Europe also reported that the use of vitamin and mineral supplements, which contain numerous essential trace elements, was associated with later age at menopause (Stepaniak et al., 2013). These findings, which warrant further investigation, raise interesting questions regarding the role of essential metals in determining the timing of menopause which should be pursued in future work. To our knowledge, the current investigation is among the

knowledge, the current investigation is among the first studies of metal mixtures and their effects on the occurrence of natural meno­ pause in a prospective cohort of multi-racial/ethnic, midlife women. Further, we observed a strong association between metal mixtures, assessed by an integrated ERS, and natural menopause. This finding highlights the importance of considering metal mixtures to evaluate associations of metal exposures with health outcomes in epidemiologic studies. The primary strength of our study was its use of a large prospective cohort of community-based midlife women from four racial/ethnic groups with longitudinal determination of menopause events. Addi­ tionally, we examined a panel of 15 metals, which allowed us to investigate a large number of associations as an initial exploratory in­ quiry of environmental factors affecting

in­ quiry of environmental factors affecting natural menopause. Further­ more, we implemented a mixture analysis approach, ERS, to evaluate the associations between exposure to metal mixtures and age at natural menopause while accounting for statistical challenges, such as complex correlations underlying multiple metals. Several limitations should be considered as well when interpreting the findings. First, we measured all metal concentrations in urine, and urinary concentrations may not

in urine, and urinary concentrations may not reflect total body burden from all forms of metals and exposure sources. Second, metals included in the current analysis have different half-lives in the human body. Urinary concen­ trations of metals with short half-lives, such as arsenic, mainly reflect recent exposures. In contrast, metals such as cadmium are not rapidly excreted and have half-lives of years to decades. Information on the temporal variability of urinary metal concentrations,

variability of urinary metal concentrations, especially for metals with short half-lives, is needed to characterize better cumulative metal exposures in future studies. Third, only total arsenic was measured in urine samples, but information on its methylated metabolites, which play an important role in its toxicity, was not available (Drobna et al., 2009). Additional arsenic metabolism measurements will improve our understanding of its potential effects on reproductive health outcomes in

effects on reproductive health outcomes in future studies. Fourth, the coefficient estimates from ENET penalized Cox regression were conservatively biased because of shrinkage esti­ mation provided by the ENET, and standard errors and test statistics are difficult to compute (Yang and Zou, 2013). Fifth, we used cross- validation to minimize prediction errors of the ENET penalized Cox model, and ERS was further constructed, but these findings may not be generalizable to other populations. Though other prospective studies are needed to validate the effects of individual metals and the ERS, our findings from a large, multi-racial/ethnic sample are nonetheless important in indicating that exposure to metals and their mixtures may affect the timing of natural menopause, which in turn may affect sub­ sequent disease risk. Lastly, women at the SWAN-MPS baseline were between age 45 and 56 years and had menstruation, thus women who experienced

and had menstruation, thus women who experienced menopause before baseline, especially those with prema­ ture menopause (before age 40 years) or early menopause (before age 45 years), were not included in the analysis. Thus, the effects of metals on natural menopause could be underestimated. 5. Conclusions This prospective study demonstrated that metals, including arsenic and lead were associated with earlier natural menopause. The results of this study provide evidence that exposure to metal

study provide evidence that exposure to metal mixtures may affect age at natural menopause. Women in the highest ERS quartile, on average, had 1.6 years earlier age at menopause than women in the lowest quartile. This estimate was roughly equivalent to or even larger than an effect estimate of 1.1 years comparing current smokers versus never smokers in the SWAN-MPS (Ding et al., 2020b). Methods: We searched six databases (PubMed, AMED, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, RISS, and KoreaMed) from their inception to April

RISS, and KoreaMed) from their inception to April 2022 and included all placebo-controlled RCTs comparing any type of ginseng in menopausal women. The methodological quality of all studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0. Results: We included 15 RCTs with our inclusion criteria. The majority of studies considered bias a concern. Ginseng reduced menopausal symptoms in three studies (n = 515; standardized mean difference (SMD): −0.40, 95% confidence interval (CI): −0.73 to

Another three RCTs failed to demonstrate a beneficial effect of Korean red ginseng (KRG) on endometrial thickness. Conclusion: This study demonstrated that ginseng can significantly reduce hot flashes, menopausal symptoms, and quality of life in menopausal women. hormones or biomarkers, or endometrial thickness. More rigorous RCTs are needed to overcome the current limitations. 1. Introduction Menopausal women often suffer from various problems, including vasomotor symptoms, insomnia, vaginal dryness, impaired cognitive functions, and emotional disturbances [1]. Hormone replacement ther­ apy (HRT) can help alleviate some of these symptoms. However, because of the adverse effects of HRT, many postmenopausal women turn to complementary therapy, including

women turn to complementary therapy, including body therapies, acupuncture, aromatherapy, phytoestrogens, and herbal medicines. A systematic re­ view demonstrated that herbal medicines are the most popular form of complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) [2]. Some Chinese herbal medicines have been shown to be effective in relieving meno­ pausal symptoms [3]. treat menopausal symptoms, and their efficacy has been studied [4,5]. Ginseng is used to promote longevity, stabilize the dynamic balance of physiological processes, and aid in disease recovery. Methods This study was registered with the Research Registry (reviewregistry 1342). 2.1. Data sources and search strategy We searched the following databases from their inception through April 2022: PubMed, AMED, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, RISS, and KoreaMed. Articles identified through reference lists of the included studies and relevant

lists of the included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also included. The search terms used were "(ginseng OR ginseng$ OR panaxa) AND (menopause$ OR climact$ OR post menopause$ OR postmenopaus$ OR hot flash$ OR hot flash$ OR hot flush$ OR hot flush$)." 2.2. Criteria for considering studies 2.2.1. Types of studies Placebo-controlled randomized trials were included. 2.2.2. Types of participants Menopausal women were considered. Patients with breast cancer or endometrial disease as

with breast cancer or endometrial disease as well as immunocompromised patients or those taking multiple medications were excluded. 2.2.3. Types of interventions All prospective randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the effects of ginseng of any type with placebo were included. All ginseng extracts or ginseng-derived products were included in the studies, regardless of source, age, processing stage, or dosage. One complex herbal drug containing ginseng was excluded from our study.

containing ginseng was excluded from our study. Disserta­ tions and abstracts were also included. 2.2.4. Outcome measures The primary outcome was menopausal symptoms, which were measured by the Kupperman index and other questionnaires. The sec­ ondary outcomes were quality of life (QoL), adverse events (AEs), and other physiological and biochemical parameters. 2.3. Data collection, extraction, and assessment Data were extracted from all publications by two independent re­ viewers according to

by two independent re­ viewers according to prespecified criteria. We identified the authors, year of publication, country, sample size, age of participants, type of ginseng, dose, treatment duration, and main outcomes. For analysis, the extracted data are presented in tables. There were no language restrictions. 2.4. Evaluating risk of bias The review authors (LA and HWL) based their assessment on the Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (RoB 2.0) developed by the Cochrane Collab­ oration [10]. There

by the Cochrane Collab­ oration [10]. There were five aspects examined: randomization, de­ viations from planned interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes, and selection of reported outcomes. Risk of bias was graded as “low risk of bias,” “some concern,” or “high risk of bias” for each area of each study. Disagreements were resolved by involving a third reviewer when necessary. 2.5. Data analysis All statistical analyses were performed using the Cochrane Collabo­ ration

were performed using the Cochrane Collabo­ ration software program Review Manager (RevMan), V.5.3 for Windows (Copenhagen, The Nordic Cochrane Center). Differences between the intervention and placebo control groups were assessed. In the analysis of clinical effectiveness, categorical data in the form of risk ratios and continuous data in the form of mean differences (MDs) were evaluated. Categorical and continuous variables were reported as efficacy values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For outcome variables based on different scales, the standardized MD (SMD) was used instead of the weighted MD. When the meta-analysis revealed heterogeneity (defined as p < 0.1 by the chi-square test and 50% I2 by the Higgins I2 test), subgroup analyses were performed to determine the reason for the clinical heterogeneity. Because of the likelihood of clinical heteroge­ neity in the included studies due to treatment diversity, research design, and

due to treatment diversity, research design, and other factors, a random-effects model was used to estimate the cu­ mulative effect size from the efficacy variables. The Egger regression method and funnel plots were used to measure publication bias [11]. When missing data were detected, we asked the original study in­ vestigators for missing or incomplete information. We performed sub­ group analyses based on ginseng type, dose, and treatment duration. We assessed the robustness of the results

We assessed the robustness of the results of the meta-analyses by performing sensitivity analyses when appropriate. Albatross plots were also gener­ ated using STATA/SE v.16.1 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA) to visualize the effect of direction on the menopausal symptoms and biochemical outcomes. 3. Summary of the main results We included 15 RCTs involving 1256 (analyzed 1155) menopausal women, all of which compared ginseng with placebo. Our systematic review revealed that ginseng can relieve

review revealed that ginseng can relieve menopausal symptoms and hot flashes and improve quality of life. However, it may have no effect on sexual function, hormone biomarker levels, or endometrial thickness. The level of evidence for these findings was low. In addition, the number of studies and the overall size of the included studies were insufficient to draw firm conclusions. 4.2. Overall completeness and applicability of the evidence Different types of ginseng at different doses were

types of ginseng at different doses were tested and compared with placebo. The difference in significance could be due to the type of ginseng and the dosage of treatment. The dosage and fre­ quency of ginseng intake were not sufficient to produce a significant effect on the biochemical variables. Most of the included studies were conducted in South Korea. It is not known whether the cultivation re­ gions affect the therapeutic effect of ginseng by affecting the chemical formulation. Therefore,

by affecting the chemical formulation. Therefore, the extent to which the results of this review are applicable to other forms of ginseng is unclear. 4.3. Certainty of Evidence (CoE) We consistently downgraded the CoE based on study limitations. The most common reasons were lack of information on the generation of the random sequence and concealed allocation, which is known to lead to overestimation of effect sizes. The CoE regarding most menopausal symptoms was low. 4.4. Agreement and

menopausal symptoms was low. 4.4. Agreement and disagreement with other studies or reviews We found only three systematic reviews on the use of ginseng for the treatment of menopausal symptoms [5,9,29]. One review included 4 RCTs and showed limited efficacy of ginseng for menopausal symptoms [9]. The second systematic review updated the first review and included 10 RCTs that examined the effects of ginseng on menopausal women’s health [5]. The results showed beneficial effects of ginseng on

results showed beneficial effects of ginseng on sexual function and hot flashes. The third systematic review focused on the effects of ginseng on sexual function in menopausal women [29]. It included 5 RCTs and failed to demonstrate the efficacy of ginseng on sexual function. Compared with previous reviews, we identified five new RCTs [14,17,18,22,23] (seven reports: [14,17–19,22–24]) and successfully updated the evidence regarding this therapy. Implications for research The therapeutic effect of ginseng may depend on the availability and amounts of the various constituents of the

and amounts of the various constituents of the preparation. Many publica­ tions do not provide information in this regard. The optimal dose of ginseng or red ginseng is unknown. Single-dose studies have used extract amounts ranging from 200 to 3000 mg. When we analyzed the direction of outcomes based on dose, treatment duration, dosage and duration, and type of outcome, there were no clear relationships between dose and treatment duration and significant changes in different outcomes. Clinical trials of ginseng dosing comparing varying and increasing amounts of ginseng have not been published. The main limitations of the included RCTs were a lack of transparent research design and detailed reporting. This downgraded the CoE, which reduced our confidence in the pooled results. In the future, researchers should be comprehensive and transparent in

should be comprehensive and transparent in reporting the methods and results of their studies so that readers can better understand the study design, conduct, analysis, and interpretation. A sample size calculation based on accepted sample sizes should also be used, as should appro­ priate concealed allocation and optimal treatment doses. Limitations This study has several significant limitations. Although we made every effort to find all relevant RCTs, we cannot guarantee that they were all found. In addition, publication bias and inadequate reporting of clinical trials are important sources of bias. Several unpublished nega­ tive RCTs could distort the overall

nega­ tive RCTs could distort the overall picture. In addition to these limita­ tions, noncompliance with CONSORT guidelines may have placed a study at high risk for bias, regardless of whether the study was well conducted. Of note, most of the studies were sponsored by a ginseng company, which may have introduced some bias. Most of the industry- sponsored studies showed positive results [30–32]. Nine trials were funded by Korea Ginseng Corp (KRG) [12,15,16,18,20–23,27], Bifido [24], or

(KRG) [12,15,16,18,20–23,27], Bifido [24], or Pharmaton [13], which raises concerns about possible bias in our review. In addition, the primary data are often of suboptimal methodological quality because of their small number and usually poor quality. Some of the studies included in this review failed to minimize bias. These deficiencies limit the power of this systematic review. 5. Conclusions In summary, the existing studies showed positive effects of ginseng on alleviating menopausal

effects of ginseng on alleviating menopausal symptoms and hot flashes and improving quality of life. However, the included studies did not demonstrate sig­ nificant differences in sexual function, hormone levels, or endometrial thickness. Because of the small number of studies and unclear risk of bias, the level of evidence is low. More rigorous RCTs are needed to overcome the many limitations of the current evidence. ABSTRACT Whey protein is widely recognized as a high-quality protein source, primarily derived from dairy products. This type of protein is valued not only for its remarkable nutritional benefits but also for its substantial antioxi- dant properties and its capacity to reduce inflammation. Previous studies have demonstrated that whey protein hydrolysate (WPH) is effective in both the prevention and treatment of liver injury caused by acetaminophen (APAP) overdose. Pyroptosis is a form of

Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death that significantly contributes to liver damage induced by APAP, and it is associated with increased levels of oxidative stress and inflammation. However, the specific mechanisms by which WPH influences py- roptosis remain not fully understood. The present study observed a significant alleviation of APAP-induced hepatocyte injury by WPH, alongside a reduction in the release of proinflammatory factors, specifically IL-1β and -18.

factors, specifically IL-1β and -18. Moreover, the expression levels of pyroptosis- related proteins, including NLRP3, GSDMD-N (N termi- nal fragment), and cleaved CASP1, were significantly re- duced following treatment with WPH. In the subsequent phase of our research, we examined the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the expression of CTSB in hepatocytes. Increased levels of ROS resulted in height- ened permeability of lysosomal membranes, which led to the release of CTSB into the

which led to the release of CTSB into the cytosol. The liberated CTSB subsequently activated the NLRP3 inflammasome, there- by promoting pyroptosis. Our results revealed that WPH reduced the accumulation of ROS in hepatocytes and inhibited the release of CTSB. In subsequent mechanistic studies, we found that WPH upregulated the expression of PRKN, PINK1, and microtubule-associated protein 1 LC3, while downregulating the expression of P62 to activate mitophagy. We further validated these results

mitophagy. We further validated these results by introducing the mitophagy inhibitor CsA. In conclusion, our findings suggest that WPH may enhance the removal of damaged mitochondria through the activation of the mitophagy mechanism. This process may lead to a re- duction in intracellular ROS accumulation and mitigate APAP-induced activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and pyroptosis. These attributes render it useful for both the prevention and treatment of various diseases, leading to its widespread recognition and application in health food development (Minj and Anand, 2020). have shown that WPH can mitigate liver injury caused by APAP overdose and reduce hepatic oxidative stress (Athira et al., 2013). Therefore, the potential of WPH as a natural dietary ingredient for the treatment of APAP-induced liver injury is considerable. Pyroptosis refers to a form of inflammatory cell death that is mediated by an inflammasome (Wei et al., 2022). This process is characterized by the swelling of cells un- til the plasma membrane becomes permeable, leading to the efflux of

It has been established that the NLRP3 inflammasome is the primary component responsible for detecting various exogenous and endogenous danger signals. This detec- tion initiates the inflammatory response through the acti- vation of CASP1, ultimately resulting in the production of IL-1β and -18 (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010). Related studies suggest that various mechanisms may explain the activation of the

mechanisms may explain the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, including CTSB leakage, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and mitochondrial dysfunction (Hoyt et al., 2017; Ko et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021a). However, these mechanisms alone do not provide a comprehensive understanding of NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Therefore, further research is necessary to clarify the precise mechanisms underlying these interconnected cellular events. Mitochondria serve as a critical site for the

Mitochondria serve as a critical site for the action of APAP in hepatocytes, with mitochondrial dysfunc- tion playing a central role in the progression of APAP- induced liver injury (Deng et al., 2024). Excessive intake of APAP damages mitochondria through various mechanisms, including the induction of oxidative stress, disruption of mitochondrial membrane integrity, and deterioration of mitochondrial function (Ramachandran and Jaeschke, 2020). Mitochondria are a primary source of intracellular

are a primary source of intracellular ROS. When mitochondria are damaged, they produce ROS abnormally, leading to a significant accumulation of intracellular ROS. This accumulation not only damages the mitochondrial membrane structure, further exacerbating mitochondrial dysfunction, but also compromises the lysosomal membrane, thereby affect- ing its permeability (Jung et al., 2020). Alterations in lysosomal membrane permeability due to damage have been observed to facilitate the entry of CTSB

been observed to facilitate the entry of CTSB into the cytoplasm from lysosomes. This translocation has been demonstrated to activate NLRP3 inflammasome vesicles, leading to the induction of pyroptosis (Ma et al., 2024). However, mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles, and mitophagy, a self-repair mechanism, is initiated when intracellular mitochondria are damaged and lose function. Mitophagy is a critical process that eliminates damaged mitochondria and reduces the production of ROS,

mitochondria and reduces the production of ROS, thereby maintaining stable mitochondrial mass and homeostasis of the intracellular environment (Murphy et al., 2016). Notably, WPH have demonstrated the poten- tial to enhance mitochondrial function. However, further investigation is necessary to elucidate the underlying mechanisms through which WPH influences mitophagy. liver injury by WPH through the inhi- bition of pyroptosis, and to explore the effect of WPH on cellular pyroptosis through regulated mitophagy. The findings provide a theoretical basis for daily dietary in- tervention of WPH and precision nutrition to alleviate the toxicity of APAP. In-depth research on the bioactive functions of WPH will facilitate the application of its preventive and therapeutic capabilities, thereby promot- ing the development of the dairy industry toward health, safety,

to the mitochondria but also creates a vicious cycle that further weakens mitochondrial func- tion (Jiang et al., 2022). In response to APAP-induced mitochondrial damage and dysfunction, cells spontane- ously activate several complex self-repair and adaptive mechanisms. Among these, mitophagy plays a key role in removing damaged mitochondria and promoting the restoration of cellular homeostasis (Kong et al., 2022). Mitophagy is a delicate intracellular clearance pathway that can be activated in

clearance pathway that can be activated in response to signals of mitochon- drial damage, such as mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation (Jiang et al., 2022). This process plays a dual role, which not only is a means of clearing damaged mitochondria but also is a secondary signal trig- gering the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and cellular pyroptosis (Chung et al., 2020). However, when the toxic effects of APAP exceed cellular repair capacity, mitophagy may not be able to

repair capacity, mitophagy may not be able to adequately counteract the damage, ultimately leading to cell death and tissue dam- age. In view of the previous background, it is a valuable research direction to explore whether WPH can alleviate APAP-induced liver injury more effectively by activating and strengthening mitophagy. To validate our hypothesis, we introduced the mi- tophagy inhibitor CsA as a negative control experiment. With this design, we observed that the original protec- tive

we observed that the original protec- tive effect of WPH on MMP as well as the ROS scav- enging were significantly reversed in the presence of CsA. Meanwhile, in the presence of CsA, we observed a significant increase in fluorescence colocalization of CTSB and NLRP3. This result suggested that the in- hibitory effect of WPH on CTSB overexpression and NLRP3 activation is suppressed by CsA. We hypoth- esize on the basis of this finding that the positive effect of WPH on mitochondria mainly is

positive effect of WPH on mitochondria mainly is achieved by pro- moting mitophagy. The PINK1, PRKN, P62, and LC3 form a tightly interconnected regulatory network dur- ing mitophagy (Feng et al., 2024). Upon mitochondrial damage, PINK1 is activated to phosphorylate ubiquitin and recruit PRKN. The PRKN targets mitochondrial degradation by ubiquitinating proteins on the mito- chondrial surface. Subsequently, P62 acts as a linker protein to bind ubiquitinated mitochondrial substrates to LC3,

ubiquitinated mitochondrial substrates to LC3, ultimately facilitating autophagosome forma- tion and mitochondrial degradation (Liu et al., 2021b). Subsequently, we examined the expression levels of key proteins to assess the extent of mitophagy development. The results showed that WPH significantly elevated the expression of LC3, PINK1, and PRKN, which signi- fied the formation of autophagosomes with enhanced mitochondrial degradation. Meanwhile, the significant decrease in the level of P62

the significant decrease in the level of P62 reflected its effective deple- tion as a substrate for mitophagy, further confirming that mitophagy was actively performed. However, in the presence of CsA, mitophagy was inhibited and the protective effect of WPH was reversed. Fluorescence colocalization analysis of LC3 (representing autophagic lysosomes) with PINK1 (labeled mitochondria) clearly revealed that WPH was able to strengthen the binding of autophagosomes to mitochondria and mitophagy.

of autophagosomes to mitochondria and mitophagy. Conversely, CsA inhibited this colocalization, further demonstrating the positive role of WPH in activating mitophagy. Next, we explored the effect of WPH-acti- vated mitophagy on pyroptosis by detecting pyroptosis- related proteins. We found that the expression of these proteins was inhibited in the presence of WPH, and this inhibition was reversed after CsA cotreatment. This suggests that the inhibitory effect of WPH on pyroptosis is achieved

effect of WPH on pyroptosis is achieved by activating mitophagy. CONCLUSIONS Our study suggests that WPH attenuates APAP- induced liver injury by alleviating pyroptosis. Mecha- nistically, WPH removes damaged mitochondria by activating mitophagy, thereby reducing ROS production and CTSB release, ultimately inhibiting NLRP3 inflam- masome activation and pyroptosis. The findings reveal a novel therapeutic and preventive mode of action of WPH against APAP-induced hepatocyte pyroptosis. NOTES This

Middle-aged individuals also face reductions in muscle mass and strength due to aging (Holloszy, 2000; T. N. Kim et al., 2009; Melton et al., 2000; Volpi, Nazemi, & Fujita, 2004). can be exacerbated by obesity, resulting in increased risk of disability, mortality and other poor health consequences (Barazzoni et al., 2018; Batsis & Villareal, 2018) and the crosstalk mechanism involves multiple processes, such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance (Batsis & Villareal, 2018; Kalin­ kovich & Livshits, 2017). Discussions Obesity in middle age is a serious problem in China (Pan et al., 2021). In contrast to younger people, obese

al., 2021). In contrast to younger people, obese middle-aged and elderly in­ dividuals should pay more attention to muscle preservation while maintaining a healthy weight. Dietary protein is the main raw material for muscle protein synthesis. A high protein diet (HPD) is considered to be an effective dietary approach to weight loss (Westerterp-Plantenga, Lemmens, & Westerterp, 2012) and to attenuate muscle mass loss (J. E. Kim, O’Connor, Sands, Slebodnik, & Campbell, 2016; Sammarco et al.,

Slebodnik, & Campbell, 2016; Sammarco et al., 2017; Wright, Zhou, Sayer, Kim, & Campbell, 2018). The source of di­ etary protein is one of the factors affecting the benefits of HPD. WP is often used in weight loss management to reduce fat and increase muscle. Since WPH contains more bioactive peptides than WP, their efficacy in the weight loss management may differ. Therefore, this study compared the anti-obesity effect of WPH and WP in obese middle-aged mice. The results showed that WPH

middle-aged mice. The results showed that WPH significantly attenuated weight gain during the experiment. WP attenuated weight gain at week 10, but not by week 20. Although WP and WPH did not significantly affect muscle mass, they significantly improved ectopic fat deposition and antioxidant capacity in muscle. The potential anti-obesity effect of WP supplementation has been previously reported in a study showing decreased BMI and improved metabolic syndrome parameters (Simonson, Boirie, &

syndrome parameters (Simonson, Boirie, & Guillet, 2020). However, some studies showed mixed results (Larsen et al., 2018; Pal et al., 2010). Our study failed to find the anti-obesity effect of WP on middle-aged mice after a 20-week intervention, but a lessened weight gain was observed at week 10. The discrepancies in findings between studies could have been due to the variations in the age of the mice and study duration. In the present study, the age of the mice was nearly 12 months, and the

the age of the mice was nearly 12 months, and the study duration was 20 weeks. Boscaini et al. reported that WP is more effective than casein against HFD-induced obesity during a 5-week intervention, but not during a 10-week intervention (Boscaini et al., 2020). In fact, the rate of weight gain in the HFD group had slowed since week 10. This was not present in the WP group until week 18. and then decreased, and the inflection point was around week 10. We found that WPH significantly decreased the weight and fat mass gains in obese middle-aged mice with low diet and calorie intake. This result suggested that the decrement in weight gain while under the WPH regimen was highly likely caused by the reduced calorie intake. Although WP has been shown to suppress appetite (Giezenaar et al., 2018), obesity and aging can blunt this effect (Giezenaar et al., 2017; Oberoi et al., 2020),

(Giezenaar et al., 2017; Oberoi et al., 2020), and this is in agreement with our results. The results showed that the increases in the levels of some plasma-free amino acids after WP uptake are inversely correlated with calorie intake (Elovaris et al., 2019). This indicated that one of the reasons for the reduced calorie intake

one of the reasons for the reduced calorie intake associated with WPH might be the better absorption of WPH than that of WP. We aimed to assess the effect of whey protein supplementation alone or with vitamin D on lean mass (LM), strength, and function in older adults with or without sarcopenia or frailty. sarcopenia or frailty. We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and SCOPUS databases. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) that investigated the effect of whey protein supplementation with or without vitamin D on sarcopenia outcomes in healthy and sarcopenic or frail older adults were included. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were calculated for LM, muscle strength, and physical function data. The analysis showed that whey protein supplementation had no effect on LM and muscle strength;

had no effect on LM and muscle strength; nevertheless, a signiﬁcant improvement was found in physical function (SMD ¼ 0.561; 95% conﬁdence interval [CIs]: 0.256, 0.865, n ¼ 33), particularly gait speed (GS). On the contrary, whey protein supplementation signiﬁcantly improved LM (SMD ¼ 0.982; 95% CI: 0.228, 1.736; n ¼ 11), appendicular lean mass and physical function (SMD ¼ 1.211; 95% CI: 0.588, 1.834; n ¼ 16), and GS in sarcopenic/frail older adults. By contrast, co-supplementation with vitamin

By contrast, co-supplementation with vitamin D enhanced LM gains (SMD ¼0.993; 95% CI: 0.112, 1.874; n ¼ 11), muscle strength (SMD ¼2.005; 95% CI: 0.975, 3.035; n ¼ 11), and physical function (SMD ¼ 3.038; 95% CI: 2.196, 3.879; n ¼ 18) signiﬁcantly. Muscle strength and physical function improvements after whey protein supplementation plus vitamin D were observed without resistance exercise (RE) and short study duration subgroups. Moreover, the combination of whey protein and vitamin D with RE

combination of whey protein and vitamin D with RE did not enhance the effect of RE. Whey protein supplementation improved LM and function in sarcopenic/frail older adults but had no positive effect in healthy older persons. By contrast, our meta-analysis showed that co-supplementation with whey protein and vitamin D is effective, particularly in healthy older adults, which is likely owing, we propose, to the correction of vitamin D insufﬁciency or deﬁciency. Advances in Nutrition 14 (2023) 762–773 Introduction Sarcopenia is a geriatric syndrome characterized by the pro- gressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function. It is associated with falls,

physical function. It is associated with falls, fractures, disability, frailty, and an increased risk of chronic metabolic diseases. People classiﬁed as sarcopenic are more frequent users of health care systems [1–3]. Guidelines for sarcopenia treatment [4] include incorporating resistance exercise (RE), optimizing protein intake, and addressing insufﬁciency or deﬁciency of vitamin D; however, there is a lack of clarity regarding the effective com- bination of these variables. Higher habitual

com- bination of these variables. Higher habitual protein intakes are associated with lean mass (LM) preservation and improved muscle function in older adults [5,6]. A recent meta-analysis showed that protein intakes of 1.2–1.59 g/kg/d added to RE training positively affected LBM and function in older adults [7]. Whey protein is an easily digestible high-quality protein con- taining all essential amino acids, particularly leucine, a key activator of muscle protein synthesis [8]. Vitamin D has

of muscle protein synthesis [8]. Vitamin D has multiple effects on the muscle, such as regu- lation of gene expression, differentiation, neuromuscular func- tion, and production of anti-inﬂammatory cytokines [9,10]. Studies have also shown that optimizing vitamin D status is important in maintaining muscle mass and function in older adults [11], and vitamin D status is related to muscle mass and strength changes [10]. Notably, the normalization of circulating vitamin D concentration from

of circulating vitamin D concentration from deﬁcient or insufﬁcient to replete may be critical in dictating the efﬁcacy of protein (or other amino acids) supplementation [12,13]. Although some in- terventions, such as whey protein supplementation and vitamin D optimization, are suggested as effective ways to protect against sarcopenia, the efﬁcacy of such interventions is unclear. Although several systematic reviews on different populations and interventions have been published in recent years

interventions have been published in recent years [14–17], a conclusion regarding whether whey protein supplementation alone or with vitamin D is beneﬁcial for sarcopenia-related outcomes in older people is unknown. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate the effects of whey protein supplementation with or without vitamin D and with or without RE on LM, muscle strength, and physical func- tion in older adults with or without sarcopenia or frailty. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was developed ac- cording to the guidelines laid out in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [18] and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) report [19]. Asymmetry was found in the pooled models. Discussion We examined the effects of whey protein with and without vitamin D supplementation on measures relevant to sarcopenia. We found that whey protein supplementation did not increase LM in healthy older

did not increase LM in healthy older participants but did affect LM in sarco- penic or frail older persons. The result of this meta-analysis concurs with a recent analysis on protein supplementation, showing that the changes in LM were largely (if not exclu- sively) related to the effects of RE rather than protein supple- mentation [7]. Many trials have conﬁrmed that recommending protein supplementation as a stand-alone intervention for older adults has no signiﬁcant effects on muscle mass or

has no signiﬁcant effects on muscle mass or strength [21,22,30,33]. Our results are noteworthy because older adults exhibit impaired muscle anabolism in response to protein intake [50,51]. However, in a subgroup analysis, whey protein supplementation signiﬁcantly improved LM in sarcopenic or frail older adults (particularly ALM). Older adults with low LM may have higher requirements for protein, which could un- derpin the effects of whey protein in sarcopenic or frail persons [52]. The effect

in sarcopenic or frail persons [52]. The effect of vitamin D plus whey protein on increasing LM was signiﬁcant. This result was pronounced in the subgroups with a study duration of 12 weeks. Bauer et al. [11] reported an effect of co-supplementation with whey protein with vitamin D on LM. We propose that correcting vitamin D deﬁciency or insufﬁciency likely underpins this co-supplementation effect [53]. Vitamin D can improve muscle mass through genomic and nongenomic pathways [54]. The main

genomic and nongenomic pathways [54]. The main mechanisms of the anabolic effects of vitamin D on muscle anabolism are not fully understood; nevertheless, its positive inﬂuence on muscle pro- tein anabolism has been shown [53,55]. Analyzing all included RCTs showed no signiﬁcant change in muscle strength gains with whey protein supplementation; however, signiﬁcant increases were seen in subgroups who engaged in RE and consumed whey protein doses higher than 20 g. In summary, whey protein supplementation did not increase LM, even when combined with RE in healthy older adults but did improve LM (mainly ALM) in sarcopenic or frail older adults. Similarly, whey protein supplementation did not affect muscle strength, but improvements were seen with higher doses of whey (>20 g) when combined with RE. Longer duration (>12 weeks) whey protein supplementation signiﬁcantly improved physical function, particularly GS, but the

physical function, particularly GS, but the addition of RE superseded the effects of the protein supplementation and supplementation provided no further beneﬁt. Nonetheless, in all domains, the quality of evidence was low. However, whey protein did affect sarcopenia-related measures when combined with a vitamin D supplement, showing improved LM in the short term (<12 weeks). Whey protein plus vitamin D co-supplementation increased LM, muscle strength, and physical function in non- RE

muscle strength, and physical function in non- RE supplementation. We hypothesize that this effect was due to correcting deﬁcient/insufﬁcient vitamin D status. Further studies are warranted to better elucidate the exact mechanisms of action of vitamin D combined with whey protein on sarco- penia measures and muscle protein anabolism, particularly in various durations or doses.
